title: Detection != Reliable Control: Decodable Empathy Directions Yield at Most Partial Shifts in Automated Empathy Scores
comment: Under review at BlackboxNLP 2026 (EMNLP). 8 pages body, 10 figures/tables, plus appendix
summary: A decodable "empathy" direction is routinely read as a causal lever, conflating decodability, automated-metric control, and human-perceived change. We test this for two EPITOME-derived facets -- Recognition (cognitive) and Resonance (affective) -- in three instruction-tuned LLMs, scoring every intervention with two LLM judges and a discriminative EPITOME classifier, each gated by an emotional-vs-neutral positive control. The control passes for the affective facet across all automated instruments, but cognitive range is inconsistent across them. Both facets remain decodable after residualizing against a sentence-embedding-derived surface score, and steering can substantially rewrite the text. Yet adding the Resonance direction raises the affective score only partially -- in Qwen by +0.29 (approximately 26% of the natural gap). A direct between-direction contrast confirms the shift is facet-specific in Qwen and Llama (not Gemma); we do not, however, establish a matching human-perceived change. Additive cognitive steering produces no measurable change, but a within-domain control shows the cognitive instrument is too coarse to resolve the differences such steering would produce -- unmeasurable, not a clean null. By contrast, Gemma Recognition ablation lowers the classifier's cognitive score even after adjusting for response length. Detection does not imply reliable control under global interventions, and cognitive-empathy claims warrant an explicit measurement-sensitivity check.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether a decodable “empathy direction” in language models actually lets us causally control empathetic behavior, finding that detection of empathy does not reliably translate to controllable changes, especially for cognitive empathy.
AI.motivation: Many recent works identify latent “empathy” directions in language models and implicitly treat these as dials that causally control empathy in generated text. However, this conflates three things: the ability to decode a feature, the ability to steer model outputs along that feature, and actual human-perceived changes in empathy. The authors want to rigorously test whether these directions genuinely function as causal levers for different empathy facets, rather than just being correlational signals picked up by automated metrics.
AI.method: The authors focus on two EPITOME-derived empathy facets: Recognition (cognitive empathy) and Resonance (affective empathy). They study three instruction-tuned LLMs and construct interventions along these latent directions. Each intervention is evaluated using: (1) two LLM-based judges, and (2) an EPITOME classifier, all gated by an emotional-vs-neutral positive control to ensure the instruments are responsive. They also residualize the directions against a sentence-embedding-based surface score to rule out trivial surface-form artifacts. They analyze both additive steering (boosting the facet) and ablation (removing it), and compare directions directly to test facet specificity, while checking for response-length confounds.
AI.result: The emotional control passes for the affective (Resonance) facet across all automated instruments, but for the cognitive (Recognition) facet the range and consistency across instruments are weak. Both empathy facets remain decodable even after controlling for surface features, and steering interventions can strongly alter the text content itself. However, adding the Resonance direction only partially increases affective scores—for Qwen the score rises by +0.29, covering about 26% of the natural gap between low and high empathy. Direction contrasts show facet-specific shifting in Qwen and Llama but not Gemma. They do not demonstrate a corresponding change in human-perceived empathy. Additive steering along the cognitive direction shows no measurable change, but a within-domain control reveals that the cognitive instrument is too insensitive to detect plausible changes, so the apparent null is due to measurement limits. Conversely, ablation of Gemma’s Recognition direction decreases cognitive scores even after adjusting for response length, indicating some causal influence under local manipulations.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that the mere decodability of an empathy-related latent direction does not guarantee reliable causal control over that empathy facet, particularly under broad or global steering interventions. Affective empathy shows only partial controllability and cognitive empathy is hampered by measurement insensitivity and model differences. The authors argue that claims about cognitive empathy in LLMs must include explicit checks of measurement sensitivity, and they caution against equating detection of empathy features with genuine, controllable changes in behavior or human-perceived empathy.

title: Semantic Variability of Replies Across LLMs: Implications for Designing Conversation-Based Assessment
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, two tables. Accepted to the AI in Measurement and Education Conference 2026
summary: This study examines whether LLM-generated replies remain semantically consistent when the underlying LLM changes. Using messages from real collaborative conversations, we compared the semantic similarity of generated replies across LLMs under two conditions: with and without preceding chat history. Results show that model choice and conversational context both affect response similarity and alignment with human replies. These findings indicate that prompting and conversational context alone may not be sufficient to preserve response consistency across LLMs, highlighting the need for infrastructure and design strategies that can maintain stable and comparable responses amid the rapid and continuous evolution of LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether responses generated by different LLMs stay semantically consistent when models are swapped, and how chat history affects this consistency.
AI.motivation: As LLMs rapidly evolve and are frequently swapped in real systems, there is a practical need to know if the same prompt or conversation will yield stable, comparable outputs across models, especially in collaborative or longitudinal applications.
AI.method: The authors use messages from real collaborative conversations as prompts, then generate replies from multiple LLMs in two conditions: (1) with preceding chat history included and (2) without it. They then compute semantic similarity between replies across models and compare these to human replies to assess alignment and consistency.
AI.result: They find that both the specific LLM chosen and the presence or absence of conversational context significantly influence the semantic similarity of replies across models and their alignment with human responses.
AI.conclusion: Prompting strategies and conversational context alone are insufficient to guarantee consistent responses across different LLMs, suggesting a need for additional infrastructure and interaction design methods to maintain stable, comparable behavior as LLMs change over time.

title: The Dialect Tax: Dialectal Biases Persist throughout the Language Modeling Pipeline
comment: To be published at EMNLP 2026 under the full author name "Elle"
summary: Systematic dialectal performance gaps in language models (LMs) are well documented, but the source of these disparities within the modern language modeling pipeline remains unclear. Our study traces this "dialect tax" across the natural language processing pipeline. Using parallel English dialect corpora that hold meaning fixed while varying surface form, we first confirm that LMs recognize matched Standard American English (SAE) and dialectal texts as semantically equivalent. However, we discover further representational gaps corresponding to downstream performance gaps. Across model families and generations, modern LMs still encode dialectal texts unequally during tokenization, pre-training, post-training, and inference. Strikingly, bypassing traditional subword segmentation via a character-level counterfactual tokenizer removes neither input and output asymmetries nor dialectal accuracy gaps. During pre-training, dialect pairs induce more divergent gradient updates than pairs of entirely unrelated SAE documents, indicating that models find semantically equivalent dialectal content harder to learn from than unrelated SAE documents. During post-training, reward models show contextual, unstable dialect preferences, assigning higher values to isolated AAVE-exclusive tokens than to SAE-exclusive tokens, while full reasoning contexts receive task- and model-dependent dialect penalties. Overall, our findings suggest that the dialect tax is encoded and accumulated not by any one step in isolation, but at every step of the language modeling process.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why language models perform worse on certain English dialects, showing that bias arises and accumulates at every stage of the modeling pipeline rather than from a single source.
AI.motivation: There are known accuracy gaps in how language models handle different English dialects, but it is unclear which parts of the modern language modeling pipeline cause these disparities. The authors aim to pinpoint where and how these dialect-related performance gaps emerge.
AI.method: The authors use parallel English dialect corpora that keep semantic content constant while varying surface dialect (e.g., Standard American English vs. other dialects). They analyze model behavior at multiple pipeline stages—tokenization, pre-training, post-training, and inference—across different model families and generations. They also test a character-level counterfactual tokenizer to bypass subword segmentation, examine gradient updates during pre-training for dialect vs. SAE pairs, and study reward model preferences for dialect-specific tokens and full reasoning contexts.
AI.result: Language models recognize dialectal and Standard American English texts as semantically equivalent, but still encode them unequally. Representational and performance gaps persist at tokenization, pre-training, post-training, and inference stages, across different models. Using a character-level tokenizer does not remove asymmetries or accuracy gaps. During pre-training, semantically equivalent dialect pairs produce more divergent gradient updates than unrelated SAE document pairs. During post-training, reward models display unstable and context-dependent dialect preferences, favoring isolated tokens from one dialect but penalizing full contexts in that dialect, depending on task and model.
AI.conclusion: Dialect-related performance disparities in language models are not attributable to any single stage of the pipeline. Instead, a "dialect tax" is encoded and compounded across all stages—tokenization, pre-training, post-training, and inference—indicating that mitigating such bias requires holistic changes throughout the entire language modeling process.

title: Unsupervised Post-Training of Foundation Models: A Survey
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 20 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables
summary: Foundation-model post-training usually relies on human labels, preference data, stronger teachers, or executable verifiers. We study Unsupervised Post-Training (UPT): update-bearing adaptation on unlabeled inputs whose learning signal is derived from same-lineage model artifacts rather than an external oracle. We catalog 80 strict UPT methods and organize them by the object that supplies the update signal: a prediction statistic, a sample relation, a self-generated target, or an internal evaluator. Beyond inventory, we show how the choice of internal signal and task structure determines whether post-training improves the model or recursively amplifies error. An orthogonal Input Visibility $\times$ Update Persistence view maps deployment regimes and defines a unified framework for UPT selection and evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys and systematizes 'Unsupervised Post-Training' (UPT) methods that adapt foundation models using only signals derived from the model lineage itself, and proposes frameworks to understand when such methods help or harm.
AI.motivation: Most post-training of foundation models (like reinforcement learning from human feedback, distillation, or verifier-based training) depends on external supervision—human labels, stronger teacher models, or executable verifiers—which is expensive, limited in scale, and sometimes unavailable. There is growing interest in adapting models using only their own outputs or internal signals, but these approaches are fragmented and poorly systematized, and it is unclear under what conditions they improve models versus reinforcing their existing errors. The paper aims to define, categorize, and analyze such purely unsupervised post-training methods to guide their design and deployment.
AI.method: The authors define 'Unsupervised Post-Training' (UPT) as update-bearing adaptation based solely on unlabeled inputs and signals derived from models of the same lineage (no external oracle). They compile and curate a catalog of 80 strict UPT methods from the literature. They then introduce an organizing taxonomy based on what provides the learning signal: (1) prediction statistics (e.g., likelihoods, entropy, surprise), (2) sample relations (e.g., consistency across augmentations or views), (3) self-generated targets (e.g., self-training or pseudo-labeling), and (4) internal evaluators (e.g., internal critics or reward models derived from the model itself). They analyze, theoretically and/or empirically, how the interaction between the chosen internal signal and the task structure governs whether UPT corrects or amplifies errors. Additionally, they develop an orthogonal framework based on two dimensions—Input Visibility and Update Persistence—to map different deployment regimes (online vs offline, transient vs permanent updates) and to provide a unified lens for selecting and evaluating UPT strategies.
AI.result: The paper provides: (1) a structured catalog of 80 strict UPT methods, clarifying which methods qualify under their definition and how they differ; (2) a taxonomy that groups these methods by the nature of their internal learning signals; (3) an analysis showing that some combinations of internal signal and task structure are prone to error amplification or feedback loops, while others are more stable and beneficial; and (4) an Input Visibility × Update Persistence framework that positions existing methods and deployment settings, helping to compare and reason about them systematically. The results highlight both promising settings where UPT reliably improves models and risky regimes where it can degrade performance.
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised Post-Training can meaningfully adapt foundation models without external supervision, but its success is highly contingent on the choice of internal learning signals, the structure of the underlying task, and how and when updates are applied. By cataloging existing methods and organizing them under signal-type and deployment-regime frameworks, the paper offers a unified foundation for understanding, designing, and evaluating UPT approaches. It warns that naive applications can recursively amplify errors, but also identifies principled conditions and configurations under which UPT is a powerful and scalable alternative or complement to supervised post-training.

title: VLM-based automatic multi-granularity graph representation of building layouts for design informatics
summary: Architectural floorplan images encode rich relational knowledge among functional spaces, which underpins design retrieval, knowledge-based reasoning, and BIM enrichment through the building lifecycle. However, it remains challenging to automatically construct task-adaptive graph representations for public buildings. To address this gap, we first define a multi-granularity Level-of-Graphs (LoGs) for public building layouts. Methodologically, we present a Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based automatic LoG construction through node identification, edge inference, text parsing, and graph coarsening. VLM-generated representations are systematically evaluated and tested in real-world tasks, using 147 academic library floorplans worldwide as a case study. Experiments showed VLM-generated graphs were broadly consistent with human-labeled graphs (matched node ratio >= 92%; 509.3 s per floor plan for three-LoG graph generation). Meso-grained graphs yield the best node-level zone prediction (Macro F1 = 0.647, at 65% of fine-grained complexity), while coarse-grained graphs are most effective for graph-level layout quality evaluation (Spearman's \r{ho} = 0.610, at 16% of fine-grained complexity). By enabling scalable, annotation-free extraction of structured layout information from floorplan images, this study advances design informatics by converting plan images into knowledge representations, thereby enhancing the utilization of design information across the building life cycle.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method to automatically convert public-building floorplan images into multi-level graph representations using a vision-language model, and validates it on 147 academic library layouts.
AI.motivation: Architectural floorplans contain rich spatial and functional relationships that are valuable for tasks like design retrieval, reasoning, and BIM enrichment, but it is difficult to automatically and scalably derive suitable, task-adaptive graph representations from these images, especially for public buildings.
AI.method: The authors define a multi-granularity Level-of-Graphs (LoGs) framework for public building layouts, then develop a VLM-based pipeline that automatically constructs these graphs from floorplan images via node identification, edge inference, text parsing, and graph coarsening. They evaluate the generated graphs against human-labeled ones and test their usefulness in real tasks using 147 academic library floorplans.
AI.result: The VLM-generated graphs align closely with human-labeled graphs (matched node ratio ≥ 92%), and the full three-level LoG construction takes about 509.3 seconds per floorplan. Meso-grained graphs provide the best performance for node-level functional zone prediction (Macro F1 = 0.647) at about 65% of the fine-grained graph complexity, while coarse-grained graphs perform best for graph-level layout quality evaluation (Spearman’s rho = 0.610) at only 16% of fine-grained complexity.
AI.conclusion: Automatically constructed, multi-granularity graph representations of floorplan images using a VLM can reliably approximate human annotations and support downstream tasks, enabling scalable, annotation-free extraction of structured layout knowledge from building plans and thereby improving the use of design information throughout the building lifecycle.

title: Does Fine-Tuning Undo Activation Steering? Behavioural Recovery Without Weight-Edit Reversal
comment: Accepted at EMNLP 2026 Main. Earlier version at ICLR 2026 Re^4-Align Workshop
summary: Activation steering can be embedded directly into a language model's weights, shaping behaviour without inference-time intervention and offering a way to encode alignment prior to release. However, models are routinely fine-tuned after deployment, and it is unknown whether embedded interventions survive this. We study the stability of embedded steering for refusal suppression and brevity induction across five instruction-tuned models (3B-14B) under non-adversarial SFT and RLHF. Behaviourally, preservation tracks the training data: steering degrades when optimisation pressure contradicts the targeted behaviour and persists otherwise, with refusal ablation losing 64% of its effect on average under SFT. Mechanistically, however, the weight edit survives almost untouched even where behaviour reverts: mean vector recovery is $ρ= 0.004$, and the fine-tuning update along the steering direction is near-orthogonal to its pre-edit weight pattern (mean $\cosθ= 0.074$). When steered behaviour degrades, fine-tuning does not achieve it by dismantling or reversing the steering mechanism itself. Embedded steering is therefore mechanistically durable but functionally vulnerable, and requires behavioural re-validation after downstream training.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether activation steering edits embedded in model weights remain effective after standard post-training, finding that the underlying weight changes persist but their behavioural effects can be weakened or lost by later fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: To understand if alignment-related interventions implemented directly in a model’s weights (activation steering embedded pre-release) remain stable and reliable after typical downstream fine-tuning procedures like SFT and RLHF, which are common in real-world deployment.
AI.method: The authors embed activation steering edits into several instruction-tuned language models of varying sizes, targeting two behaviours: reducing refusals and inducing brevity. They then apply non-adversarial supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RLHF to these models, measuring both the behavioural persistence of the intervention (e.g., refusal rates, output length) and the mechanistic persistence (e.g., recovery of the steering vector, alignment of fine-tuning updates with the steering direction).
AI.result: Behaviourally, the effectiveness of embedded steering depends on whether downstream fine-tuning data reinforces or opposes the targeted behaviour; where there is conflict (e.g., refusal suppression under SFT), steering degrades substantially, with refusal ablation losing about 64% of its effect on average. Mechanistically, the original steering weight edits remain nearly intact: the mean vector recovery correlation is about ρ=0.004 (indicating negligible distortion), and the fine-tuning update is nearly orthogonal to the steering direction with mean cosθ≈0.074.
AI.conclusion: Embedded activation steering is robust at the weight/mechanism level but fragile at the behavioural level: fine-tuning typically does not dismantle or reverse the steering circuitry itself, but can still override its functional impact via other changes. As a result, steering-based alignment interventions encoded in weights must be behaviourally re-validated after any downstream training, since mechanistic durability does not guarantee preserved aligned behaviour.

title: SIMGUIDE: Procedurally Grounded Multi-Context Representations for Personalized Agent Planning
summary: Personalized AI agents overwhelmingly treat users as single entities: a flat profile concatenated into a prompt. This fails when the same person holds different priorities across life contexts -- and fails catastrophically when those priorities conflict. The core problem is not that agents lack information about users; it is that the format of user representations determines whether an agent can act on that information at all. We introduce SIMGUIDE, a method that structures user context into typed, domain-specific blocks called Sims and grounds each constraint with procedural examples drawn from past decisions. To evaluate this, we construct SIMBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 47 preference-conditioned planning tasks where the correct plan depends on which user context is active -- a property no existing benchmark tests. Declarative Sim constraints alone do not outperform retrieval-based personalization (RAG). Procedurally grounded Sims outperform RAG on GPT-4o (+7.9 Preference Adherence points, $p = 0.013$), and this advantage replicates on 100 $τ$-bench tasks across both GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet~4.5 ($p \leq 0.023$). At the parametric level, the same principle holds: training distribution dominates whether parametric adaptation succeeds at all. Task-matched LoRA fine-tuning improves generation quality by 12.8 ROUGE-L points over the unadapted base model, and routing adapters by Sim type rather than user identity adds a further 7.3 points, robust to 28% routing error. Representation format -- not representation content -- is the first-order design variable.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SIMGUIDE, a structured way to represent user preferences via typed, procedural context blocks (Sims), and shows that representation format strongly improves preference-conditioned planning and personalization over standard flat profiles and RAG.
AI.motivation: Most AI agents treat a person as a single, flat profile in prompts, which breaks down when one user has different, even conflicting, priorities across contexts. Existing systems and benchmarks don’t test whether models can choose actions that depend on which context is active. The authors aim to fix this by rethinking how user information is represented so that agents can correctly condition on nuanced, context-dependent preferences.
AI.method: They introduce SIMGUIDE, which organizes user information into typed, domain-specific blocks called Sims, each encoding constraints and grounded with procedural examples from past decisions. They build SIMBENCH, a benchmark of 47 preference-conditioned planning tasks whose correct solution depends on the active Sim. They compare: (1) baseline retrieval-based personalization (RAG), (2) Sims with only declarative constraints, and (3) procedurally grounded Sims, across GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.5. At the parametric level, they perform LoRA fine-tuning with task-matched data and evaluate routing strategies, including routing adapters by Sim type versus user identity, measuring gains with ROUGE-L and robustness to routing errors.
AI.result: Procedurally grounded Sims outperform RAG personalization on SIMBENCH for GPT-4o by +7.9 Preference Adherence points (p = 0.013), and the improvement replicates on 100 τ-bench tasks for both GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (p ≤ 0.023). Declarative Sims without procedural grounding do not beat RAG. For parametric adaptation, task-matched LoRA fine-tuning improves ROUGE-L by 12.8 points over the base model. Routing LoRA adapters by Sim type instead of user identity yields an additional 7.3 ROUGE-L gain and remains robust even with 28% routing error.
AI.conclusion: The way user information is structured—its representation format—is more critical than how much information is available. Organizing user context into typed, procedurally grounded Sims enables models to better follow context-specific preferences than flat profiles or naive RAG retrieval. Similarly, for fine-tuned models, aligning training and routing with Sim types rather than users notably improves performance. Overall, representation format is the key design lever for building reliable, preference-aware AI agents.

title: The Imperfective Paradox Is Not Necessarily in Large Language Models: A Benchmark Failure Before a Model Failure
summary: The imperfective paradox provides a useful test of compositional semantic analysis. Recent work constructs an NLI benchmark and reports that models frequently infer completed telic events from progressive descriptions, attributing this behavior to a Teleological Bias. It further argues that prompting interventions cause a Calibration Crisis. We reexamine the benchmark and conclusions and show that it is substantially affected by conceptual and evaluation mis-specifications. We identify three conceptual mis-specifications. In particular, Aspectual Reduction affects the benchmark construction, analysis, experiments, and conclusions. Under a strict NLI standard, 76% of Group A instances do not explicitly rule out culmination. In our native-speaker annotation, 38% of Group A examples and 29% of the Group C examples were judged to permit an alternative interpretation. To control these issues and lexical variation, we construct Lexically Matched Minimal Pairs. At the evaluation level, we formulate event-semantic NLI as a Multi-step Reasoning Problem and assess both intermediate semantic decisions and final predictions. Our results show that models often do not affirm culmination but nevertheless accept the corresponding simple-past hypothesis, a pattern we characterize as Sufficiency Bias. We further show that prompting interventions produce a Decision Shift among labels without reliably improving the underlying semantic understanding and reasoning. Intermediate and oracle-guided analyses identify two additional failure modes: errors in compositional aspectual classification and Surface-form Attraction toward surface-associated answers. Our experiments on Qwen-7B with suitable prompts, GPT-5.4, and Qwen-72B provide initial evidence for the context sensitivity of aspectual classification and suggest that these models can achieve performance comparable to that of human annotators.

AI.tldr: The paper reexamines an NLI benchmark on imperfective aspect, shows it is conceptually and evaluatively mis-specified, builds better-controlled data and evaluation, and finds models show a Sufficiency Bias and other failure modes rather than a simple Teleological Bias, while also demonstrating context-sensitive but competitive aspectual reasoning.
AI.motivation: To test compositional semantic analysis using the imperfective paradox, prior work built an NLI benchmark and claimed that models wrongly infer completion (Teleological Bias) and that prompting causes a Calibration Crisis. This paper suspects those conclusions are undermined by problems in how the benchmark is conceptually framed and evaluated, and seeks to provide a more accurate assessment of what models actually do and how well they understand aspect and event semantics.
AI.method: The authors critically analyze the existing benchmark and identify three conceptual mis-specifications, including Aspectual Reduction, and quantify how many NLI items truly exclude culmination under a strict NLI standard. They run native-speaker annotations to measure interpretive variability in key groups. To address these issues, they construct Lexically Matched Minimal Pairs controlling for lexical variation. On the evaluation side, they recast event-semantic NLI as a multi-step reasoning task, separately evaluating intermediate semantic decisions and final labels. They perform experiments on Qwen-7B with carefully designed prompts, GPT-5.4, and Qwen-72B, and conduct intermediate and oracle-guided analyses to uncover error patterns such as compositional aspectual misclassification and Surface-form Attraction.
AI.result: They find that 76% of Group A instances in the original benchmark do not actually rule out culmination under strict NLI, and human annotators often judge examples as permitting multiple interpretations (38% for Group A, 29% for Group C), undermining the original claims. With Lexically Matched Minimal Pairs and a multi-step evaluation, they show that models frequently do not explicitly affirm culmination, but still tend to accept simple-past hypotheses, which they term a Sufficiency Bias. Prompting interventions mainly cause a Decision Shift in label distributions rather than genuine semantic improvement. Further, they identify systematic failure modes in compositional aspectual classification and Surface-form Attraction. Their experiments indicate that aspectual classification is context-sensitive, and that Qwen-7B, GPT-5.4, and Qwen-72B can, under suitable prompting, reach performance levels comparable to human annotators.
AI.conclusion: The original NLI benchmark and its Teleological Bias and Calibration Crisis conclusions are significantly weakened by conceptual and evaluation mis-specifications, notably Aspectual Reduction and underspecified exclusion of culmination. A more controlled, event-semantic, multi-step evaluation reveals that models exhibit a Sufficiency Bias and other specific failure modes rather than simply inferring completion from progressives. Prompting mostly reshapes decision distributions without reliably improving semantic reasoning. Nevertheless, with improved data and prompting, large language models can show context-sensitive aspectual understanding and performance similar to human annotators, suggesting that careful benchmark design and multi-step evaluation are crucial for accurately assessing semantic competence.

title: Reliable LLM-Powered Decision Engines for Large-Scale Supply Chain Operations: Architecture, Safety, and Performance Guarantees
summary: Current large-scale supply chains are highly uncertain, dynamic, and disruption prone that are challenging to serve up timely and resilient decisions through traditional rule-based and optimization-only systems. The increasing supply of heterogeneous data sources, such as transactional demand signals and unstructured disruption report, presents a chance of intelligent systems, which could reason, adapt and optimize at the same time. A hybrid architecture that combines large language models (LLMs) with mathematical optimization, probabilistic forecasting, and safety-constrained decision filtering is proposed in this paper as a performance of a Decision Engine, which is called LLM-Powered Decision Engine (LLM-DE). In comparison to purely data-driven or heuristic solutions, LLM-DE integrates semantic reasoning with LLM with a set of performance and safety guarantees that allow safe decision-making in large-scale supply chain processes. The suggested framework enables the end-to-end decision making such as demand forecasting, inventory optimization, and transportation routing and disruption mitigation. The findings affirm that language-based reasoning combined with optimization and formal constraints can be used to come up with not only smarter but also safer and more scalable supply chain decisions. This research provides a new architecture, a complete pipeline of algorithm, and a formulation based on mathematical constructs of the operational decision systems incorporating LLM. The proposed model offers a pragmatic and theoretical basis of the next-generation intelligent supply chain infrastructures that can be implemented to work dependably in the face of uncertainty and massive complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an LLM-powered decision engine that combines language-based reasoning with forecasting, optimization, and safety constraints to improve robustness and scalability of supply chain decision-making.
AI.motivation: Traditional rule-based and optimization-only systems struggle with modern supply chains that are uncertain, dynamic, disruption-prone, and fed by heterogeneous data (structured and unstructured). There is a need for intelligent systems that can understand rich contextual information, adapt to disruptions, and still provide reliable, safe, and scalable decisions.
AI.method: The authors design a hybrid architecture, the LLM-Powered Decision Engine (LLM-DE), which couples large language models for semantic reasoning with mathematical optimization, probabilistic demand forecasting, and safety-constrained decision filtering. The framework forms an end-to-end pipeline to support tasks like demand forecasting, inventory optimization, transportation routing, and disruption mitigation, with formal performance and safety guarantees embedded in the optimization and constraint components.
AI.result: Experimental or conceptual findings (as suggested in the abstract) show that LLM-DE can generate decisions that are more intelligent, resilient, and scalable than purely data-driven or heuristic baselines, while maintaining explicit safety and performance guarantees via optimization and constraint mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Language-based reasoning from LLMs, when integrated with formal mathematical optimization, probabilistic models, and safety filters, can serve as the core of next-generation intelligent supply chain decision systems. This architecture provides both a practical pipeline and a theoretical formulation for deploying dependable, end-to-end, LLM-enabled decision engines in complex, uncertain supply chain environments.

title: A Primer on Computational Semantics for Artificial Intelligence Systems
summary: As people adopt transformer-based language models (e.g., ChatGPT and Gemini) for an increasing number of use-cases, it is important to know how such models learn and represent the meaning of the language, and to be more informed about what language is. This document is an attempt to help the reader understand how linguistic meaning (i.e., semantics) is approached from different fields of scientific and philosophical examination. I also explain three primary semantic theories: formal semantics, grounded semantics, and distributional semantics then compare how transformer-based language models differ from how humans learn language.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys how different disciplines understand linguistic meaning and explains three major semantic theories, then contrasts them with how transformer-based language models acquire and represent meaning.
AI.motivation: With the rising use of transformer-based language models like ChatGPT and Gemini, there is a need to clarify what "meaning" in language is and how different scientific and philosophical traditions conceptualize it, in order to better understand what these models are actually doing when they process language.
AI.method: The author reviews and synthesizes perspectives on semantics from multiple fields, then presents and explicates three core semantic frameworks—formal semantics, grounded semantics, and distributional semantics—and analyzes them in relation to the learning and representational mechanisms of transformer-based language models.
AI.result: The paper characterizes each semantic theory, shows the conceptual differences among them, and identifies mismatches between human language learning (which involves grounding and rich context) and the largely distributional, text-based learning of transformer models.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based language models primarily embody a form of distributional semantics and differ in important ways from human language learning, especially in grounding and conceptual understanding; appreciating the distinctions among formal, grounded, and distributional semantics helps clarify both the capabilities and limits of such models.

title: AI-Powered Mental Health Chatbots in Africa: A Systematic Review and Culturally Adaptive Framework
summary: Mental health challenges in Africa remain under-addressed due to inadequate infrastructure, stigma, and a chronic shortage of professionals. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots are emerging globally as low-cost, accessible tools that can offer psychological support. This paper presents a systematic review of 52 empirical studies published between 2017 and 2025, critically analysing their cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural relevance to African contexts. The findings demonstrate the potential of AI chatbots to improve accessibility, reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, and expand psychosocial support, yet reveal limited African-specific adaptation. Most systems remain rooted in Western models and English-language designs, leaving critical gaps in local relevance, inclusivity, and sustainability. Based on the findings, the authors develop a Culturally Adaptive Digital Mental Health (CADMH) framework that integrates African cultural values, multilingual design, mobile-first optimisation, and ethical safeguards. The study highlights opportunities and barriers for integrating AI chatbots into African healthcare, offering guidance for research, practice, and policy.

AI.tldr: Systematic review of AI mental health chatbots and proposal of an Africa-focused, culturally adaptive framework for their design and deployment.
AI.motivation: Mental health needs in Africa are high, but services are constrained by infrastructure gaps, workforce shortages, cost, and stigma. While AI chatbots are being explored globally as scalable, low-cost psychological support tools, it is unclear how relevant, effective, and appropriate these systems are for African populations with diverse cultures, languages, and access conditions. The paper aims to understand the current evidence base and to address the mismatch between existing chatbot designs and African contexts.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic review of 52 empirical studies on AI-powered mental health chatbots published between 2017 and 2025. They critically analyse these studies for their cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural relevance to African settings, assessing aspects such as target populations, languages used, theoretical models, delivery platforms, and adaptation strategies. Based on synthesis of these findings, they then derive a conceptual framework for culturally adaptive digital mental health in Africa.
AI.result: The review finds that AI chatbots can improve access to psychological support and show promise in reducing symptoms of anxiety and depression and extending psychosocial support. However, only a small subset of systems are tailored to African users. Most chatbots are grounded in Western therapeutic models, predominantly use English, and assume high-connectivity, smartphone-rich environments, leading to gaps in cultural fit, linguistic inclusivity, and long-term sustainability in African contexts. These observations inform the construction of the new CADMH framework.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that AI mental health chatbots are a promising component of digital mental health strategies in Africa but currently lack sufficient cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural adaptation. To close this gap, the authors propose the Culturally Adaptive Digital Mental Health (CADMH) framework, which emphasizes integrating African cultural values, multilingual and mobile-first design, and robust ethical safeguards. They argue that this framework can guide future research, implementation, and policy to more effectively integrate AI chatbots into African healthcare systems while promoting equity, relevance, and sustainability.

title: Behind the [MASK]: Disentangling Representation and Faithfulness in DAPF-Based Dementia Detection
comment: 16 pages, 1 figure, 19 tables. Under review at ACL Rolling Review
summary: Spoken-language analysis via prompt-based domain-adaptive models is a promising direction for low-resource, non-invasive dementia screening, but such models remain internally opaque. We study the interpretability of the Domain-Adapted models via Prompt-based Fine-tuning (DAPF) framework, which casts dementia detection as diagnosis-related masked-token prediction. We interpret DAPF and strong baselines using a variety of probing and analysis techniques, finding that DAPF achieved the best overall performance (accuracy=0.83 and macro-F1=0.83) with diagnosis most recoverable from its [MASK] representation. However, this representational advantage did not extend to token-level explanation faithfulness. DAPF attributions primarily reflected language task vocabulary, discourse markers, and transcription artifacts, with perturbation tests showing weak or negative effects. This suggests that its masked-token interface determines diagnosis information without producing faithful token-level explanations.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how interpretable a prompt-based, domain-adaptive model (DAPF) is for dementia detection from speech transcripts, finding strong predictive performance but limited faithfulness of token-level explanations.
AI.motivation: To enable low-resource, non-invasive dementia screening using spoken-language models while addressing the key concern that such models are opaque and hard to interpret, especially in clinical settings where explanation and trust are crucial.
AI.method: They use the DAPF framework that treats dementia detection as a masked-token prediction task, adapt language models via prompt-based fine-tuning, and compare DAPF to strong baselines. They apply multiple probing and analysis techniques to examine how diagnosis information is represented in the model and evaluate token-level explanation faithfulness through attribution and perturbation tests.
AI.result: DAPF achieves the best overall detection performance (accuracy=0.83, macro-F1=0.83). Diagnosis information is most easily recoverable from the [MASK] representation in DAPF compared to baselines, showing a representational advantage. However, token-level explanations derived from DAPF are not faithful: attributions focus on vocabulary tied to the language task, discourse markers, and transcription artifacts, and perturbing high-attribution tokens yields weak or even negative effects on predictions.
AI.conclusion: Although DAPF is strong for dementia detection and encodes diagnosis information effectively in its masked-token representation, its interface does not yield faithful token-level explanations. The model appears to use global or abstract features rather than specific tokens in a way that clinicians might expect, indicating a gap between performance and interpretable, trustworthy explanations.

title: Measurement-Budget Allocation in Quantum Learning with Finite-Shot Generalization Guarantees
summary: On near-term quantum hardware, estimating a Born probability requires repeated circuit executions. A quantum learning experiment with a fixed measurement budget $B$ must therefore decide how many distinct training states $n$ to use and how many shots $S$ to allocate to each state. We study this tradeoff for binary quantum classifiers with fixed or independently selected measurement operators $M$, where the ideal score is $\Tr(Mρ)$. We prove a distribution-free generalization bound that separates the finite-sample and finite-shot contributions. The sample term scales as $\sqrt{d/n}$, while the shot term scales as $\sqrt{(\log n)/S}$; under the constraint $B=nS$, these two terms move in opposite directions. Minimising a conservative closed-form surrogate of the bound gives the allocation rule $\nstar = 2\sqrt{2dB/\log(2B/δ)}$ and $\Sstar = B/\nstar$. This surrogate has the same asymptotic scaling as the exact minimizer and yields a worst-case rate of $B^{-1/4}$. The guarantee is intentionally conservative, since it applies to the full class of binary quantum measurements. We complement the theory with PennyLane simulations using 2-qubit and 4-qubit variational quantum circuits on nine synthetic binary classification benchmarks. In all tested configurations, the one-sided empirical generalization gap remains below the theoretical bound. The result provides a conservative statistical guideline for allocating measurement budgets in finite-shot evaluation and pre-experimental planning for near-term quantum learning systems, complementing hardware-level scheduling and circuit-design considerations. Extending the guarantee to fully adaptive shot-noisy training remains an open problem.

AI.tldr: They derive and validate a conservative statistical rule for how to split a fixed number of quantum measurement shots across training states in near-term quantum classifiers.
AI.motivation: Near-term quantum devices are noisy and require many repeated circuit executions (shots) to estimate measurement outcomes. In quantum machine learning, one often has a fixed total measurement budget, but it is unclear how best to distribute this budget between using more distinct training states versus using more shots per state. A principled, distribution-free guideline for this tradeoff is missing.
AI.method: The authors analyze binary quantum classifiers whose ideal outputs are expectation values Tr(Mρ) of fixed or independently chosen measurement operators M. They derive a distribution-free generalization bound that explicitly separates errors due to limited training samples (finite-sample) from errors due to limited shots (finite-shot). They study how these two error components scale with the number of training states n and shots per state S under a fixed budget B=nS. Using a conservative closed-form surrogate of their bound, they analytically optimize over n and S, then validate the resulting allocation rule via PennyLane simulations on 2- and 4-qubit variational circuits across nine synthetic binary classification tasks.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows that the finite-sample term of the generalization bound scales as sqrt(d/n), while the finite-shot term scales as sqrt((log n)/S). Under the constraint B=nS, these behave antagonistically as functions of n and S. Minimizing a surrogate bound yields an explicit allocation rule: n* = 2 sqrt(2 d B / log(2B/δ)) training states and S* = B / n* shots per state. This allocation achieves a worst-case convergence rate in the total budget of order B^{-1/4}. Simulations on small variational quantum circuits confirm that the empirical one-sided generalization gap stays below the theoretical bound in all tested cases.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a conservative, distribution-free statistical prescription for how to allocate a fixed measurement budget between training set size and shots per state in binary quantum classifiers on near-term hardware. Their bound cleanly separates sample and shot errors, leading to an explicit allocation rule with provable worst-case scaling and empirical support from simulations. This offers a practical guideline for pre-experimental planning and finite-shot evaluation in quantum learning, complementing hardware and circuit-design considerations. They highlight extending the analysis to fully adaptive, shot-noisy training procedures as an important open direction.

title: Padamitra: Grounded Glossary Generation for Classical Sanskrit
comment: Accepted in the Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: We introduce grounded glossary generation, a structured task requiring models to recover semantically meaningful Sanskrit phrases and produce translation-grounded meanings from a sloka-translation pair, formalizing the traditional patha commentary practice as an evaluable NLP objective. We construct a benchmark of 31,316 sloka-translation-glossary triples from the Valmiki Ramayana and Srimad Bhagavatam, paired with two metrics: Jaccard for phrase recovery and Meaning Faithfulness for semantic consistency. Across zero-shot, few-shot, and instruction fine-tuned variants of Gemma-3n-E4B, Gemma-3-12B, Phi-4, and Qwen3.5-9B, instruction fine-tuning substantially outperforms prompting, while explicit segmentation yields gains. Error analysis identifies over-segmentation of sandhi and samasa compounds as the dominant failure mode, pointing to morphological modeling as the key bottleneck for faithful Sanskrit lexical decomposition.

AI.tldr: The paper defines and benchmarks a new NLP task: generating translation-grounded Sanskrit glossaries from sloka-translation pairs.
AI.motivation: To formalize the traditional Sanskrit patha commentary practice as a concrete, evaluable NLP objective and to advance computational methods for Sanskrit phrase segmentation and interpretation.
AI.method: They define a grounded glossary generation task, build a dataset of 31,316 sloka-translation-glossary triples from Valmiki Ramayana and Srimad Bhagavatam, and evaluate multiple LLMs (Gemma-3n-E4B, Gemma-3-12B, Phi-4, Qwen3.5-9B) in zero-shot, few-shot, and instruction-finetuned settings using Jaccard for phrase recovery and a Meaning Faithfulness metric for semantic consistency. They also test the impact of explicit segmentation and conduct error analysis.
AI.result: Instruction fine-tuning significantly outperforms pure prompting across models; explicit segmentation further improves performance. The main errors stem from over-segmentation of sandhi and samasa compounds.
AI.conclusion: Grounded glossary generation is a viable benchmark that exposes morphological modeling, especially accurate handling of sandhi and samasa compounds, as the primary bottleneck for faithful Sanskrit lexical decomposition, and instruction fine-tuned models with segmentation cues perform best on this task.

title: Natural Language Input, Semantic Track Representation, and LLM Inference: Making the Maritime Information Exchange Model Tractable
summary: We describe a practical architecture for making the Maritime Information Exchange Model (MIEM) and the broader Rich Semantic Track model tractable using current large language model (LLM) technology. The barrier to adoption of semantic track models in defense and law enforcement has been the requirement that operators learn formal ontology languages and manually encode observations as typed logical assertions. We propose eliminating this barrier entirely: operators contribute observations in natural language; an LLM translates these into typed Semantic Assertion Records (SARs), which are named case frames that capture n-ary relations in a single compact structure; a knowledge graph accumulates the SARs; and a second LLM pass performs inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking over the graph. We work through two detailed examples (a 9/11-era pre-attack indicator scenario and a maritime cargo inspection scenario) showing the full pipeline from natural language input to SAR representation to inference output. We argue that this architecture makes the Track Model and MIEM immediately deployable with current technology, establishes prior art against proprietary enclosure of the approach, and grounds the method in a theoretical framework connecting semantic track representations to neural manifold geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an LLM-based architecture that makes rich semantic track models (like MIEM) usable in practice by letting operators work in natural language instead of formal ontologies.
AI.motivation: Semantic track models such as MIEM promise powerful multi-entity, multi-event reasoning for defense and law enforcement, but in practice they are hard to adopt because they require users to understand and manually author formal ontological assertions. This complexity blocks real-world deployment even though the models themselves are valuable.
AI.method: The authors propose a pipeline where (1) human operators describe observations in plain natural language, (2) a large language model converts these descriptions into structured Semantic Assertion Records (SARs) that encode n-ary relations, (3) a knowledge graph stores and aggregates these SARs, and (4) a second LLM pass reasons over the graph for inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking. They demonstrate the approach on two example scenarios and connect it to a theoretical view of semantic tracks as structures in neural manifold geometry.
AI.result: The paper shows end-to-end examples in which natural language descriptions of complex, multi-actor situations are successfully mapped into SAR-based knowledge graphs that support non-trivial inference and anomaly detection using current LLMs. The examples illustrate that the full pipeline—from free-text input through structured representation to analytic output—can work in realistic defense and maritime contexts.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that their LLM-centered architecture removes the main usability barrier to semantic track models, making MIEM and related rich semantic tracks practically deployable today. They also claim the design as prior art to discourage proprietary lock-in and argue that their approach is theoretically grounded in the relationship between symbolic track representations and the geometric structure of neural network embeddings.

title: DataKernelBench: Can LLMs Optimize Database Queries on GPUs?
summary: GPUs increasingly accelerate database systems, but query-specific peak performance still often relies on hand-written kernels. Existing LLM kernel benchmarks focus on machine learning operators, leaving irregular, heterogeneous, data-movement-heavy database-style operators untested. We introduce DataKernelBench, which translates SQL into validated PyTorch TorchPlan programs and evaluates LLMs that optimize either the core tensor-bounded snippet or the full query in CUDA or Triton through execution-guided repair. Across ten proprietary and open-weight models on TPC-H SF10 with an H100 GPU, the strongest full-query CUDA configuration achieves $2.11\times$ speedup over torch.compile at full pass rate. We find that higher-performing implementations commonly use kernel fusion and execution-strategy changes, stronger models benefit most from full-query specialization, and workload context matters more than hardware context. To handle data larger than GPU memory, we extend TorchPlan with Dask-cuDF for on-demand partition loading on TPC-H SF100 with four H100 GPUs, achieving $2.54\times$ speedup

AI.tldr: DataKernelBench evaluates how well large language models can generate and optimize GPU kernels for database-style workloads, showing significant speedups over standard compilation baselines.
AI.motivation: While GPUs are used to accelerate databases, optimal performance still typically needs hand-written kernels. Existing LLM kernel benchmarks target ML operators and miss irregular, data-movement-heavy database operators, so we lack a way to measure LLMs' ability to optimize such queries.
AI.method: The authors build DataKernelBench, which translates SQL queries into PyTorch TorchPlan programs. They then task various LLMs (both proprietary and open-weight) with generating optimized CUDA or Triton kernels, either for a key tensor-bound code snippet or for the entire query, using execution-guided repair to ensure correctness. Experiments are run on TPC-H SF10 with an H100 GPU, and TorchPlan is extended with Dask-cuDF to support partitioned, out-of-core execution on TPC-H SF100 with four H100 GPUs.
AI.result: On TPC-H SF10 with an H100, the best LLM-generated full-query CUDA kernels achieve 2.11x speedup over torch.compile while retaining a 100% pass rate. Higher-quality models gain more from full-query optimization than snippet optimization, and effective kernels often employ fusion and change execution strategies. Workload-specific information is more critical to performance than hardware-specific context. For larger-than-memory data on TPC-H SF100 using four H100s, their extended TorchPlan pipeline reaches 2.54x speedup.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can automatically produce high-performance GPU kernels for complex, database-style workloads when guided by DataKernelBench, often matching or surpassing generic compiler baselines. Full-query specialization and workload-aware optimization are key, and the framework scales to multi-GPU, out-of-core settings while preserving significant speedups.

title: Same-Player Verification for Account Consistency in Counter-Strike 2
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: In competitive first-person shooter (FPS) games such as Counter-Strike 2 (CS2), account-integrity review often asks whether an account's recent behavior remains consistent with its historical operator. This consistency question arises in cases such as temporary substitution, rank boosting, and high-skill players using lower-ranked accounts, where manual review requires comparing a current match against multiple historical matches. We formulate this review task as same-player verification: we encode the behavioral trajectory of a single player in a match replay (demo) as a demo-player behavioral fingerprint, and train a model to judge whether two behavioral observations come from the same real player. Grounded in CS2 game understanding, the fingerprints cover crosshair control, movement-stop-fire coordination, economy/buy, combat/engagement, and temporal rhythm. From 1,330 CS2 demos we extract 13,300 demo-player observations, and sample 663,590 same/different pairs from an 88.4M candidate-pair space for supervised training and evaluation. The final pairwise model reaches an average ROC AUC of 0.931 and achieves 0.722 different-player recall at 95% precision. Feature analysis shows that the strongest identity signals come from low-level operations, especially crosshair control, firing rhythm, and movement-stop-fire coordination, indicating that stable low-level mechanical habits are more informative for this verification task than single-match performance outcomes. In the account-history aggregation evaluation, increasing history depth raises AUC from the K=1 single-pair baseline of 0.931 to 0.986 at K=10. These results show that CS2 demo behavior can support supervised same-player verification and account-level identity-consistency modeling through multi-demo history aggregation.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a behavioral fingerprinting method to verify whether two CS2 match demos come from the same player, achieving high accuracy and showing that low-level mechanical behavior is most distinctive.
AI.motivation: Manual account-integrity reviews in competitive FPS games are labor-intensive because reviewers must judge if recent gameplay is consistent with an account’s historical operator, especially in scenarios like smurfing, boosting, or temporary substitutions. The authors aim to automate this process by turning it into a same-player verification problem based on in-game behavioral data extracted from match demos.
AI.method: They encode each player’s behavior in a single CS2 match demo into a structured behavioral fingerprint capturing crosshair control, movement-stop-fire coordination, economy/buy patterns, combat/engagement behavior, and temporal rhythm. From 1,330 demos they derive 13,300 demo-player observations and construct 663,590 labeled pairs (same vs different player) from a large candidate pair space. A supervised pairwise model is trained to predict if two fingerprints belong to the same real-world player. They also perform feature-importance analysis and test an aggregation method that combines multiple historical demos (K > 1) to evaluate an account’s identity consistency over time.
AI.result: The pairwise same-player verification model achieves an average ROC AUC of 0.931 and a different-player recall of 0.722 at 95% precision, indicating strong discriminative power at high precision. Feature analysis reveals that low-level mechanical features—especially crosshair control, firing rhythm, and movement-stop-fire coordination—are the most informative identity signals, more so than high-level metrics like single-match performance. In experiments aggregating multiple demos per account, verification AUC improves from 0.931 with a single pair (K=1) to 0.986 with history depth K=10.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral data from CS2 match demos can effectively support supervised same-player verification. Stable low-level mechanical habits provide strong, persistent identity signatures, enabling accurate modeling of account-level identity consistency when multiple historical demos are aggregated. This suggests that automated, behavior-based tools can aid account-integrity review in competitive FPS environments by detecting inconsistencies such as smurfing or unauthorized account use.

title: HealthBench-Psych: A Mental Health Subset of OpenAI's HealthBench
comment: 21 pages (6-page main text plus appendices), 2 figures. Code: https://github.com/mindbench-ai/healthbench-psych Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/mindbench-ai/healthbench-psych
summary: General-purpose health benchmarks increasingly anchor claims about LLM medical performance, but they are not always resolved by clinical specialty, making domain-specific performance hard to isolate. Mental health is of acute public-health concern as millions of people turn to LLMs for psychological support, and most existing evaluations are bespoke academic benchmarks that are difficult to integrate into developer workflows. We introduce HealthBench-Psych and HealthBench-Psych-Hard. We screened HealthBench's 5,000 physician-rubric conversations for mental-health relevance with a transparent LLM-applied rubric, then validated the subset through two rounds of blinded clinician review with concealed known-exclude controls, yielding 610 conversations (12.2% of the corpus). Evaluating 20 frontier and open models under a cross-vendor panel of three LLM judges, we find a statistically tied frontier cluster, measurable refusal behavior in two models, and near-identical rankings across judges ($τ\ge 0.92$). We release the subset, pipeline, model responses, grades, and analysis code as a reusable resource.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a mental-health-specific benchmark (HealthBench-Psych and HealthBench-Psych-Hard) derived from an existing large health benchmark to evaluate LLMs in psychological-support contexts.
AI.motivation: Existing general-purpose medical benchmarks for LLMs are not specialty-specific and thus do not clearly measure performance in mental health, an area where many users already rely on LLMs for psychological support. Current mental-health evaluations are mostly custom academic setups that don’t integrate well into developer workflows. There is a need for a standardized, reusable, clinically validated benchmark focused on mental health conversations.
AI.method: The authors start from HealthBench, a corpus of 5,000 physician-rubric conversations. They use an explicit rubric applied by an LLM to screen for mental-health relevance. The resulting candidate subset is then validated through two rounds of blinded clinician review, including hidden known-exclude controls, to ensure quality and relevance, ending with 610 conversations (12.2% of the original corpus). They then evaluate 20 state-of-the-art and open-source LLMs using a cross-vendor panel of three different LLM judges that score model responses; they analyze rankings, refusals, and agreement between judges.
AI.result: The mental-health-relevant subset (HealthBench-Psych and a harder subset HealthBench-Psych-Hard) is created and validated. When 20 models are evaluated, they find a statistically tied group of top frontier models, detect significant refusal behavior in two models, and observe that different LLM judges produce highly consistent model rankings with Kendall’s tau at least 0.92. All artifacts from the creation and evaluation—data subset, pipeline, model outputs, grades, and code—are prepared for release.
AI.conclusion: HealthBench-Psych and HealthBench-Psych-Hard provide a rigorously constructed, reusable benchmark for assessing LLM performance in mental-health contexts, with strong inter-judge consistency and evidence that current frontier models perform similarly at the top. The released resources can be integrated into developer workflows and future research to more systematically test, compare, and improve LLMs used for psychological support.

title: Semantic Graph Unification for Industrial Digital Threads: Bridging 11 Heterogeneous Manufacturing Systems Through Ontology-Driven Knowledge Graphs
summary: Modern manufacturing enterprises operate heterogeneous systems -- ERP, MES, PLM, SCADA, QMS, SCM -- each with its own data model and API. The resulting silos prevent holistic analysis, delay root-cause investigation, and obstruct Industry 4.0 traceability. Point-to-point integration scales as O(n^2) and accumulates brittle dependencies. This paper presents an open framework for semantic graph unification of industrial digital threads. An ontology-driven RDF knowledge graph unifies data from 11 simulated sources across nine domains through a five-stage ETL pipeline with automated entity resolution spanning 97 owl:sameAs identity links. The ontology encompasses 78 RDFS classes, 108 object properties, and 243 data properties, drawing on ISA-95, OPC UA, eClass, the Asset Administration Shell, RAMI 4.0, and additional standards. An automated discovery engine applies nine strategy categories -- cross-station correlation, alarm coverage, ECN impact, CUSUM/EWMA drift detection -- to surface insights spanning system boundaries. The primary empirical result: blocking 24 cross-system tools reduces recall from 1.00 to 0.31 (F1 from 1.00 to 0.48), showing that 69% of discoverable signals require cross-system graph joins. Leave-one-out ablation confirms six of nine strategies contribute unique signals. Verification against a 65-signal manifest (16 positive, 49 null) yields F1 = 1.00 (95% Clopper-Pearson CI [0.79, 1.00]); as the manifest was author-constructed, this constitutes verification not independent validation. The graph is exposed to LLM agents via 287 Model Context Protocol tools as a SPARQL-native semantic layer. Five industry templates (aerospace, CPG, pharma, medical devices, turbine blades) demonstrate schema stability across manufacturing verticals.

AI.tldr: They build an ontology-driven RDF knowledge graph to unify heterogeneous manufacturing systems and show that most useful signals require cross-system joins.
AI.motivation: Manufacturers run many heterogeneous systems (ERP, MES, PLM, SCADA, etc.) that create data silos, making end-to-end traceability, root-cause analysis, and Industry 4.0 use cases difficult. Point-to-point integration does not scale and becomes brittle, so a more principled, scalable integration approach is needed.
AI.method: They design an open framework using an ontology-driven RDF knowledge graph that unifies data from 11 simulated sources across nine domains via a five-stage ETL pipeline. Automated entity resolution creates owl:sameAs links. The ontology, grounded in multiple industrial standards (ISA-95, OPC UA, eClass, Asset Administration Shell, RAMI 4.0), defines classes and properties. On top of this graph, they implement an automated discovery engine with nine strategy categories (e.g., cross-station correlation, alarm coverage, ECN impact, CUSUM/EWMA drift detection). They then run ablation and blocking experiments and verify results against an author-created manifest. The graph is also exposed to LLM agents via hundreds of Model Context Protocol tools, and they instantiate five industry templates to test schema stability.
AI.result: The ETL and ontology successfully unify the simulated multi-domain data, including 97 owl:sameAs links across 11 sources. The discovery engine shows that blocking 24 cross-system tools drops recall from 1.00 to 0.31 and F1 from 1.00 to 0.48, indicating 69% of signals depend on cross-system joins. Leave-one-out ablations show six of nine strategy categories contribute distinct, non-redundant signals. Verification against a 65-signal manifest yields F1 = 1.00 with a 95% Clopper-Pearson confidence interval [0.79, 1.00]. Five vertical templates demonstrate that the schema generalizes across several manufacturing sectors.
AI.conclusion: A standards-based semantic knowledge graph can serve as a unifying digital thread across heterogeneous manufacturing systems, and most valuable analytic signals rely on cross-system integration. Their framework provides a reusable, ontology-driven approach, shows high performance on a constructed benchmark, and can be consumed by automated discovery engines and LLM agents. However, evaluation is based on simulated data and an author-defined manifest, so independent validation on real industrial deployments is still needed.

title: MTDiag: A Multi-Turn Diagnostic Dataset Towards Clinically Meaningful LLM Evaluation
comment: 20 pages, published in the SIGDIAL 2026 conference proceedings, see https://aclanthology.org/2026.sigdial-1.58/
summary: Clinical diagnosis is fundamentally interactive and incremental, yet the dominant paradigm for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) in medicine remains static QA benchmarks or template-based dialogues. These benchmarks say little about whether a model can serve as a diagnostic agent in a dynamic clinical encounter, with LLMs showing significant accuracy and reliability degradation in multi-turn settings. To address this issue, we present MTDiag, a large multi-turn diagnostic dialogue dataset constructed from three heterogeneous sources: DDXPlus, MIMIC-IV, and published case reports (AJCR), covering common ED presentations as well as long-tail rare and atypical conditions. All cases are normalized into a canonical schema anchored in the most comprehensive and widely-adopted medical knowledge bases (UMLS concept identifiers, with ICD-10 diagnosis codes). We release the schema, a UserLM-8B-based utterance-generation pipeline, and the physician-validated dataset that converts structured clinical evidence into natural-language utterances. Importantly, we introduce and motivate clinical knowledge-grounded metrics for evaluating LLMs as diagnostic agents, beyond diagnostic accuracy, for the task of multi-turn differential diagnosis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MTDiag, a large multi-turn diagnostic dialogue dataset and evaluation framework to better assess LLMs as interactive clinical diagnostic agents.
AI.motivation: Existing medical LLM benchmarks are mostly static QA or simple template dialogues, which do not capture the interactive, incremental nature of real clinical diagnosis. LLMs often lose accuracy and reliability in multi-turn dialogues, and current evaluations overlook this. There is a need for realistic, knowledge-grounded benchmarks and metrics that reflect how LLMs would function as diagnostic agents over multi-step encounters.
AI.method: The authors build MTDiag, a multi-turn diagnostic dialogue dataset, by transforming structured clinical data from three heterogeneous sources—DDXPlus, MIMIC-IV, and AJCR case reports—into natural-language, multi-turn conversations. They normalize all cases into a canonical schema tied to UMLS concept identifiers and ICD-10 diagnosis codes. Using a UserLM-8B-based utterance-generation pipeline and physician validation, they convert structured evidence into realistic clinical utterances. They further define clinical knowledge-grounded metrics tailored to multi-turn differential diagnosis evaluation of LLMs, extending beyond simple end-diagnosis accuracy.
AI.result: The result is a large, physician-validated dataset of natural-language multi-turn diagnostic dialogues spanning both common emergency department presentations and rare or atypical cases, all mapped to standardized medical ontologies. Additionally, they provide an open schema, the utterance-generation pipeline, and a set of specialized evaluation metrics designed for assessing LLMs as diagnostic agents in multi-turn settings.
AI.conclusion: MTDiag enables more realistic and rigorous evaluation of LLMs for interactive clinical diagnosis by providing a standardized, ontology-linked, multi-turn dialogue dataset and knowledge-grounded metrics. This framework addresses the limitations of static QA benchmarks and lays groundwork for developing and assessing LLMs that can function more safely and effectively as diagnostic agents in dynamic clinical encounters.

title: post-graph-rag: A PostgreSQL-Native Graph RAG Engine
summary:
Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation connects facts that no single passage states, but current implementations pay for that three times: in infrastructure, requiring a vector store, graph database and document store to be kept consistent; in graph quality, because an extraction pipeline that never refuses output fills the graph with edges that assert nothing; and over time, because a graph that only accumulates treats superseded and current facts alike.
  post-graph-rag is an open-source engine addressing all three. Text chunks with embeddings, a canonical entity graph and community summaries live in one PostgreSQL database, with pgvector for search and edge tables for traversal. Extraction-time invariants run before anything is written: vague predicates, pronominal names and bare quantities are rejected; predicates are normalised onto an optional vocabulary; entities resolve to one vertex per canonical name via model-supplied aliases; and denied relations keep the positive predicate under a negation flag. A temporal layer lets relations carry a validity period from the prose, lets a later document supersede an earlier incompatible assertion from document order alone, and answers as-of queries.
  Against LightRAG on three corpora under identical extraction and embedding models, post-graph-rag builds a denser graph everywhere, up to $2.4\times$ the relations per entity, and a more queryable one: distinct edge labels run at 0.46 to 0.58 per relation, 0.11 under a controlled vocabulary, against 0.77 to 1.33. It answers comparably with lower query latency, and supports temporal evolution the baseline lacks: 13 and 8 relationships superseded on a novel sequence and a decade of filings, against zero. These are engineering measurements, not a benchmark result.
  Code: https://github.com/crajah/post-graph-rag, https://github.com/crajah/post-graph

AI.tldr: Post-graph-rag is an open-source, PostgreSQL-based graph RAG engine that unifies embeddings, entities, and summaries, enforces strict extraction-time quality checks, and adds temporal reasoning to build denser, more queryable and time-aware knowledge graphs than LightRAG.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based RAG systems require separate vector, graph, and document stores, making infrastructure complex and hard to keep consistent. Their extraction pipelines tend to over-generate low-value or noisy edges (vague predicates, unresolved entities), degrading graph quality. They also treat all facts as timeless, failing to distinguish superseded information from current facts, which limits temporal reasoning and leads to incorrect answers over evolving corpora.
AI.method: The authors implement post-graph-rag, an engine that stores text chunks, embeddings, a canonical entity graph, and community summaries in a single PostgreSQL database using pgvector for similarity search and relational tables for graph traversal. At extraction time, they enforce invariants: reject vague predicates, pronouns as names, and bare quantities; normalize predicates to an optional controlled vocabulary; canonicalize entities so aliases map to a single vertex; and explicitly encode denied relations with a negation flag. They add a temporal layer in which relations carry a validity interval derived from text, and later documents can automatically supersede earlier conflicting assertions using document order, enabling as-of queries. They then empirically compare this system to LightRAG under identical extraction and embedding models on three corpora.
AI.result: Compared with LightRAG, post-graph-rag yields consistently denser graphs, with up to 2.4× more relations per entity. Its edge labeling is more disciplined and queryable: distinct edge labels per relation are reduced to 0.46–0.58 (or 0.11 with a controlled vocabulary) versus LightRAG’s 0.77–1.33, indicating less label fragmentation. Query answering quality is comparable, but query latency is lower. Crucially, the system supports temporal evolution: in experiments on a synthetic document sequence and a decade of filings, it identifies 13 and 8 superseded relationships respectively, while LightRAG detects none. The authors emphasize that these are engineering metrics rather than formal benchmark scores.
AI.conclusion: Post-graph-rag demonstrates that graph-based RAG can be implemented with simpler infrastructure by consolidating embeddings, graph data, and documents in PostgreSQL, while also improving graph quality and enabling temporal reasoning. Strong extraction-time constraints and canonicalization yield denser but cleaner graphs, and the temporal layer allows the system to distinguish current from superseded facts and answer time-specific queries. The work is positioned as a practical engineering contribution and open-source toolkit, not as a state-of-the-art benchmark submission.

title: Apples to Apples? Towards Comparable Crosslingual Language Model Evaluation
