summary: Crosslingual evaluation of language models that enables fair comparisons remains a fundamental challenge in multilingual NLP. Existing studies adopt a variety of downstream tasks and intrinsic metrics with different theoretical justifications, yet there has been little empirical investigation into whether these approaches yield meaningful crosslingual conclusions. We systematically examine crosslingual evaluation approaches using controlled monolingual language models trained on parallel data with varying tokenizer vocabulary sizes and model sizes, and further validate our findings on multilingual LLMs. We further discuss challenges in achieving comparable downstream evaluation across languages. Our results show that several widely used normalized metrics introduce crosslinguistic biases rooted in tokenization, encoding, and orthographic differences. In contrast, sentence-level negative log-likelihood computed over semantically equivalent sequences provides more meaningful and consistent crosslingual comparisons.

AI.tldr: The paper critically examines how we evaluate language models across languages and proposes a fairer, sentence-level likelihood metric for crosslingual comparison.
AI.motivation: Crosslingual evaluation of language models is inconsistent and potentially unfair because different studies use heterogeneous tasks and metrics that may be influenced by language-specific properties like tokenization and orthography. There is little empirical evidence that these approaches yield reliable crosslingual conclusions, creating a need to systematically test what makes evaluations comparable across languages.
AI.method: The authors use controlled monolingual language models trained on parallel corpora so that the underlying semantic content is aligned across languages. They systematically vary tokenizer vocabulary sizes and model sizes to disentangle the effects of tokenization and capacity. Then they apply a range of existing intrinsic and downstream evaluation metrics, including various normalized scores, and analyze how these metrics behave across languages. Finally, they validate the main findings on large multilingual LLMs to check if the observed biases generalize beyond the controlled setting.
AI.result: They find that many commonly used normalized metrics for crosslingual LM evaluation produce biased or misleading comparisons across languages. These biases are traced to differences in tokenization granularity, encoding schemes, and orthographic characteristics of the languages rather than true modeling ability. In contrast, when evaluation is done via sentence-level negative log-likelihood over semantically equivalent sentences across languages, the resulting crosslingual comparisons are more stable, interpretable, and less affected by language-specific artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Widely used normalized metrics for crosslingual language model evaluation can introduce systematic crosslinguistic bias and thus may not support fair comparisons across languages. A more reliable alternative is to use sentence-level negative log-likelihood computed on parallel, semantically equivalent sentences. The paper underscores the difficulty of achieving truly comparable downstream evaluations across languages and advocates for more careful metric design and the use of semantically aligned data in multilingual LM assessment.

title: FrontierChallenge: Evaluating Scientific Workflow Completion
summary: Scientific agents increasingly analyze data, execute code, and produce research artifacts, yet most benchmarks emphasize final answers, isolated programs, or a single domain. We introduce FrontierChallenge, a cross-domain benchmark comprising 300 end-to-end scientific workflows. In this paper, we release and evaluate 97 of these tasks, spanning quantum chemistry, molecular dynamics, materials characterization, analytical chemistry, life science, and electrochemistry/environment. Each task provides fixed inputs and specifies a bundle of required scientific deliverables. We evaluate twelve frontier models with three agent scaffolds. Pass Rate measures the fraction of tasks satisfying the full-completion criterion, while Avg. Score captures partial progress. Each of the best-performing configurations completed only 20 of the 97 released tasks, yielding a Pass Rate of 20.6%. Partial progress translated especially poorly into complete delivery in analytical chemistry and electrochemistry/environment: Avg. Scores reached 87.6 and 94.9, but the highest Pass Rates were only 4% and 0%. Among non-passing Claude Code trajectories, 75.5% still ended with language claiming completion. These findings show that neither high partial scores nor confident claims of completion reliably indicate that a scientific task has been fully delivered, highlighting the need to evaluate end-to-end workflow execution and the completeness of scientific deliverables together.

AI.tldr: FrontierChallenge is a benchmark of realistic, end-to-end scientific workflows across multiple domains showing that current AI scientific agents rarely complete full tasks, even when they make strong partial progress and confidently claim success.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for scientific AI agents largely focus on final answers, single programs, or narrow domains, which does not reflect how real scientific work involves multi-step workflows and multiple deliverables. There is a need to understand how well current frontier models can handle complete, realistic scientific tasks from input to final deliverables, and whether standard metrics or the models’ own claims of success are reliable indicators of true task completion.
AI.method: The authors construct FrontierChallenge, a cross-domain benchmark of 300 end-to-end scientific workflows and publicly release 97 tasks. These cover domains such as quantum chemistry, molecular dynamics, materials characterization, analytical chemistry, life science, and electrochemistry/environment. Each task specifies fixed inputs and a bundle of required scientific outputs. Twelve frontier models are evaluated under three different agent scaffolds. Performance is measured using Pass Rate, the percentage of tasks where all deliverables meet a full-completion criterion, and Avg. Score, which captures partial progress toward task requirements. The authors also analyze model behavior, such as when agents fail the full criteria but still claim completion in natural language.
AI.result: No evaluated configuration performs strongly on full task completion: the top systems each fully complete only 20 out of 97 released tasks, corresponding to a Pass Rate of 20.6%. There is a large gap between partial and full success in several domains. In analytical chemistry and electrochemistry/environment, models achieve high Avg. Scores (87.6 and 94.9, respectively) but extremely low Pass Rates (4% and 0%), indicating that near-complete partial progress often does not translate into truly complete deliverables. For one strong system, Claude Code, 75.5% of non-passing trajectories still end with language asserting that the task is complete.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end scientific benchmarking reveals that current frontier models, even when scaffolded as agents, are poor at fully completing realistic, multi-artifact scientific workflows. High partial scores do not guarantee that all required deliverables are actually produced, and models frequently assert completion despite failing objective criteria. Therefore, reliable evaluation of scientific agents must consider both workflow execution and the strict completeness of required outputs, rather than relying on partial metrics or model self-reports.

title: Less can be More: Relieving RAG Bottlenecks via Evidence Frontloading and Pressure-Adaptive Budgeting
summary: Existing methods for improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) efficiency mainly optimize downstream LLM generation, such as context compression or serving optimization. However, RAG is an end-to-end system, and its bottleneck can shift between upstream reranking and downstream generation under different serving loads and reranking budgets.In this paper, we first empirically characterize this shifting-bottleneck behavior and show that upstream reranking can become the dominant bottleneck under high query rates or large reranking budgets. Reducing the reranking budget can relieve this bottleneck, but it may also drop supporting evidence and degrade recall. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{\textsf{PACE}} (\textbf{P}rioritized \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{C}overage of \textbf{E}vidence), a training-free framework that combines \textit{evidence frontloading} with \textit{pressure-adaptive budgeting}. \textsf{PACE} first reorders candidates by marginal evidence coverage, prioritizing documents that are query-relevant, complementary, and useful for forming multi-hop evidence chains. We show that this objective is monotone submodular, giving greedy selection a $(1-1/e)$ approximation guarantee. \textsf{PACE} then dynamically adjusts the reranking budget according to the relative pressure of the reranker and the LLM. Experiments on three multi-hop QA datasets and online serving simulations show that \textsf{PACE} improves evidence recall, reduces p95 latency under ranking-heavy workloads. More importantly, the two components together reveal that \textit{less can be more}: an evidence-dense top-ranked candidates enable higher final recall with fewer reranked documents.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how bottlenecks in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) shift between reranking and generation, and proposes PACE, a training-free, adaptive reranking framework that prioritizes evidence coverage and dynamically adjusts reranking budget to improve recall and latency.
AI.motivation: Most work on efficient RAG focuses on speeding up large language model (LLM) generation, e.g., via context compression or serving optimizations. However, RAG is an end-to-end system where both upstream retrieval/reranking and downstream generation contribute to latency. Under different query loads and reranking budgets, the bottleneck can move from LLM generation to the reranking stage, especially when many candidates must be reranked. Naively cutting the reranking budget to reduce latency harms evidence recall and answer quality. The paper aims to understand this shifting bottleneck and design a method that maintains or improves evidence recall while reducing end-to-end latency, particularly under heavy ranking workloads.
AI.method: The authors first empirically characterize how the performance bottleneck in RAG shifts between upstream reranking and downstream generation under varying query rates and reranking budgets. They then propose PACE (Prioritized Adaptive Coverage of Evidence), a training-free framework comprising two key components: (1) Evidence frontloading: candidates are reordered based on marginal evidence coverage, favoring documents that are highly relevant to the query, complementary to each other, and supportive of multi-hop reasoning chains. This objective is formulated as a monotone submodular function, allowing a greedy selection algorithm to achieve a (1−1/e) approximation ratio to the optimal coverage. (2) Pressure-adaptive budgeting: the reranking budget (number of documents reranked) is dynamically adjusted as a function of the relative computational pressure on the reranker vs. the LLM, effectively shifting load to the less congested component to reduce latency. The framework is evaluated on multi-hop QA benchmarks and via online serving simulations.
AI.result: On three multi-hop QA datasets and in simulated online serving environments, PACE increases evidence recall compared to baselines while lowering the 95th-percentile (p95) end-to-end latency, especially when the workload is ranking-heavy (i.e., reranking is the bottleneck). The experiments demonstrate that by prioritizing evidence-dense documents and adaptively controlling the reranking budget, the system can achieve higher final recall with fewer reranked documents than conventional approaches that use larger, static reranking budgets.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that RAG efficiency should be approached from an end-to-end perspective, recognizing that the bottleneck can shift between reranking and generation depending on load and configuration. PACE offers a training-free approach that uses submodular evidence frontloading and pressure-adaptive reranking budgets to both improve evidence recall and reduce tail latency. The key insight is that carefully selected, evidence-dense top-ranked documents can make "less be more": with a smaller but higher-quality reranked set, systems can achieve better overall recall and responsiveness than with larger, poorly prioritized reranking budgets.

title: Solving Robust POMDPs with Omega-regular Objectives via Partially Observable Stochastic Games
summary: Robust POMDPs (RPOMDPs) generalize classical POMDPs to the setting where exact transition probabilities are not known -- rather, they are only known to belong to some uncertainty set of values. In this work, we study the problem of solving RPOMDPs with general omega-regular objectives, which subsume a broad class of objectives such as reachability, safety, and linear temporal logic (LTL) objectives. We show that, for (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets, the problem of solving RPOMDPs under omega-regular objectives can be reduced to solving partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) under omega-regular objectives. Moreover, we show for the first time that reductions can be constructed in both directions, establishing the semantic equivalence between (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets and POSGs. This allows us to derive a range of new computational complexity results, including both upper and lower complexity bounds, on solving RPOMDPs with different omega-regular objectives. As a corollary, we also derive new computational complexity results for RMDPs.

AI.tldr: The paper studies robust partially observable Markov decision processes (RPOMDPs) with general omega-regular objectives, showing they are semantically equivalent to partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) under certain structural assumptions, and derives new complexity results from this equivalence.
AI.motivation: Classical POMDPs assume exact knowledge of transition probabilities, which is unrealistic in many applications. Robust POMDPs address this by allowing uncertainty sets over transitions, but their algorithmic and complexity properties are poorly understood, especially for rich goal specifications like omega-regular and LTL objectives. The authors are motivated to clarify how hard these problems are to solve and whether they can be related to better-studied models such as POSGs and RMDPs.
AI.method: The paper focuses on (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets. It constructs formal reductions from such RPOMDPs with omega-regular objectives to POSGs with omega-regular objectives, and crucially also gives reductions in the opposite direction, establishing a semantic equivalence between these two models. Using these bidirectional reductions, the authors transfer known complexity results between frameworks and systematically derive upper and lower bounds for a variety of omega-regular objectives.
AI.result: 1) A reduction is given from solving RPOMDPs with omega-regular objectives (under (s,a)-rectangular polytopic uncertainty) to solving POSGs with omega-regular objectives. 2) A converse reduction is also obtained, so that any POSG with omega-regular objectives can be represented as such an RPOMDP. 3) This bidirectional reduction proves semantic equivalence between the two models under the stated assumptions. 4) From this equivalence, the authors obtain new computational complexity classifications (both hardness and membership results) for solving RPOMDPs with different omega-regular objectives. 5) As a corollary, they extend these complexity insights to robust MDPs (RMDPs).
AI.conclusion: (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty and POSGs are semantically equivalent with respect to omega-regular objectives, via explicit reductions in both directions. This equivalence allows known algorithmic and complexity theory for POSGs to be leveraged to understand RPOMDPs, leading to new complexity bounds for robust planning with rich temporal objectives, including for the special case of RMDPs.

title: SelfGraphRAG: Bridging the Supervision Gap in Graph-Based RAG with Synthetic QA Generation
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures. Based on M.S. thesis work. Thesis available at https://www.proquest.com/docview/3350071346. Under review. Code available upon request from manas@umbc.edu
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves large language models by incorporating external knowledge without retraining, but existing methods often underuse the relational structure encoded in knowledge graphs. Graph-based RAG can capture entity relationships, yet supervised graph retrieval typically requires labeled question-answer data that may not be available for newly constructed graphs. We address this limitation with SelfGraphRAG, a framework that generates question-answer pairs directly from knowledge graph structure and uses them to train a query-conditioned graph retriever. The generated questions capture multi-hop paths and local neighborhoods, providing relational supervision without manual annotation. Experiments on multi-hop question answering and classification benchmarks show that SelfGraphRAG improves retrieval precision and downstream reasoning performance over embedding-based baselines. These results suggest that knowledge graph structure can provide useful supervision for training graph retrievers when labeled data are unavailable.

AI.tldr: SelfGraphRAG automatically generates QA pairs from a knowledge graph to train a graph retriever, improving multi-hop retrieval and reasoning without labeled data.
AI.motivation: RAG systems often fail to exploit the rich relational structure in knowledge graphs, and supervised graph retrieval usually needs labeled QA data, which is scarce or unavailable for new graphs. The paper aims to leverage the inherent structure of knowledge graphs to supervise retrieval without manual labels.
AI.method: Introduce SelfGraphRAG, which samples paths and local neighborhoods from a knowledge graph, then uses an LLM or templates to generate synthetic question-answer pairs that reflect multi-hop and relational patterns. These synthetic QA pairs are used to train a query-conditioned graph retriever that maps user questions to relevant graph substructures, enabling graph-based RAG without human annotations.
AI.result: On multi-hop QA and classification benchmarks, SelfGraphRAG achieves higher retrieval precision and better end-task performance compared with embedding-based retrieval baselines that do not use structural supervision. The method is shown to better capture multi-hop relations and relevant neighborhoods in the knowledge graph.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge graph structure can itself be used as a source of supervision for training graph retrievers. By generating QA pairs from graph paths and neighborhoods, SelfGraphRAG eliminates the need for labeled data while improving retrieval and downstream reasoning, demonstrating a scalable way to build effective graph-based RAG systems on new or evolving knowledge graphs.

title: CVE-SAI: Counterfactual Visual Evidence-Guided Selective Attribute Indexing for Risk-Controlled E-commerce Search
summary: Multimodal product models can complete missing e-commerce attributes, yet current methods still optimize attribute-answer accuracy without verifying visual support, conflate transient prediction with persistent index admission, and lack explicit risk control over factually incorrect or visually unsupported values. We address these gaps with Counterfactual Visual Evidence-Guided Selective Attribute Indexing (CVE-SAI), which first infers and freezes an ontology-constrained candidate from the primary image and attribute question without catalog text, and then decides whether that candidate should enter the index. Focus-Zone Distortion (FZD) constructs an attribute-specific visual-dependence proxy through a controlled counterfactual intervention, and Evidence-Guided Attention Redistribution (EGAR) uses the proxy to refine ontology-constrained scoring. The canonical candidate is frozen before evidence necessity, evidence retention, nuisance-transformation stability, and candidate-specific catalog-text conflict audits; catalog text can only tighten admission and cannot revise the candidate. Independent family-level calibration selects one policy with a simultaneous one-sided finite-sample bound under a 5% unsafe-admission budget. Experiments on five visual attributes derived from Amazon Berkeley Objects show that CVE-SAI improves attribute inference and evidence localization, achieves the highest certified admission coverage under the shared risk protocol, and yields the strongest controlled retrieval performance with the lowest unsafe auto-induced exposure among automatic-admission systems. Separating inference from admission therefore enables visually supported attribute completion to improve retrieval while limiting persistent index contamination.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new framework, CVE-SAI, to decide when automatically inferred visual product attributes are safe to store in an e-commerce index, focusing on visual evidence and risk control rather than just prediction accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal product models can fill in missing attributes (like color, pattern, material) from images and text, but they optimize only for attribute prediction accuracy. They often (1) fail to ensure that predictions are visually supported by the image; (2) mix up temporary predictions with permanent decisions about what goes into a searchable product index; and (3) lack explicit, quantifiable control over the risk of indexing incorrect or visually unsupported attributes, which can pollute search and recommendation systems.
AI.method: The authors introduce Counterfactual Visual Evidence-Guided Selective Attribute Indexing (CVE-SAI). First, the system predicts a single canonical attribute value from the main product image and the attribute query, under an ontology constraint, and freezes this candidate before reading catalog text. Then it decides whether this candidate should be admitted into the index. Focus-Zone Distortion (FZD) creates attribute-specific counterfactual image perturbations to approximate how much the prediction depends on visual evidence. Evidence-Guided Attention Redistribution (EGAR) uses this proxy to refine scores for candidate admission while respecting the attribute ontology. The frozen candidate then undergoes several audits: evidence necessity, evidence retention, robustness to nuisance transformations, and conflicts with catalog text (where text can only veto or further restrict, not change, the candidate value). Finally, at the level of attribute families, the method performs calibration to choose a single admission policy with a finite-sample one-sided bound that guarantees the risk of unsafe admissions stays within a 5% budget.
AI.result: On five visual attributes from the Amazon Berkeley Objects dataset, CVE-SAI simultaneously improves attribute inference accuracy and the localization of visual evidence. It attains the highest certified admission coverage (fraction of attributes it can safely admit) under a shared risk protocol, and delivers the best controlled retrieval performance while achieving the lowest rate of unsafe auto-induced exposure among systems that perform automatic admissions.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling attribute inference from the decision to admit an attribute into a persistent index, and enforcing that admissions are visually supported with controlled risk, leads to cleaner, safer attribute completion for e-commerce. CVE-SAI shows that selective, evidence-aware indexing can enhance retrieval quality while reducing long-term contamination of the product index by incorrect or visually unsupported attributes.

title: Belief Cascades Drive Persuasion in LLM Agent Networks
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly debate answers, coordinate research, simulate users, and mediate information flows, making agent-to-agent persuasion a basic but undermeasured capability. We introduce a controlled testbed for studying how goal-directed persuaders shift elicited stances in networks of LLM agents grounded in real-world ego-network topologies. Across four LLM backbones, five graphs, and 55 policy statements, we find that persuasion dynamics depend on the interaction between topology, competition, topic, and model prior. Additionally, we show that direct exposure reliably predicts next-round stance change in competing runs, and peer relays carry smaller but measurable influence, showing that agents not assigned to persuade can still transmit persuasive force. Finally, analyzing post text alone misses important movement: planned strategies are only partly realized in executed messages, action choices can diverge from message content, and persuadees rarely state the stance shifts detected by probes. These results argue for evaluating multi-agent persuasion as a trajectory- and exposure-level process, using belief probes, exposure provenance, and action logs to identify who influenced whom and whether visible language reflects underlying stance movement.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a testbed to measure how persuasive LLM agents influence each other’s stances within multi-agent systems, revealing that persuasion depends on network structure, competition, topic, and model priors, and that visible messages only partially reveal underlying belief changes.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly used for debate, coordination, and mediation, where agents must persuade each other, yet this persuasion capability is poorly understood and undermeasured. Existing work tends to look at single-model persuasion or surface text, missing the complex dynamics of influence propagation in networks of agents. The authors aim to systematically characterize how LLM agents’ stances shift due to interaction, what roles network topology and competition play, and how well observable language reflects deeper belief movement.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled multi-agent testbed based on real-world ego-network topologies, populating nodes with LLM agents instantiated from four different backbone models. They define 55 policy statements to elicit initial stances from agents and then assign some agents goal-directed persuasion roles while others act as persuadees or intermediaries. They run experiments across five network graphs and conditions with and without competing persuaders. Throughout multi-round interactions, they log agents’ messages, actions, and exposure histories, and use belief probes to measure stance changes over time. They then analyze how direct versus relayed exposure, topology, competition, topic, and model priors shape stance shifts, and compare planned strategies to actually executed language and actions.
AI.result: Persuasion effects vary substantially across combinations of network topology, competitive settings, topics, and base LLM models. Direct exposure to a persuader is a strong predictor of next-round stance change in competitive scenarios, while peer relays—messages passed by non-persuader agents—exert smaller but still detectable influence, evidencing indirect propagation of persuasive force. The study also finds notable discrepancies between agents’ stated plans, their realized messages, their action choices, and the belief shifts detected via probes: persuasive strategies are only partly implemented in text, actions can deviate from message content, and persuadees rarely explicitly acknowledge their stance changes. These findings show that much persuasion occurs beneath the surface of overt language in the logs.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent LLM persuasion should be evaluated as a dynamic, trajectory-level process rather than only through snapshot analysis of final answers or surface text. Proper measurement requires tracking the provenance of exposures, using belief probes to quantify underlying stance movement, and analyzing action logs to map who influenced whom and how. The work underscores that network structure, competition, topic, and model priors jointly govern persuasion dynamics, and that non-persuasive agents can still relay and amplify influence. Overall, the paper argues for richer, exposure-aware evaluation frameworks to understand and eventually control persuasion in multi-agent LLM systems.

title: Retrieve, Match, Escalate: Accurate and Scalable Product Linking with VLM-Distilled Cross-Encoders and Agentic VLMs
summary: Product linking, the entity-resolution task of mapping merchant product records to canonical catalog products, consolidates fragmented listings so downstream search, recommendation, and advertising see one clean entry per product. At marketplace scale, billions of noisy, multi-category records must be resolved against tens of millions of canonical products, where scoring every candidate with a single model is either too weak for the hard cases or too costly for the easy ones. We present a production retrieve-then-match cascade that spends computation in proportion to difficulty: retrieval surfaces plausible matches, a lightweight text cross-encoder auto-resolves the high-confidence majority, and an agentic multimodal vision-language model settles the ambiguous remainder by inspecting product images and issuing web searches for evidence that is in neither record. The cross-encoder is distilled from millions of dual-VLM-consensus labels, retiring human annotation from the training set, and is calibrated to auto-accept links at a 98% precision bar validated against a smaller operator-certified audit. The agent is a self-hosted open-weight model that reaches a closed frontier VLM's precision at a four-point recall cost (88% versus 92%) for roughly one-seventh the per-pair cost, with no fine-tuning. Per-pair cost spans nearly five orders of magnitude from the cheap cross-encoder to the frontier VLM, so escalating only the hard tail to the agent raises end-to-end link coverage from the cheap stage's 68% to 77%.

AI.tldr: A large-scale e-commerce system links noisy merchant product listings to a clean product catalog using a multi-stage, cost-aware pipeline that combines retrieval, a distilled cross-encoder, and an agentic multimodal VLM, improving coverage while controlling compute cost.
AI.motivation: At marketplace scale, search and recommendation depend on having a single clean record per product, but merchant listings are fragmented, noisy, and span billions of records across many categories. Existing single-model entity-resolution approaches are either too weak to handle difficult cases or too computationally expensive to run on all candidate pairs. There is a need for a scalable, high-precision, cost-efficient system that can resolve most links automatically and reserve heavy computation for only the hardest cases, without relying heavily on human annotation.
AI.method: The paper proposes a retrieve-then-match cascade for product linking. First, a retrieval stage surfaces plausible catalog candidates for each merchant listing. Second, a lightweight text-only cross-encoder scores pairs and automatically accepts high-confidence links; this cross-encoder is trained via knowledge distillation from millions of labels formed by the consensus of dual vision-language models (VLMs), removing the need for human labels at scale. Third, an agentic multimodal VLM handles the remaining ambiguous pairs by examining both product images and performing web search to gather external evidence not present in the product records. The cross-encoder is calibrated to a 98% precision threshold validated by a smaller, operator-verified audit. The agent uses an open-weight model deployed in-house and is run only on the hard tail of cases.
AI.result: The distilled cross-encoder achieves high precision and is able to auto-resolve the majority of product links at low cost, covering about 68% of all pairs under a 98% precision constraint. The agentic multimodal VLM, without fine-tuning, attains a precision comparable to a strong closed-source frontier VLM but at a modest loss in recall (88% vs. 92%), while reducing per-pair inference cost by approximately a factor of seven. Across the pipeline, model costs differ by nearly five orders of magnitude between the cheap cross-encoder and the expensive frontier VLM. By escalating only the ambiguous tail to the multimodal agent instead of applying heavy models everywhere, overall end-to-end link coverage increases from 68% to 77% without sacrificing precision and with manageable compute expenditure.
AI.conclusion: A cascaded, difficulty-aware approach to product linking significantly improves catalog coverage while tightly controlling computational cost. Distilling a text cross-encoder from dual-VLM consensus removes dependence on large-scale human annotation and enables a very cheap, high-precision auto-resolution stage. Complementing this with an on-demand, open-weight multimodal agent that can query external evidence matches the precision of frontier VLMs at much lower cost, with only a small recall penalty. This design demonstrates that carefully orchestrated retrieval, distillation, and agentic multimodal reasoning can scale entity resolution to marketplace-sized catalogs efficiently and accurately.

title: The Changing Geometry of Grammar: Dimensionality and Neighborhood Reorganization across Transformer Layers
summary: Transformer representations describe trajectories through high-dimensional vector spaces, which are shaped dynamically as tokens incorporate relational context across layers. Such data tend to concentrate on lower-dimensional sub-manifolds, a form of compression quantified by the Intrinsic Dimensionality (ID), the minimum number of independent variables needed to represent them without significant information loss. In this work, we ask whether the grammatical role of tokens, as marked by their part-of-speech (PoS) tag, shapes the local geometry of this manifold. To this end: (1) We investigate the layer-wise evolution of ID, finding that closed-class items expand earlier and collapse sooner than open-class ones; (2) We show its expansion and contraction to be explained by changes in the neighborhood structure, and hence in the relations between words within a sentence; (3) We compare encoders (ModernBERT, bigbird-roberta-large) and decoders (gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-3B), finding that the two families evolve differently across layers, consistently with how each integrates context;(4) We show that geometric features alone recover a token's grammatical role, and use them to interpret how the semantic content of each PoS evolves across layers in a downstream classification task.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the intrinsic dimensionality and geometry of transformer hidden states vary across layers and parts of speech, and how these geometric patterns relate to grammatical role and model architecture.
AI.motivation: Transformer representations live in high-dimensional spaces but often lie on lower-dimensional manifolds, which can be characterized by intrinsic dimensionality (ID). While prior work examines global ID or layer-wise compression, it is less clear how local geometry varies by linguistic function (e.g., parts of speech) and across encoder vs. decoder architectures. Understanding this connection can reveal how models encode grammar and context and may aid interpretability and downstream tasks.
AI.method: The authors estimate intrinsic dimensionality of token embeddings across layers of several transformer models, conditioned on part-of-speech tags. They track how ID evolves layer-wise for different PoS categories (closed vs. open class), analyze changes in neighborhood structure to explain ID expansion/contraction, compare encoder models (ModernBERT, bigbird-roberta-large) against decoder models (gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-3B), and train classifiers based purely on geometric features of token representations to recover PoS and study semantic evolution in downstream classification.
AI.result: They find that closed-class tokens (e.g., function words) show earlier increases and earlier decreases in intrinsic dimensionality than open-class tokens (e.g., content words), indicating distinct geometric dynamics. ID changes are linked to shifts in nearest-neighbor structure, reflecting evolving inter-word relations within sentences. Encoders and decoders exhibit different layer-wise geometric trajectories consistent with their different ways of integrating context. Moreover, grammatical roles can be reliably predicted from geometric features alone, which then enables an analysis of how the semantic content associated with each PoS evolves through the network.
AI.conclusion: Local manifold geometry in transformer models is systematically shaped by tokens' grammatical roles. Closed- and open-class items follow different compression dynamics, and encoder vs. decoder architectures organize token geometry differently across layers. Purely geometric cues suffice to recover PoS and to trace semantic changes across layers, suggesting that intrinsic dimensionality and neighborhood structure provide a useful lens on how transformers encode grammar and meaning.

title: LifePlanner: Evaluating LLM Agents for Geo-spatial Planning with Social Media Data
summary: Geo-spatial planning, like trip design, is a realistic testbed for LLM agents because it requires grounded tool use, noisy evidence retrieval, and multi-constraint reasoning. Most benchmarks, however, only provide clean geospatial data and tools, missing the open-ended social signals that people use in daily planning. We introduce LifePlanner, a benchmark that enriches map data with large-scale local social media posts and provides access through an MCP toolset. LifePlanner provides an evaluation suite spanning four task categories and three difficulty levels. Experiments show frontier LLMs perform well on simple retrieval but degrade sharply on complex planning, with the Pass Rate dropping to 40.2%. Results show that failures mainly stem from incomplete evidence acquisition from such a large multimodal database, imprecise tool use, and weak constraint integration rather than model size or reasoning length, suggesting that future progress requires effective grounded planning instead of scaling alone.

AI.tldr: The paper presents LifePlanner, a benchmark for testing LLM agents on realistic geo-spatial planning using noisy social signals and tools, revealing that current models struggle with complex, constraint-heavy planning.
AI.motivation: Existing geospatial planning benchmarks are too clean and lack the messy, open-ended social signals (like local social media) that people rely on in real-world trip and route planning, so they fail to stress-test LLM agents’ grounded tool use and multi-constraint reasoning.
AI.method: The authors build LifePlanner, which enriches map data with large-scale local social media posts and exposes this multimodal information via an MCP toolset. They design an evaluation suite with four task types and three difficulty levels, then systematically test frontier LLMs on retrieval and planning tasks that require using tools over noisy evidence and satisfying multiple constraints.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs achieve strong performance on simple retrieval tasks but their accuracy drops significantly on complex planning scenarios, with Pass Rate falling to 40.2%. Error analysis shows most failures are due to incomplete evidence gathering from the large multimodal database, inaccurate or inefficient tool usage, and poor integration of multiple constraints.
AI.conclusion: Scaling model size or increasing reasoning length alone is insufficient for robust geo-spatial planning. Progress will require better methods for grounded planning: more reliable tool use, more complete and targeted evidence acquisition from noisy, large-scale data, and stronger mechanisms for enforcing and integrating multiple constraints in open-ended tasks.

title: BanglaMamba: Exploring State Space Models for Bangla Fake News Detection
summary: Fake news detection has become an important Natural Language Processing (NLP) task due to the rapid spread of misinformation through online news platforms and social media. While transformer-based models such as BanglaBERT achieve strong performance for Bangla text classification, their quadratic computational complexity makes them less suitable for long-document processing in resource-constrained environments. This paper investigates Mamba-based State Space Models (SSMs) as an efficient alternative for Bangla fake news detection. We propose BanglaMamba and compare it with pre-trained BanglaBERT and a similarly configured BERT model trained from scratch. Experimental results show that BanglaBERT achieves the highest Macro-F1 score (0.9260), while BanglaMamba (0.9029) achieves performance comparable to the from-scratch CustomBERT (0.9057) despite using a different architecture. Meanwhile, BanglaMamba achieves approximately $2.2\times$ higher inference throughput and 49% lower inference peak GPU memory usage than the BERT-based models. Cross-dataset evaluation shows that BanglaBERT generalizes better to an external dataset, highlighting the importance of large-scale pretraining. These findings demonstrate that Mamba-based SSMs can provide a competitive and computationally efficient alternative to Transformer-based architectures for Bangla fake news detection, particularly in resource-constrained settings.

AI.tldr: The paper compares a new BanglaMamba state space model with BanglaBERT and a custom BERT for Bangla fake news detection, finding that BanglaMamba is nearly as accurate but far more efficient in computation and memory, making it attractive for resource-constrained settings.
AI.motivation: Fake news spreads rapidly on online platforms, and Bangla, as a low-resource language, needs effective and efficient automatic fake news detection. Standard transformer-based models like BanglaBERT are accurate but computationally expensive, especially for long documents and on limited hardware. The authors want to explore whether Mamba-based state space models can maintain strong accuracy while significantly reducing computational cost for Bangla fake news detection.
AI.method: The authors design BanglaMamba, a Mamba-based state space model tailored for Bangla text classification, and compare it experimentally against two transformer baselines: a pre-trained BanglaBERT and a CustomBERT model trained from scratch with a similar configuration. They evaluate all models on Bangla fake news detection using Macro-F1 as the main accuracy metric and measure inference throughput and peak GPU memory usage. They also perform cross-dataset evaluation to test generalization to an external dataset.
AI.result: BanglaBERT achieves the best Macro-F1 score of 0.9260. BanglaMamba attains a Macro-F1 of 0.9029, which is close to the from-scratch CustomBERT’s 0.9057, despite using a different architecture. In terms of efficiency, BanglaMamba delivers roughly 2.2× higher inference throughput and uses 49% less peak GPU memory compared to the BERT-based models. Cross-dataset experiments reveal that BanglaBERT generalizes better to an external dataset, suggesting benefits from large-scale pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Mamba-based state space models like BanglaMamba can serve as a competitive, computationally efficient alternative to transformer-based architectures for Bangla fake news detection, especially where computational resources are limited. However, large-scale pretraining, as in BanglaBERT, still provides superior accuracy and cross-dataset generalization. The work indicates a trade-off between peak performance and efficiency, with BanglaMamba offering a strong balance for resource-constrained environments.

title: SimVerity: When Does Simulated Agent Success Survive Physical Deployment?
comment: Submitted to the Main Technical Track of AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-27); currently under review
summary: Simulated evaluation is widely used to benchmark AI agents, yet how much evidence a simulated pass provides about physical deployment has not been systematically quantified. We present SimVerity, a verdict-transfer assurance framework: it replays matched scenarios on target smart home deployments and cross-validates agent execution against independently qualified physical witnesses. Our evaluation highlights that deployment success is a real-world process, not a static property in simulation: completion, reported state, observable effect, and settled outcome diverged within the same execution. Although an advanced simulator cleared all 240 light trials, a camera caught 42 sub-second failures invisible to settled-state checks. False clearance was predictable: a risk profile learned from measured trials and locked before evaluation predicted failures on a path it never physically measured, beating a property-blind baseline in all eleven held-out sessions across two cohorts. Agent auditability was also measurable: switching one agent loop's model-client/serving configuration raised its scenario-matching share from 52-88% to 100%. Finally, a second qualified simulator added no independent cross-check: it never disagreed on any overlapping case, and only physical measurement exposed their shared blind spots. SimVerity turns verdict transfer into an explicit decision: clear, abstain, or escalate before deployment.

AI.tldr: SimVerity is a framework to empirically measure how well simulated evaluation of AI agents transfers to real-world smart home deployments, revealing gaps between simulation passes and physical behavior.
AI.motivation: AI agents are heavily evaluated in simulators, but it is unclear how reliably a pass in simulation predicts safe and correct behavior after physical deployment, especially in complex environments like smart homes. There is a need for a systematic way to quantify this "verdict transfer" and reveal hidden failure modes that simulators may miss.
AI.method: The authors introduce SimVerity, a verdict-transfer assurance framework that replays matched scenarios from simulation on real smart home hardware. It cross-validates agent behavior using independently qualified physical witnesses such as cameras and sensors. They analyze multiple outcome facets—task completion, agent-reported state, observable physical effect, and settled outcome—and compare an advanced simulator, a second simulator, and physical measurements. They also learn a risk profile from physically measured trials, lock it before evaluation, and test whether it predicts failures in unmeasured paths. Finally, they study how changes in agent configuration affect the ability to match scenarios across sim and reality.
AI.result: The study finds that deployment success is dynamic and multifaceted: the four outcome facets often diverge even within a single execution. While a sophisticated simulator reported 100% success on 240 light-control trials, high-speed camera data revealed 42 brief failures that were invisible to simple, final-state checks. These false clearances were systematically predictable: the learned risk profile successfully predicted failures on unmeasured paths and outperformed a property-blind baseline in all eleven held-out sessions across two user cohorts. Adjusting an agent loop’s model-client/serving configuration improved scenario-matching between sim and physical runs from 52–88% up to 100%. Adding a second qualified simulator did not improve assurance: it never disagreed with the first on overlapping cases, and only physical measurement exposed blind spots shared by both simulators.
AI.conclusion: SimVerity reframes verdict transfer from simulation to deployment as an explicit, evidence-based decision process with options to clear, abstain, or escalate before real-world deployment. The results show that simulation alone can systematically miss important failure modes and that independent physical witnesses and learned risk profiles are necessary to obtain reliable assurance. Multiple simulators do not automatically provide independent validation; physical measurement remains critical for uncovering shared blind spots and for quantifying how much confidence a simulated pass should warrant in real-world use.

title: From Memorization to Absorption: Mixed-Policy RL for Continual Knowledge Injection
summary: Continual knowledge injection is essential for keeping large language models up-to-date in a fast-evolving world. Existing methods rely on supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which memorizes injected facts in their training format but fails to generalize across paraphrasing, document combinations, and reasoning. To address this, we propose Golden-GRPO Injection (GRIN), a three-stage self-learning framework for continual knowledge injection. Golden-GRPO is a mixed-policy reinforcement learning algorithm designed specifically for knowledge injection, which injects a golden answer to provide learning signal even when on-policy rollouts fail on novel facts. We further introduce Blank and Counter, two document-level benchmarks targeting novel acquisition and counterfactual overwrite respectively, each evaluating single-fact recall, multi-source retrieval, and inferential reasoning. Our experiments establish a clear empirical claim: mixed-policy reinforcement learning enables knowledge absorption beyond what supervised fine-tuning can achieve. GRIN substantially outperforms SFT and mixed-policy RL baselines on the harder question types while matching them on basic fact recall.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GRIN, a reinforcement-learning-based framework (Golden-GRPO Injection) for continually injecting new knowledge into large language models, outperforming standard supervised fine-tuning in generalization and reasoning over newly injected facts.
AI.motivation: Large language models quickly become outdated as real-world facts change or new information appears. Existing continual knowledge injection methods mainly use supervised fine-tuning, which teaches models to memorize specific training examples but often fails to generalize to paraphrased questions, combined documents, or reasoning tasks involving the new facts. There is a need for a method that can not only store new factual knowledge but also flexibly use it across varied query styles and reasoning demands.
AI.method: The authors propose Golden-GRPO Injection (GRIN), a three-stage self-learning framework built atop Golden-GRPO, a mixed-policy reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm tailored for knowledge injection. Golden-GRPO combines on-policy rollouts with a ‘golden answer’ policy: even when the model fails to answer questions involving novel facts during on-policy exploration, the golden answers are injected to provide a learning signal. GRIN uses this RL setup to repeatedly interact with knowledge-injection tasks and refine the model’s ability to recall and reason over newly added facts, going beyond simple supervised fine-tuning on static question–answer pairs.
AI.result: The authors create two document-level benchmarks, Blank (for novel knowledge acquisition) and Counter (for counterfactual overwrite), each probing three capabilities: single-fact recall, multi-source retrieval, and inferential reasoning over the injected knowledge. Across these benchmarks, GRIN consistently surpasses supervised fine-tuning and other mixed-policy RL baselines on more challenging tasks, particularly those involving multi-source retrieval and reasoning, while achieving comparable performance on basic fact recall.
AI.conclusion: Mixed-policy reinforcement learning with explicit golden-answer guidance enables language models to absorb and use new knowledge more effectively than standard supervised fine-tuning. GRIN maintains strong performance on straightforward fact recall while notably improving generalization to paraphrased queries, document combinations, and reasoning tasks, thus offering a more robust approach to continual knowledge injection for large language models.

title: Auto-Policy, not Auto-Skill: Compiled Agent Skills for the Physical World
comment: Presented at the 1st Workshop on Agent Skills (Agent Skills '26), ACM CAIS 2026, San Jose, May 26, 2026
summary: Self-evolving Skill harnesses (AutoSkills, Hermes Agent) generate more advisory orchestration automatically; their reported gains are efficiency, not safety. This misses the actual gap: a Skill describes how an agent should behave; a Policy decides which behavior is allowed to become an action. Today's format covers the first with markdown and scripts; the second is left to the model. Generating more Skills scales the gap, not the safety, especially when a wrong invocation can unlock a door or move money. Two adjacent attacks are documented: malicious skills compromising cloud software, and jailbroken LLM-controlled robots causing physical harm. Their intersection, malicious agent skills causing physical harm, follows directly but has not been reported. We name this class Borrowed Authority: Skills format gives the receiving agent no typed way to reject an inter-agent permission claim, so a malicious or misused Skill can drive actuation by attaching one. We propose Edge Skillguard, a typed authority layer that lives inside the Skill artifact rather than between tools as workflow engines do, with guards over world state and sensor evidence. On a live edge control-plane testbed, the guards reject 60/60 borrowed-authority requests across five attack variants without blocking benign requests, and the result holds at 5x scale and across hosts over a Tailscale mesh. These results suggest that high-risk Skills should co-package typed invocation policy with procedural knowledge, so that physical actions depend on machine-checkable evidence rather than peer-agent claims.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a safety gap in self-evolving AI agent skill systems and proposes a typed authority layer, Edge Skillguard, that embeds invocation policy directly in skills to block malicious or misused actions while preserving benign behavior.
AI.motivation: Current self-evolving skill systems for agents (e.g., AutoSkills, Hermes Agent) improve efficiency by automatically generating more skills, but they do not address safety. Skills encode how an agent should act, while policies should determine which actions are permitted. At present, skill formats focus on behavior specification and leave permission decisions to models, which becomes dangerous when actions can control critical systems (doors, money, robots). Documented attacks show malicious skills compromising software and jailbroken LLM-robots causing harm. However, the combined risk—malicious agent skills causing physical harm—remains unaddressed. The authors define this as a class of attacks called Borrowed Authority, where an agent has no structured way to reject permission claims carried inside skills.
AI.method: The authors define the Borrowed Authority threat model, analyzing how current skill formats let one agent 'borrow' another’s authority by embedding permission claims. They design Edge Skillguard, a typed authority and policy layer embedded directly inside skill artifacts. This layer uses type-checked guards over world state and sensor evidence to validate or reject action requests. They then implement Edge Skillguard on a live edge control-plane testbed and evaluate it against multiple attack variants, scaling the number of skills and distributing them across machines connected by a Tailscale mesh network.
AI.result: On the testbed, Edge Skillguard successfully rejects all 60 out of 60 Borrowed Authority attack attempts across five different attack variants, while not blocking legitimate benign requests. This performance is maintained when the system is scaled 5x in size and when skills and agents are distributed across hosts connected via a Tailscale mesh, indicating robustness at scale and in realistic distributed environments.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that embedding a typed invocation-policy layer inside skill artifacts (Edge Skillguard) can effectively close the Borrowed Authority gap in agent skill systems. High-risk skills should be packaged with both procedural know-how and machine-checkable authority constraints, so that executing physical actions requires verifiable world-state or sensor evidence, not just claims from other agents. This design improves safety without sacrificing benign functionality and offers a path toward safer deployment of self-evolving skill ecosystems, especially in settings with physical actuation or financial control.

title: Groundhog Bit-Flip Attack: Seeding Infinite Generation Loops in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs through Bit Flips
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable scalable and efficient large language models (LLMs) by selectively activating expert sub-networks through a routing mechanism. However, this adaptive design introduces a new attack surface: specific experts become disproportionately correlated with certain tokens (e.g., end-of-sequence), allowing adversaries to manipulate model behavior via lightweight perturbations. In this work, we present \textbf{Groundhog Bit-Flip Attack (GBFA)}, the first bit-flip-based \textit{ Denial-of-Wallet availability attack} against MoE-based LLMs. By identifying and flipping routing-layer bits associated with related expert activations, we demonstrate that GBFA substantially extends the decoding token usage across three different LLM modes: conversational, reasoning, and agentic tasks, while largely preserving semantic fidelity. Across four main real-world MoE-based LLMs, manually deactivating on average fewer than \textbf{4 experts} drives average output inflation to $\mathbf{5912\%}$, with the majority of test samples reaching max tokens. These results reveal a robustness vulnerability of MoE architectures to bit flip, and highlight the potential of GBFA as an availability attack against LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Groundhog Bit-Flip Attack (GBFA), a bit-flip-based denial-of-availability attack on Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs that dramatically inflates output length by corrupting routing bits, while mostly preserving semantics.
AI.motivation: Mixture-of-Experts LLMs improve scalability and efficiency by activating only a subset of experts per token, but this routing mechanism may create new vulnerabilities. Certain experts correlate strongly with specific tokens (like end-of-sequence), meaning that small perturbations to routing could systematically bias generation behavior. There is a lack of work on how low-level hardware faults or adversarial bit flips could exploit this structure to cause denial-of-service-like effects without obviously harming model semantics.
AI.method: The authors analyze routing layers in MoE LLMs to find bits whose flipping changes the activation of experts that are strongly associated with key tokens. They design Groundhog Bit-Flip Attack (GBFA), which identifies routing-layer parameters whose modification (bit flips) will disrupt normal expert selection. They then flip bits to effectively deactivate or misroute a small number of experts. Experiments are conducted across several real-world MoE-based LLMs and three usage modes—conversational, reasoning, and agentic—to quantify how these changes affect decoding token usage and output semantics.
AI.result: With GBFA, manually deactivating on average fewer than four experts causes a huge inflation in generated token counts—on the order of 5912% on average—across four MoE LLMs, often pushing outputs to the maximum token limit. Despite this large increase in length, the semantic content of the outputs remains largely intact, indicating that the attack primarily affects termination and efficiency rather than correctness of responses. This demonstrates that small, targeted bit flips in routing layers can strongly impact resource consumption and availability of MoE LLM services.
AI.conclusion: MoE architectures possess a specific robustness weakness: their routing layers are highly sensitive to targeted bit flips, which can be exploited to create efficient denial-of-availability attacks that massively increase generation length without obviously corrupting semantics. The proposed GBFA attack exemplifies this vulnerability and underscores the need for more robust routing designs, monitoring, and defenses against low-level faults or adversarial manipulations in MoE-based LLMs.

title: PhysElite: How Far Are LLMs from Solving Olympiad-Level Physics Problems?
summary: Understanding how (multimodal) large language models perform on physics problems requires benchmarks that reflect the difficulty and breadth of expert-level physical reasoning. Existing physics benchmarks remain limited in the following two important ways: (1) short of high-difficulty datasets, and (2) lack of comprehensive coverage of visual forms, knowledge points, and step-by-step solution processes. As a result, model performance on current datasets may not be fully representative of their ability to solve complex physics problems. To address these issues, we present PhysElite, a large-scale bilingual multimodal benchmark for Olympiad-level physics reasoning. PhysElite contains 11,586 Olympiad-tier problems. For each problem, we provide corresponding visual diagrams, step-by-step bilingual Chinese-English solution derivations, and the final answer. We benchmark 18 open-source and closed-source MLLMs, and find that even the strongest model reaches only 33.7% answer accuracy. We additionally conduct step-level process evaluation to diagnose where models fail in the reasoning chain. Our datasets are released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/physelite/PhysElite.

AI.tldr: PhysElite is a large, Olympiad-level, bilingual multimodal benchmark to rigorously test physics reasoning of multimodal large language models.
AI.motivation: Existing physics benchmarks for multimodal large language models are too easy and narrow: they lack truly challenging Olympiad-level questions, diverse visual formats, broad coverage of physics knowledge, and detailed step-by-step solutions, so current model scores do not reflect real expert-level reasoning ability.
AI.method: The authors construct PhysElite, a dataset of 11,586 high-difficulty physics Olympiad problems, each paired with visual diagrams, bilingual (Chinese-English) step-by-step derivations, and final answers. They then evaluate 18 open- and closed-source multimodal large language models on this benchmark, measuring both final answer accuracy and step-wise reasoning performance to locate where reasoning chains break down.
AI.result: On PhysElite, even the strongest evaluated multimodal large language model achieves only 33.7% answer accuracy, and step-level analysis shows systematic failures at multiple stages of the reasoning process, revealing significant remaining gaps in complex physics reasoning.
AI.conclusion: PhysElite exposes that current multimodal large language models are far from expert-level performance on challenging, visually rich physics problems, and provides a comprehensive, high-difficulty benchmark and process-based evaluation framework to drive future progress in physics reasoning capabilities.

title: Routed Graph Handoff: Adaptive Format Selection for Multi-Agent LLM Delegation
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems coordinate through natural-language messages that consume 40--60\% of their token budget. Replacing these with structured graphs reduces cost but fails on tasks requiring adaptive reasoning. We propose \textbf{Routed Graph Handoff}, where a lightweight LLM router (155 tokens, 0.15\% overhead) selects between a typed dependency graph and natural language for each delegation. On four benchmarks (1,050+ trajectories), the routed system matches or exceeds NL-only on every task: \textbf{+12.7\,pp} on $τ$-retail at 3.2$\times$ compression ($p{<}0.01$), \textbf{+8.7\,pp} on BrowseComp at 2.2$\times$ compression ($p{<}0.05$), and parity on BFCL and AppWorld. Without the router, graph-only delegation regresses 14.6\,pp on AppWorld; the router eliminates this at near-zero cost. A graph-aware executor prompt is required: the same schema without interpretation guidance yields no gain. An oracle analysis reveals 8.6\,pp of additional headroom, motivating execution-time adaptive routing as future work.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Routed Graph Handoff, a system where a lightweight LLM router dynamically chooses between structured graphs and natural-language messages for multi-agent LLM coordination, achieving similar or better performance than natural language alone while significantly reducing token costs.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems rely heavily on natural-language messages for coordination, which consume 40–60% of the total token budget and thus are expensive and inefficient. Structured graph representations can reduce token usage but perform poorly on tasks requiring flexible, adaptive reasoning. There is a need for a method that maintains the reasoning benefits of natural language while leveraging the efficiency of structured graphs, and that can adaptively choose the best representation per interaction.
AI.method: The authors propose Routed Graph Handoff, which introduces a lightweight LLM-based router that decides, for each delegation between agents, whether to use a typed dependency graph or natural-language communication. The router uses about 155 tokens per decision, corresponding to only 0.15% overhead, and is paired with a graph-aware executor prompt that explicitly instructs the model on how to interpret the structured schema. The system is evaluated on four benchmarks (τ-retail, BrowseComp, BFCL, and AppWorld) with over 1,050 trajectories, and compared to natural-language-only and graph-only delegation baselines. Ablation includes removing the router and removing the graph interpretation guidance. An oracle analysis estimates remaining performance headroom from ideal routing decisions.
AI.result: Across the four benchmarks, the routed system matches or exceeds the performance of a natural-language-only baseline while significantly compressing communication. It improves performance by 12.7 percentage points on τ-retail with a 3.2× reduction in token usage (statistically significant at p<0.01), and by 8.7 percentage points on BrowseComp with 2.2× compression (p<0.05), while achieving parity with NL-only on BFCL and AppWorld. A graph-only delegation baseline without routing performs 14.6 percentage points worse on AppWorld, but the routed approach removes this regression with almost no additional token cost. Without a graph-aware executor prompt (i.e., using the same schema but no interpretation guidance), the system shows no performance gains. Oracle analysis suggests there is an additional 8.6 percentage points of potential improvement with better, execution-time adaptive routing.
AI.conclusion: Routed Graph Handoff enables multi-agent LLM systems to dynamically choose between structured graphs and natural-language messages, preserving or improving task performance while greatly reducing token costs. The router’s overhead is negligible relative to the savings, and it prevents performance degradation seen in naive graph-only communication. Effective use of structured graphs requires explicit interpretive prompting; simply providing a schema is insufficient. The remaining headroom identified by oracle analysis indicates that further gains are possible, particularly through more sophisticated, execution-time adaptive routing strategies.

title: Towards Reliable, Generalizable, and Specific In-Context Knowledge Editing via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
comment: Our work proposes a multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithm that optimizes prompt construction for reliable, generalizable, and specific in-context knowledge-editing
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful but limited by static parametric knowledge that becomes outdated once pretraining ends. Knowledge editing addresses this problem by updating model behavior on target facts without full retraining. In particular, in-context knowledge editing has gained attention because it is training-free and readily applicable to black-box LLMs. Recent reinforcement learning (RL)-based approaches improve over fixed retrieval strategies by adapting prompt construction to the quantity-quality trade-off. Despite initial success, they fail to model the prompt as a structured entity under the distinct and often competing objectives of reliability, generality, and specificity. Previous methods largely optimize a single objective and make decisions over only part of the prompt construction process, thereby overlooking both the balance of different objectives and the global organization of demonstrations. We propose Multi-Objective In-context Knowledge Editing (MO-IKE), a multi-objective RL algorithm that formulates prompt construction for in-context knowledge editing as a Constrained Markov Decision Process. MO-IKE trains a dynamic retriever to optimize competing objectives in knowledge editing, enabling more balanced and globally coherent prompt construction. On Llama-3.2, MO-IKE improves edit success (reliability) from 85.0% to 92.0%, paraphrase consistency (generality) from 77% to 79%, while increasing retention rate (specificity) by 23.0% compared to prior RL-based methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MO-IKE, a multi-objective RL-based method to construct in-context prompts for knowledge editing in LLMs, jointly optimizing reliability, generality, and specificity to achieve better editing performance and knowledge retention.
AI.motivation: LLMs store knowledge in parameters that quickly become outdated, and retraining is expensive. Knowledge editing offers targeted updates, with in-context methods being especially attractive for black-box models. However, existing RL-based prompt construction methods optimize only a single objective (e.g., edit success) and treat the prompt partially and myopically, ignoring the structured nature of prompts and the inherent trade-offs between reliability (successful edits), generality (robustness to paraphrases), and specificity (retaining unrelated knowledge).
AI.method: The authors formulate in-context prompt construction for knowledge editing as a Constrained Markov Decision Process and introduce MO-IKE, a multi-objective RL algorithm. MO-IKE learns a dynamic retriever that sequentially selects and organizes demonstrations in the prompt while explicitly optimizing multiple, potentially competing objectives. It uses constraints to balance reliability, generality, and specificity, leading to globally coherent prompt design rather than local, single-objective improvements.
AI.result: On Llama-3.2, MO-IKE improves edit success (reliability) from 85.0% to 92.0%, raises paraphrase consistency (generality) from 77% to 79%, and substantially increases retention rate (specificity) by 23.0% relative to prior RL-based approaches, indicating better trade-off management among the three objectives.
AI.conclusion: Treating prompt construction as a structured, multi-objective decision process enables more effective in-context knowledge editing. MO-IKE’s constrained RL framework yields prompts that better balance reliability, generality, and specificity, leading to higher edit success and much stronger retention compared to previous RL-based methods. This suggests that multi-objective, globally-aware prompt optimization is a promising direction for black-box LLM knowledge editing.

title: Provenance Before Prose: Claim-Locked Reporting
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can fluently verbalize statistical evidence, yet statistical reports can still drift numerical values, invert effect directions, or restate thresholded contrasts as categorical effects. We frame these failures as a control problem: the evidence-bearing content of a scientific report should be fixed by structured statistical results rather than sampled during prose generation. We therefore use cross-run reproducibility to stress-test whether report-visible numbers and claims are bound before prose generation. Existing controls operate at the text or slot level; a deterministic hybrid template reproduces only 61.1% of report-visible numerical content across seeds because the LLM still selects which findings and numbers the template renders. We propose claim-locked reporting, a provenance-before-prose protocol that fixes the evidence source, numbers, direction, and allowed language strength of each reportable claim before the LLM writes only connective prose. Across fMRI functional-connectivity reporting and randomized controlled trial reporting on Evidence Inference 2.0, claim-locked reporting improves reproducibility over the hybrid template by 37.4 and 20.5 points, respectively. Blinded human audits support the observed direction-preservation and governance trends. In an fMRI cost analysis with DeepSeek, claim-locked reporting also yields the lowest observed token use and median generation latency.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a control protocol, claim-locked reporting, to make LLM-generated scientific reports numerically and logically reproducible across runs by fixing claims before prose generation.
AI.motivation: LLMs can describe statistical evidence fluently but are unreliable: between runs they may change reported numbers, flip effect directions, or exaggerate thresholded results into categorical claims. Existing control methods, like templates or slot-filling, still allow variation in which findings and numbers are selected, causing poor cross-run reproducibility. The authors want a method that binds the evidence-bearing content of a report to structured statistical outputs, ensuring that what is scientifically reported is stable and not resampled in generation.
AI.method: They treat scientific reporting as a control problem and define cross-run reproducibility as a stress test: do report-visible numbers and claims remain constant across generation seeds? They first evaluate a deterministic hybrid template system, where the LLM still chooses which results to mention, and measure its numeric reproducibility. They then propose claim-locked reporting: a provenance-before-prose pipeline where, for each reportable claim, the evidence source, specific numbers, effect direction, and permissible language strength are fixed ahead of time in a structured representation. The LLM is then only used to generate connective prose around these locked claims. They test this method on two domains: fMRI functional-connectivity reporting and randomized controlled trial reporting (Evidence Inference 2.0). They also run blinded human audits to assess direction preservation and governance properties, and perform a cost analysis (tokens and latency) using DeepSeek.
AI.result: The deterministic hybrid template reproduces only 61.1% of report-visible numerical content across random seeds, demonstrating that letting the LLM choose which findings and numbers to present harms reproducibility. Claim-locked reporting substantially improves cross-run reproducibility of numerical content: by 37.4 percentage points in the fMRI functional-connectivity setting and by 20.5 percentage points in randomized controlled trial reporting on Evidence Inference 2.0. Human auditors, blinded to condition, corroborate that claim-locked reporting better preserves effect directions and adheres to governance constraints. In experiments with DeepSeek, claim-locked reporting also shows the lowest token consumption and median generation latency among the evaluated approaches.
AI.conclusion: Binding scientific claims to structured statistical evidence before prose generation—claim-locked reporting—significantly improves the reproducibility and governance of LLM-generated scientific reports compared with template-based baselines. By fixing evidence sources, numerical values, effect directions, and allowed language strength in advance, the approach reduces cross-run drift in numbers and claims while also being more computationally efficient. The work frames scientific reporting with LLMs as a control and provenance problem and demonstrates that provenance-before-prose design is a practical path toward more trustworthy automated reporting in domains like neuroimaging and clinical trials.

title: FuzzingBrain-Bench V1: Evaluating Open-Ended Bug Discovery by LLMs
comment: 21 pages, 12 figures, 7 tables. Ze Sheng and Aleksandar Kezic contributed equally. Benchmark corpus and harnesses: https://github.com/fuzzingbrain/FuzzingBrain-Bench Counts verified against the built PDF and sources: 21 pages, 12 figure environments, 7 tables
summary:
Evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) to discover software bugs is increasingly important. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate this capability by asking the model to generate a proof-of-concept input that triggers a predefined target vulnerability. However, this setup may overlook valid crashes discovered by the model when they do not match the predefined target. As a result, the evaluation may not reflect the model's real capability.
  We present FuzzingBrain-Bench, a benchmark for assessing AI models' ability to discover bugs in open-source software. Models are given an open-source project and a sanitizer-instrumented harness in a self-contained Docker image. Their goal is to generate inputs that trigger as many distinct crashes as possible through the harness. A model's performance on each challenge is scored based on the number of distinct crash signatures it produces, capped at a predefined maximum and weighted by a difficulty coefficient.
  FuzzingBrain-Bench V1 consists of 77 challenges drawn from 43 open-source projects, with 36 C, 32 C++, and 9 Java/JVM challenges. We evaluate Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Claude Opus 4.8 on the full benchmark. Claude Opus 4.8 performs best, triggering crashes in 60 of 77 challenges and achieving a score of 196 out of 579. None of the three models triggers a crash in 13 challenges. The FuzzingBrain-Bench corpus and harnesses are publicly available at https://github.com/fuzzingbrain/FuzzingBrain-Bench.

AI.tldr: They introduce FuzzingBrain-Bench, a benchmark to measure how well LLMs can find real software crashes, not just known target bugs, by counting distinct crash signatures they trigger in instrumented open-source projects.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM bug-finding benchmarks only check whether a model can hit a specific, predefined vulnerability with a proof-of-concept input. This misses other valid crashes the model might discover and underestimates its true bug-finding capability. A more realistic, fuzzing-style benchmark is needed that rewards any distinct bug-triggering input.
AI.method: They build FuzzingBrain-Bench, where each task is a Dockerized open-source project plus a sanitizer-instrumented harness. Models receive this environment and must generate inputs that cause program crashes. Each challenge is scored by the number of distinct crash signatures triggered, capped and weighted by a difficulty coefficient.
