The benchmark includes 77 challenges from 43 open-source projects (C, C++, Java/JVM). They then run several Claude model variants on all tasks and record how many challenges each model can crash and the resulting scores.
AI.result: The benchmark contains 77 challenges (36 C, 32 C++, 9 Java/JVM). In their evaluation, Claude Opus 4.8 is the strongest, triggering crashes in 60 of 77 challenges and obtaining a score of 196 out of a possible 579. Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 perform worse. Thirteen challenges remain unsolved by any of the three models, indicating headroom for improvement.
AI.conclusion: FuzzingBrain-Bench offers a more faithful and challenging way to evaluate AI models’ bug-discovery capabilities by focusing on distinct crash signatures rather than predefined single vulnerabilities. Initial results show that even top models only solve a subset of challenges and leave many crashes undiscovered, demonstrating both current capabilities and substantial room for progress. The corpus and harnesses are publicly released for the community to use, extend, and compare models.

title: GUIDE: Generative Unsupervised Chinese Query Correction via Phonetic and Visual Shared-ID Encoding
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Industry Track; 7 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables
summary: Chinese query correction (CQC) is important for search and query recommendation on content platforms, but supervised methods rely on large annotated correction pairs that are costly to maintain as query vocabularies evolve. Unsupervised correction with language models is attractive, yet in the short-query setting, unconstrained generation often over-corrects ambiguous inputs toward high-frequency phrases, causing intent drift. We propose \textsc{GUIDE}, a generative unsupervised framework for CQC based on a confuse-then-clarify paradigm. \textsc{GUIDE} encodes phonetically or visually confusable characters with shared-IDs and reconstructs the original query with an encoder--decoder architecture, which constrains correction to plausible confusion neighborhoods while learning from unlabeled query streams. A time-decayed, query-frequency-weighted objective further supports adaptation to rapidly changing query vocabularies. Experiments on \textit{QSpell 250K} and a large-scale real-world dataset (\textit{KwaiSearch}) show that \textsc{GUIDE} consistently outperforms strong baselines, while online A/B testing further confirms gains in correction quality and downstream engagement.

AI.tldr: GUIDE is an unsupervised generative framework for Chinese query correction that reduces over-correction and adapts to evolving query vocabularies, outperforming strong baselines and improving online engagement.
AI.motivation: Chinese query correction is critical for search and query recommendation, but existing supervised approaches depend on large, manually annotated correction pairs. These are expensive to create and quickly become outdated as users’ query vocabularies and trending phrases change. Unsupervised methods using language models avoid annotation but, in short-query scenarios, tend to over-correct ambiguous queries toward common phrases, leading to intent drift and harming user experience. The paper aims to build an unsupervised system that can correct queries accurately without large labeled datasets, while remaining stable to ambiguity and adaptive to fast-evolving vocabularies.
AI.method: The authors propose GUIDE, a generative unsupervised CQC framework built around a confuse-then-clarify paradigm. First, they construct confusion neighborhoods by assigning phonetically or visually similar Chinese characters to shared IDs, effectively encoding potential error sets. An encoder–decoder model is then trained to reconstruct the original query from this confusion-encoded representation, which constrains generation to likely corrections within these neighborhoods. Training uses only unlabeled query streams. To handle temporal drift and evolving vocabularies, the training objective is weighted by query frequency and decayed over time, emphasizing recent and frequent queries so the model stays up-to-date with new terms and trends.
AI.result: On the public QSpell 250K benchmark and a large industrial dataset KwaiSearch, GUIDE consistently outperforms strong supervised and unsupervised baselines in standard query-correction metrics. Moreover, large-scale online A/B tests on a production platform show that using GUIDE for query correction yields higher correction quality as judged by user behavior, and translates into improved downstream engagement metrics (e.g., clicks or time spent).
AI.conclusion: GUIDE demonstrates that a generative, unsupervised confuse-then-clarify approach can deliver effective Chinese query correction without labeled data, mitigating the over-correction and intent drift issues common in short-query settings. By constraining corrections via character confusion neighborhoods and incorporating a time-decayed, frequency-aware objective, the method adapts well to rapidly changing query vocabularies and provides both offline performance gains and measurable online business impact.

title: Tunable Tool-Call Rates in LLM Agents via Representation Steering
summary: Deciding whether to call a tool is a core competence of an LLM agent, and a costly one to get wrong: needless calls add latency, accrue cost, and may trigger irreversible side effects, while missing calls leave the model confidently wrong on questions it could only answer through tool-calls. Models manage this balance poorly, both over-using and under-using tools. Existing methods such as post-training and prompt engineering are expensive and difficult to modify at inference time. We show that whether an instruction-tuned model calls a tool can be controlled by a single linear direction in its residual stream, extracted without any training from the model's own tool-use preference signal and turned into an inference-time intervention with no prompt change. Adding the direction with strength $α$ moves the call rate monotonically from near $0\% $ to over $90\%$ while keeping calls well-formed. The steering works in both directions: dialing it down suppresses calls, and dialing it up induces new calls that land precisely on the questions the model cannot answer from its own knowledge. We also show that the direction generalizes to unseen tools with strength comparable to each tool's own direction and without favoring any specific tool choice. With live tool execution, a single sweep of the steering traces a cost/accuracy Pareto frontier and nearly doubles open-domain QA accuracy ($0.29 \! \rightarrow \! 0.56$); the same recipe transfers across a diverse range of models spanning dense, MoE, and multimodal architectures, without any training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/YuqiChen4188/Steering-Tool-Use-Propensity.

AI.tldr: The paper discovers a single linear direction in an instruction-tuned LLM’s residual stream that controls how often it calls tools, allowing inference-time control of tool-use propensity without retraining or prompt changes.
AI.motivation: Tool calls in LLM agents are costly when unnecessary and harmful when omitted, yet current models tend to both over-use and under-use tools. Existing solutions like post-training or prompt engineering are expensive, hard to tune at inference time, and not easily adaptable across models or tools. The authors want a simple, training-free, model-internal mechanism to smoothly control the rate and quality of tool use during inference.
AI.method: They analyze the internal representations of instruction-tuned models to find a single linear direction in the residual stream that encodes the model’s preference for calling tools versus responding directly. This direction is extracted from the model’s own behavior (its tool-use preference signal) without any additional training. At inference time, they intervene by adding or subtracting this direction with a tunable scalar strength α, effectively steering the model toward more or fewer tool calls, while leaving the prompt unchanged. They evaluate this steering across different models (dense, MoE, multimodal) and tools, including unseen tools, and test with live tool execution on open-domain QA.
AI.result: Varying the strength α monotonically changes the rate of tool calls from near 0% to over 90%, while preserving well-formed tool invocations. Increasing α induces tool calls particularly on questions where the base model lacks sufficient knowledge, and decreasing α suppresses calls. The learned direction generalizes to new tools with strengths comparable to each tool’s own direction and does not bias which tool is chosen. With live tool execution, sweeping α traces a clear cost/accuracy Pareto frontier and nearly doubles open-domain QA accuracy from 0.29 to 0.56. The same intervention strategy works across multiple architectures without any retraining.
AI.conclusion: A single linear direction in an instruction-tuned model’s residual stream provides effective, training-free, inference-time control over tool-use propensity. This steering can smoothly trade off cost (number of tool calls) against accuracy, preserves call quality, generalizes to unseen tools, and transfers across diverse model architectures. This offers a practical way to optimize LLM agent behavior in real deployments without changing prompts or performing additional post-training.

title: Short Horizons and Sparse Concepts: a Mathematical View of the Readout in the J-lens
summary: The Jacobian lens (J-lens) has been proposed as a way to read verbalizable representations from language models. However, its principle and meaning lack a detailed and theoretical discussion. We provide a mathematical view of this interpretation and of its assumed causal structure. Besides treating the J-lens as a heuristic probe, we further regard it as a first-order causal transfer operator from intermediate activations to expected future readouts. We study the Jacobian matrix as the optimal local linear approximation of the downstream mapping, analyze its global approximation behavior and bias, and identify its mathematical meaning as an expectation over anticipated future readouts. Further analysis of the Jacobian energy distribution reveals that its causal geometry is highly sparse. The energy decays with depth, concentrates in an extremely small proportion, and decomposes into diagonal pathways and specific critical positions. This decomposition further resolves the expectation of the J-lens over future outputs into short-horizon and sparse concept predictions, providing a more intuitive attribution and explanation for the ability of the J-lens to visualize concepts during the thinking process. Based on the theory, we propose a simple but effective improvement strategy and decoupling method for the J-lens, which significantly enhances the ability of the J-lens to read out correct intermediate concepts.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a theoretical and mathematical analysis of the Jacobian lens (J-lens) for interpreting language models, clarifying its causal meaning and improving its effectiveness at reading intermediate concepts from model activations.
AI.motivation: The J-lens has been used as a heuristic tool to read verbalizable representations from intermediate activations in language models, but its underlying principle, causal interpretation, and mathematical meaning remain unclear. The authors aim to give a rigorous theoretical foundation, understand its limitations and biases, and thereby improve its reliability as an interpretability method.
AI.method: The authors formalize the J-lens as a first-order causal transfer operator that maps intermediate activations to expected future readouts. They analyze the Jacobian matrix as the optimal local linear approximation to the downstream mapping, study its global approximation behavior and bias, and interpret it mathematically as an expectation over anticipated future readouts. They then examine the Jacobian energy distribution across the network to characterize its causal geometry, sparsity, depth-wise decay, and decomposition into diagonal pathways and critical positions. Based on these analyses, they design an improved, decoupled variant of the J-lens to better separate and enhance relevant causal pathways for concept readout.
AI.result: The analysis shows that the Jacobian underlying the J-lens is highly sparse, with energy that decays with depth and concentrates in a tiny subset of pathways and critical positions. This structure allows the J-lens to be decomposed into short-horizon, sparse concept predictions aligned with specific causal pathways. Leveraging these insights, the proposed improvement and decoupling strategy significantly increases the accuracy of reading out intermediate concepts from language models compared to the original J-lens.
AI.conclusion: The J-lens can be rigorously understood as a first-order causal transfer operator that approximates expected future readouts from intermediate activations. Its behavior is governed by a sparse, pathway-like causal geometry that explains its ability to visualize concepts during a model’s "thinking" process. By exploiting this structure, the authors introduce simple modifications that substantially improve the J-lens, making it a more principled and effective tool for interpreting intermediate representations in language models.

title: Federation Is Nearly Free, Reasoning Is Not: Tradeoffs for AI Co-Scientists in Protein Characterization Workflows
comment: 24 Pages, 4 main figures, 5 main tables, 2 supplementary figures
summary: Natural language driven autonomous co-scientist workflows involve a fundamental trade-off between flexibility and reasoning at the expense of determinism, reproducibility, and observability. Such agents increasingly must communicate across institutional boundaries, where federation topology can shape latency and cost. We systematically evaluated these tradeoffs using a controlled ablation on a production agentic platform for science. We use a verifiable task: given a protein sequence, we ask an agent to confidently characterize its function by routing across common tools. We compare federation topology, classic RL vs LLM-driven harnesses, language model, and prompt expertise. We also stratify results by protein novelty. We find that the choice of LLM dominated prediction quality far more than topology or prompting (Opus ~92%-94% vs o4-mini ~40%-50%). The PPO policy was nearly as accurate as the best LLM (88%) at zero token cost, fastest latency, and perfect consistency, but yields no reasoning trace. Expert prompted LLMs reached the highest accuracy but were high-cost and less consistent; prompt dependence was largest when the task was hardest. Federation imposed a negligible penalty on performance. These results offer actionable guidance for deploying agents for scientific workflows: for routine, verifiable tasks, a cheap deterministic policy delivers near-frontier accuracy with complete reproducibility, while flexible LLM reasoning is best reserved for open-ended discovery.

AI.tldr: Study benchmarked different agent architectures and models for an autonomous ‘co-scientist’ that annotates protein function from sequence, quantifying trade-offs between LLM-based reasoning and deterministic RL policies across federated tool workflows.
AI.motivation: Autonomous scientific agents are increasingly orchestrated via natural language over distributed tools and institutions, but this flexibility can undermine determinism, reproducibility, observability, and cost. There is limited empirical evidence on how factors like federation topology, LLM choice, prompting strategy, and RL vs LLM control affect performance on real scientific tasks. The authors aim to provide quantitative guidance for building reliable, cost-effective co-scientist agents.
AI.method: On a production scientific agent platform, the authors run controlled ablation experiments on a verifiable task: given a protein sequence, an agent must confidently infer its function by routing among common analysis tools. They vary (1) federation topology of tools, (2) RL (PPO) policy vs LLM-based orchestration harnesses, (3) underlying language model (e.g., Opus vs o4-mini), (4) prompt design and expertise, and (5) protein novelty level. They then compare accuracy, latency, token cost, consistency, and presence/absence of reasoning traces across these configurations.
AI.result: The dominant factor in prediction quality is the underlying LLM: a stronger model (Opus) achieves about 92–94% accuracy, while a weaker one (o4-mini) yields around 40–50%. A PPO-based deterministic policy attains nearly comparable accuracy to the best LLM (≈88%) with zero token cost, lowest latency, and perfect run-to-run consistency, but it does not emit interpretable reasoning traces. Expert-crafted prompts for LLMs push accuracy slightly higher but increase cost and reduce consistency, with prompt sensitivity most pronounced on the most novel/difficult proteins. Changes in federation topology introduce only negligible accuracy penalties.
AI.conclusion: For routine, well-specified and verifiable scientific tasks, simple deterministic RL policies can match or closely approach frontier LLM performance while offering maximal reproducibility, zero token cost, and minimal latency, making them preferable as default controllers. LLM-based, prompt-sensitive reasoning harnesses should be used more sparingly, primarily when open-ended exploration or interpretability is required. Federation across institutions and tools, while an architectural concern, does not substantially degrade prediction quality, so system design can prioritize cost and latency over accuracy when choosing federation topology.

title: Leveraging Speech Acts for Low-Data and Cross-Domain Conversation Derailment Forecasting
summary: Conversational derailment forecasting aims to predict when online discussions will escalate into hostility, enabling proactive moderation. Existing approaches often struggle in low-data settings and to generalize across domains. This poses a challenge for new platforms and smaller communities where annotated data is limited. We propose modeling pragmatic representations of conversations to reduce lexical noise and improve generalizability. Specifically, speech act information is used as an auxiliary learning signal alongside textual semantics. Experimental results show improved performance across three datasets, particularly in low-data and cross-domain settings.

AI.tldr: The paper improves forecasting of when online conversations will turn hostile by incorporating speech-act-based pragmatic representations as an auxiliary signal, boosting robustness in low-data and cross-domain settings.
AI.motivation: Online platforms need to identify conversations that are likely to become hostile before they escalate, but existing models require substantial labeled data and do not transfer well to new domains or small communities. There is a need for methods that are less sensitive to surface lexical variation and can generalize with limited annotations.
AI.method: The authors propose a model that jointly learns from textual semantics and pragmatic representations of conversations, where pragmatics are captured via speech act information. Speech act labels (e.g., questioning, agreeing, attacking) are used as an auxiliary learning signal, effectively encouraging the model to abstract away from specific wording and focus on conversational roles and intentions. This multi-task or auxiliary-training setup is applied to conversational derailment forecasting across multiple datasets.
AI.result: Across three conversational datasets, the proposed method outperforms baselines on predicting future hostility. Gains are strongest in low-resource settings (few labeled examples) and in cross-domain evaluations, suggesting better robustness and generalization than purely lexical/semantic models.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating speech act–based pragmatic information as an auxiliary signal leads to more generalizable and data-efficient models for conversational derailment forecasting. This approach reduces dependence on specific lexical cues and is particularly beneficial for new or small online communities with limited annotated data.

title: LLM-Driven, Datasheet-Aware Automated Hardware Compatibility Verification for Early-Stage, Pre-Schematic Embedded System Design
summary: We present an LLM-driven, datasheet-aware framework for early-stage hardware compatibility verification that identifies documentation-level interface incompatibilities based on hardware datasheets and high-level component connectivity descriptions. It does not require, and can therefore be used, before detailed schematic simulation and implementation. We view trustworthy LLM-assisted design automation not as directly generating answers from documents, but as transforming engineering information through traceable verification stages. Given hardware datasheets and high-level component connectivity descriptions, the framework constructs a design graph that captures device connectivity and shared interaction domains, retrieves only the engineering properties required by explicit, domain-oriented verification criteria , and generates deterministic scripts for compatibility evaluation. By decomposing compatibility analysis into modular stages and preserving intermediate results, the framework reduces context overhead, improves transparency and tractability, enables scaling, and avoids reliance on LLMs for numerical computation. Evaluated on seven embedded-system designs comprising 34 datasheets, our framework achieves 97.5% compatibility-verification accuracy and an 8.6 times reduction in input context size compared with ``upload-and-query'' workflows. These results demonstrate the feasibility of LLM-assisted, specification-based hardware compatibility verification at an early design stage, as well as the need for, and substantial benefits of, modular task decomposition, formalized verification criteria, and task-aware compact context construction.

AI.tldr: An LLM-driven framework verifies early-stage hardware interface compatibility using datasheets and high-level connectivity, via modular, traceable steps instead of direct Q&A over long documents.
AI.motivation: Early in hardware design, engineers must ensure that components are electrically and logically compatible. Existing approaches often rely on manual datasheet inspection or later-stage schematic simulation, which is time-consuming, error-prone, and requires detailed designs that may not yet exist. Naive LLM workflows that simply upload and query datasheets suffer from context limits, lack of traceability, and unreliable numerical reasoning. The paper aims to enable trustworthy, scalable, and efficient LLM assistance for hardware compatibility checks at a very early design stage, before full schematics are available.
AI.method: The authors propose a datasheet-aware, LLM-driven framework that ingests hardware datasheets and high-level component connectivity descriptions. It builds a design graph representing components, their connections, and shared interaction domains (e.g., power, I/O, buses). Using predefined, domain-oriented verification criteria, the system retrieves only the necessary engineering parameters from datasheets and then auto-generates deterministic, non-LLM scripts to perform compatibility checks. The process is decomposed into modular stages—graph construction, property retrieval, criteria mapping, and script-based evaluation—while preserving all intermediate artifacts for traceability and reduced context size.
AI.result: On seven embedded-system designs involving 34 datasheets, the framework achieves 97.5% accuracy in compatibility verification, closely matching expert judgments, and reduces the required LLM input context size by 8.6× compared to simple “upload-and-query” workflows. This shows that the system can both reliably detect documentation-level interface incompatibilities and significantly improve efficiency in handling large documentation sets.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that LLMs are most effective in hardware design automation when used as controlled transformers of engineering information rather than as monolithic question-answering engines. Modular task decomposition, explicit verification criteria, and compact, task-aware context construction are key to achieving trustworthy, scalable, and efficient early-stage hardware compatibility verification. The demonstrated accuracy and context reduction validate the feasibility and benefits of specification-based, LLM-assisted verification using datasheets and high-level connectivity descriptions.

title: Adaptive Triggering for Bias Correction in LLM Reasoning
summary: Chain-of-thought prompting can expose and amplify demographic stereotypes within an LLM's intermediate reasoning and create a failure mode that final-answer debiasing alone cannot address. Mitigating such bias during generation presents a fundamental timing problem: intervening too late allows biased reasoning to propagate, while unnecessarily intervening can disrupt otherwise correct reasoning. Existing approaches largely avoid this decision by either evaluating completed reasoning chains post hoc or intervening at predetermined steps, leaving open when a developing reasoning trajectory provides sufficient evidence to warrant correction. We formulate this decision as an online change-point detection problem. A per-step bias signal updates a CUSUM statistic and a targeted correction is injected only when accumulated evidence crosses a detector-specific threshold calibrated on held-out data. We instantiate the framework with a white-box signal derived from next-token probabilities and a black-box signal obtained from an LLM judge, enabling deployment with both open-weight and hosted models. On gpt-4o-mini adaptive black-box triggering recovers most of the disambiguated-context accuracy lost under fixed-interval intervention while requiring substantially fewer interventions. That result holds even with an independent judge. Across six open-weight models, the white-box signal improves ambiguous-item accuracy on all six but reduces disambiguated-item accuracy on five because it cannot distinguish unsupported stereotype reliance from correct, stereotype-congruent evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an online, step-by-step bias detection and intervention framework for chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs, treating it as a change-point detection problem to decide when to correct biased reasoning without over-intervening.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought prompting can surface and amplify demographic stereotypes in an LLM’s intermediate reasoning, and simply debiasing the final answer cannot fix failures caused by biased reasoning paths. Current methods either check bias only after the full reasoning chain is produced or intervene at fixed steps, sidestepping the core question of when there is enough evidence that the ongoing reasoning has become biased. The authors want a principled, dynamic method to detect and mitigate bias during reasoning, intervening only when necessary to avoid both missed bias and unnecessary disruptions to correct reasoning.
AI.method: The authors cast the decision of whether to intervene during chain-of-thought generation as an online change-point detection problem. At each reasoning step, they compute a per-step bias signal and update a CUSUM (cumulative sum) statistic. When this statistic exceeds a learned threshold, they trigger a targeted corrective intervention. Thresholds are calibrated on held-out data for each detector. They instantiate this with two types of bias signals: (1) a white-box signal based on next-token probabilities from the model (for open-weight models), and (2) a black-box signal based on judgments from an external LLM judge (for closed/hosted models). They then compare fixed-interval interventions to this adaptive triggering across multiple models.
AI.result: On gpt-4o-mini, the adaptive black-box triggering recovers most of the accuracy in disambiguated contexts that is otherwise lost when using fixed-interval interventions, while also requiring significantly fewer interventions. This benefit persists even when the judging LLM is independent from the base model. For six open-weight models, the white-box signal consistently improves accuracy on ambiguous items, but for five of the six models it decreases accuracy on disambiguated items. This suggests the white-box approach struggles to distinguish between unjustified reliance on stereotypes and correct reasoning that happens to align with stereotypical patterns.
AI.conclusion: Online, adaptive intervention framed as change-point detection is a promising strategy for mitigating bias in chain-of-thought reasoning while minimizing disruption to correct reasoning. Black-box, judge-based signals can effectively trigger interventions on closed models, improving accuracy with fewer interventions, whereas white-box probability-based signals provide benefits mainly in ambiguous cases but can harm performance when stereotypes coincide with valid evidence. More refined signals or models are needed to reliably separate harmful stereotype use from justified, stereotype-consistent reasoning.

title: FLARE: Verifying MILP Reformulations with LLM-Based Theorem Proving
summary: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) is a fundamental tool for combinatorial optimization with extensive real-world applications. A central challenge is designing computationally efficient MILP formulations. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to automate the modeling process, from deriving formulations to strengthening them. Reliable automation requires robust methods for verifying that proposed formulations preserve the underlying optimization problem. However, existing approaches evaluate formulations numerically and fail to reason about general problem instances. We resolve this limitation by introducing a constructive definition of MILP reformulation that can be formalized in Lean and machine-checked. We develop FLARE (Formulation-Level Automated Reformulation Evaluation), a method that uses an LLM-based agent and the Lean proof assistant to verify proposed reformulations against a reference formulation. To evaluate our approach, we introduce FormulationBench, a challenging dataset of 20 problems and 109 formulations. FLARE outperforms existing methods, with 100% accuracy on the NP-hard subset of FormulationBench. Furthermore, FLARE produces a machine-checkable certificate for every reformulation it accepts. For cases where formal guarantees are not necessary, we introduce FLARE-NL, a fast and cheap LLM proxy that matches FLARE's accuracy but produces no certificate. These methods enable reliable verification in automated optimization modeling.

AI.tldr: They propose FLARE, a Lean-assisted framework to formally verify that MILP reformulations are correct, achieving state-of-the-art reliability on a new benchmark.
AI.motivation: Designing good MILP formulations is hard, and current automated/LLM-based methods for generating or checking formulations rely on numerical testing, which cannot guarantee correctness for all instances. There is a need for a principled, formal-verification-based way to ensure that automatically generated or strengthened MILP formulations are truly equivalent to the original optimization problem.
AI.method: They define a constructive notion of MILP reformulation that can be encoded and proven within the Lean proof assistant. On top of this, they build FLARE, an LLM-driven agentic system that proposes and guides proofs of equivalence between a candidate reformulation and a reference formulation in Lean. They also create FormulationBench, a benchmark of 20 optimization problems with 109 associated MILP formulations. In addition, they design FLARE-NL, a lightweight LLM-only proxy that imitates FLARE’s decisions without generating formal proofs.
AI.result: On FormulationBench, FLARE surpasses existing numerical or heuristic verification baselines and attains 100% verification accuracy on the NP-hard subset of problems. It outputs machine-checkable Lean proof certificates for all reformulations it accepts. FLARE-NL attains comparable accuracy to FLARE while being faster and cheaper but does not provide formal certificates.
AI.conclusion: Formal methods, integrated with LLMs, can reliably verify MILP reformulations and overcome the limitations of purely numerical validation. FLARE demonstrates that proof-assistant-backed verification is practical for nontrivial optimization problems, while FLARE-NL offers a more efficient but non-certified alternative. Together, they provide a foundation for trustworthy automation in optimization modeling workflows.

title: OmniPhys: A Unified Multimodal Benchmark for Physics Understanding and Generation from Chinese Educational Corpora
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong abilities in solving diverse visual and textual reasoning tasks. However, their development in the physics domain is significantly hindered by the lack of a comprehensive benchmark. To fill this gap, we introduce OmniPhys, a large-scale benchmark for multimodal physics understanding and reasoning, covering middle school through university-level problems from Chinese Educational Corpora. OmniPhys consists of 15,246 questions and 19,850 images, accompanied by detailed annotations that support fine-grained analysis of reasoning processes and knowledge usage. Beyond conventional evaluation, OmniPhys is a benchmark that systematically evaluates multimodal outputs in the physics domain, including models' ability to generate structured physics diagrams, which constitute a fundamental component of authentic physics problem solving. Extensive evaluations reveal critical gaps in the capabilities of current MLLMs, especially in complex reasoning and visual generation. To address this, we release OmniPhys to serve as a foundational resource for advancing multimodal intelligence in physics and scientific domains. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ECNU-RAIL/OmniPhys-EMNLP2026.

AI.tldr: OmniPhys is a large-scale benchmark to evaluate multimodal large language models on physics understanding, reasoning, and diagram generation.
AI.motivation: MLLMs are strong on general vision-language tasks but lack a dedicated, comprehensive benchmark for physics, especially with authentic educational problems and detailed reasoning analysis. This gap prevents systematic measurement and progress in multimodal physics intelligence.
AI.method: The authors construct OmniPhys from Chinese educational corpora spanning middle school to university levels, collecting 15,246 physics questions and 19,850 images. They add rich annotations for reasoning steps and knowledge usage, and design evaluation protocols that go beyond answer accuracy to include multimodal outputs such as structured physics diagrams. They then benchmark existing MLLMs on these tasks.
AI.result: Experiments on current state-of-the-art MLLMs show substantial performance gaps, particularly for complex multi-step reasoning, knowledge-intensive questions, and the generation of accurate, structured physics diagrams. The benchmark reveals that current models are far from human-level performance on authentic physics problem solving.
AI.conclusion: OmniPhys provides a much-needed, large-scale, and fine-grained benchmark for multimodal physics understanding, enabling systematic evaluation of both textual reasoning and visual diagram generation. By making the dataset and code public, the authors aim to catalyze research toward more capable multimodal models in physics and broader scientific domains.

title: Hierarchical MoE for Multi-Modal ILD Diagnosis
summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models combine specialized predictors under learned routing, offering a principled mechanism for leveraging heterogeneity in medical data. We present a hierarchical multimodal MoE for interstitial lung disease (ILD) classification that integrates a frozen, pre-trained imaging expert with structured electronic health records (EHR) via two-stage gating. A modality-level gate assigns patient-specific weights to imaging and EHR predictions, while a sub-gating module decomposes the EHR branch into clinically defined feature groups with learned, group-specific contributions. This design preserves stable imaging representations while enabling input-dependent clinical weighting and explicit EHR specialization. Under strict patient-level cross-validation, the model achieved the highest mean AUC among the evaluated methods (0.8750 +- 0.0443), compared with 0.8646 for imaging-only REN and 0.7685 for SwinUNETR. The framework extends interpretability across anatomical regions, imaging--EHR utilization, and clinically defined EHR feature groups.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical multimodal mixture-of-experts model for ILD classification combining frozen imaging expert with structured EHR via two-stage gating, improving AUC and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Interstitial lung disease diagnosis benefits from both imaging and clinical data, but effectively integrating heterogeneous modalities while maintaining interpretability and stability of pretrained imaging models is challenging. Existing approaches often either rely mainly on imaging, treat modalities uniformly, or lack clinically meaningful decomposition of EHR features.
AI.method: Propose a hierarchical multimodal MoE architecture that integrates a frozen pre-trained imaging expert with structured EHR. A modality-level gating network learns patient-specific weights between imaging and EHR predictions. Within the EHR branch, a sub-gating module partitions features into clinically defined groups and learns group-specific contributions. Imaging features are kept frozen to preserve representations, while gates are trained to provide input-dependent weighting and specialization.
AI.result: Using strict patient-level cross-validation on ILD classification, the proposed model achieves the highest mean AUC (0.8750 ± 0.0443), outperforming an imaging-only REN model (AUC 0.8646) and SwinUNETR (AUC 0.7685).
AI.conclusion: A hierarchical multimodal MoE that combines a frozen imaging expert with structured EHR and clinically meaningful EHR sub-gating improves ILD classification performance and provides extended interpretability across anatomical regions, modality usage, and clinical feature groups.

title: DCGC: Draft-Conditioned Global Correction for Complex Reasoning with Masked Diffusion Models
summary: Correcting flawed reasoning traces remains a significant challenge for Large Language Models (LLMs), whose autoregressive generation can propagate early mistakes into subsequent reasoning. We introduce DCGC, a Masked Diffusion Model (MDM) framework for global correction that uses an imperfect solution draft from an upstream solver as auxiliary context. DCGC combines task-specific Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with a novel inference-time mechanism called Dynamic Dual-CFG. This mechanism separates problem-only and joint problem-draft branches and scales the draft-conditioned residual using a relative confidence gap. Across math, code, and knowledge reasoning benchmarks, DCGC outperforms standard sampling and simpler CFG variants, with additional results suggesting transfer to different diffusion backbones. In test-time setting where ground-truth failure labels are unavailable, DCGC improves full test set accuracy by correcting low-consensus upstream outputs, highlighting its utility as a verifier-free global correction module for difficult reasoning instances.

AI.tldr: They propose DCGC, a masked diffusion framework that globally corrects flawed reasoning drafts from LLMs, outperforming standard methods across math, code, and knowledge tasks.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive LLMs tend to propagate early reasoning mistakes, making it hard to correct flawed reasoning traces and improve final accuracy, especially without explicit failure labels or external verifiers.
AI.method: They design DCGC, a Masked Diffusion Model that takes both the original problem and an imperfect solution draft as input. The training uses task-specific supervised fine-tuning. At inference, a new Dynamic Dual-CFG mechanism maintains two branches—a problem-only branch and a problem-plus-draft branch—and modulates the influence of the draft via a confidence-gap-based scaling of the draft-conditioned residual.
AI.result: On multiple benchmarks involving mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge tasks, DCGC yields higher accuracy than standard sampling and simpler classifier-free guidance (CFG) baselines, and shows signs of transferability across different diffusion model backbones. In a realistic test-time setting without ground-truth failure labels, DCGC improves performance by selectively correcting low-consensus outputs from the upstream solver.
AI.conclusion: DCGC is an effective, verifier-free global correction module that can refine difficult reasoning instances by leveraging imperfect drafts, mitigating error propagation issues of autoregressive LLMs and improving overall test accuracy across domains.

title: PhaseShift: Topology-Aware Data Harmonization and Model Consolidation Across Signalized Intersections
summary: Learned traffic-behavior models are commonly trained separately for each intersection, creating model portfolios that cannot share evidence across sites. We present PhaseShift, a topology-aware framework that harmonizes heterogeneous roadside trajectories into a shared actor-centric representation and trains one reusable backbone. Ego-relative coordinates, trajectory-induced movement paths, normalized signal context, and variable-cardinality interaction tokens remove site conventions while preserving behaviorally relevant topology. The backbone supports pooled operation, zero-shot at a held-out intersection, and low-data adaptation. We evaluate five intersections in two Florida regions on balanced field data, 100k training windows and equal-sized test sets per site under a replay-conditioned, best-of-sampled-trajectory protocol. At 10s, one pooled model lowers both minADE and minFDE relative to trained local models at all five sites, with median reductions of 36.8% and 22.0%. Leave-one-intersection-out deployment, including one cross-region fold, beats local training on both 10-s metrics at four of five sites, although short-horizon performance is less uniform. Fine-tuning with 1,000 target update windows improves on zero-shot at three sites and is the strongest regime at one. At site 7, every cross-site mixture sharply lowers long-horizon error under a fixed 100k-window budget; test-likelihood gains argue against a best-of-sample dispersion-only explanation. Local models fall behind calibrated IDM at the two highest-flow sites after long autoregressive rollouts; pretrained-backbone regimes do not. Within this five-site evaluation, PhaseShift demonstrates consolidation across heterogeneous physical control settings while identifying sites that still require adaptation. The protocol measures conditional single-vehicle generation under replayed context, not closed-loop traffic simulation.

AI.tldr: PhaseShift is a shared, topology-aware trajectory model that outperforms per-intersection models for long-horizon vehicle motion prediction across multiple heterogeneous intersections.
AI.motivation: Most traffic-behavior prediction models are trained independently for each intersection, so they cannot share data or generalize well across locations with different geometries and signal setups. This leads to inefficient use of data, brittle deployments, and difficulty transferring knowledge to new sites or adapting with limited local data.
AI.method: The authors propose PhaseShift, a topology-aware framework that converts heterogeneous roadside trajectory and signal data from different intersections into a common, actor-centric representation. They use ego-relative coordinates, trajectory-induced movement paths, normalized traffic-signal context, and variable-cardinality interaction tokens to strip away site-specific conventions while preserving behaviorally important topology. On top of this harmonized representation they train a single reusable backbone model. They evaluate pooled training, zero-shot deployment to held-out intersections (including cross-region), and low-data fine-tuning, using a replay-conditioned, best-of-sampled-trajectory protocol with 100k training windows per regime and balanced test sets per site.
AI.result: On five intersections across two regions in Florida, a single pooled PhaseShift model reduces 10-second prediction errors (minADE and minFDE) compared to individually trained local models at all sites, with median reductions of 36.8% and 22.0%. In leave-one-intersection-out tests, including one fold where the target is in a different region, the pooled/backbone approach beats local training on 10-second metrics at four out of five intersections, though short-horizon performance is more mixed. Fine-tuning the shared backbone with only 1,000 target-site windows further improves performance at most sites and is best at one site. At a specific site (site 7), any cross-site training mixture significantly lowers long-horizon error under a fixed data budget, and improved test likelihood suggests genuine modeling gains rather than simply greater trajectory dispersion. Local models degrade and fall behind a calibrated IDM baseline at the highest-flow sites during long autoregressive rollouts, whereas pretrained-backbone variants remain robust.
AI.conclusion: PhaseShift shows that consolidating trajectory modeling across heterogeneous intersections is feasible and beneficial: a single topology-aware backbone can outperform site-specific models on long-horizon prediction, generalize zero-shot to new intersections (including cross-region), and be further improved with modest fine-tuning data. However, some sites still require adaptation, and the current evaluation focuses on conditional single-vehicle generation under replayed context rather than fully closed-loop multi-agent traffic simulation.

title: MathAdv: What Theorem Provers Know, Reason, Formalize, and Generalize
summary: Formal theorem proving enables machine-verifiable evaluation of mathematical reasoning, yet existing benchmarks often emphasize aggregate proof accuracy, concentrate on a narrow range of mathematics, and provide limited evidence of robustness to equivalent reformulations. We introduce MathAdv, a diagnostic benchmark spanning 13 domains across undergraduate- and graduate-level mathematics. Alongside Lean 4 theorem proving, MathAdv provides up to three auxiliary tasks: multiple-choice questions that probe mathematical knowledge, fill-in-the-blank problems that isolate informal reasoning, and expert-crafted transformations that test robustness to problem presentation. Our evaluation of contemporary theorem provers yields four findings: formalization remains a major bottleneck; performance varies substantially across mathematical domains; natural-language guidance helps general-purpose LLMs but can hinder proof-specialized models; and mathematically equivalent reformulations expose substantial robustness limitations. Together, these results show how component-wise evaluation can reveal model capabilities and failure modes that aggregate theorem-proving accuracy obscures. The dataset and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/margotyjx/MathAdv.git.

AI.tldr: MathAdv is a diagnostic benchmark for theorem-proving systems that evaluates not just proof success but also knowledge, informal reasoning, and robustness to reformulation across many math domains.
AI.motivation: Existing theorem-proving benchmarks mostly report a single aggregate accuracy number, focus on a narrow subset of math topics, and rarely test how robust models are to equivalent rephrasings of problems. This makes it hard to understand specific strengths, weaknesses, and brittleness of current theorem provers. The authors want a benchmark that gives a fine-grained, realistic picture of capabilities needed for serious mathematical reasoning.
AI.method: The authors construct MathAdv, a benchmark covering 13 areas of undergraduate- and graduate-level mathematics. For each problem, they provide: (1) a Lean 4 theorem statement for formal proving; (2) multiple-choice questions to probe underlying mathematical knowledge; (3) fill-in-the-blank items to isolate informal reasoning; and (4) expert-designed transformations that preserve mathematical meaning but change the surface form, to test robustness to reformulation. They then systematically evaluate contemporary theorem-proving systems—both general-purpose LLMs and proof-specialized models—across these tasks and domains, with and without natural-language guidance, and compare performance and failure patterns.
AI.result: Their experiments show: (1) converting problems into formal Lean statements (formalization) is a key performance bottleneck; (2) model performance differs greatly between mathematical domains rather than being uniformly strong or weak; (3) adding natural-language guidance tends to help general-purpose LLMs but can actually reduce performance of specialized theorem-proving models; and (4) mathematically equivalent rephrasings of problems often cause large performance drops, revealing poor robustness. Overall, the finer-grained tasks expose a richer set of capabilities and errors than a single theorem-proving accuracy metric would.
AI.conclusion: MathAdv demonstrates that detailed, component-wise evaluation is essential to understand and improve machine theorem provers. By spanning many domains and decomposing the reasoning pipeline into knowledge, informal reasoning, formal proving, and robustness to reformulation, the benchmark uncovers important bottlenecks and brittleness that aggregate accuracy hides. The authors release the dataset and code to encourage more nuanced progress in automated mathematical reasoning.

title: BixBench3: Benchmarking AI agents on research-study-scale computational biology tasks
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) promises to accelerate biological research by automating computational analyses. Yet the ability of AI agents to carry out computational biology at the scale of complete research studies has not been systematically evaluated. Here we introduce BixBench3, a benchmark that measures the capacity of AI agents to process raw biological data through to scientific results. We designed BixBench3 tasks to mirror the delegation of work from a scientist to an agent: the scientist chooses the research question and high-level methods, then delegates implementation of all analyses to the agent. In each task, an agent receives a research objective, methodological guidance, and raw data derived from a published scientific study, and must execute a sequence of analyses to achieve the research objective. The data artifacts resulting from these analyses - such as peak call matrices or differential expression tables - are programmatically graded against the corresponding artifacts generated and reported in the original study. Across 20 BixBench3 tasks encompassing the generation of 138 unique artifacts, we find that 13 frontier models achieve scores ranging from 0.00 for Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite to 0.48 for GPT 5.6 Sol. Agents perform worse on tasks with larger raw datasets (0.36 on tasks with <100 GB versus 0.10 on tasks with >100 GB) and on analyses requiring more sequential steps (0.36 at 1-2 steps vs 0.24 at 3+). On average, agents use 6.8 hours, 102 million tokens, and $43 to complete each task, with the longest attempts consuming 24 hours, 1.07 billion tokens, and $525. Notably, the highest-scoring agents used fewer tokens and were cheaper than less performant options. These results reveal that LLMs vary substantially in their ability to (1) execute multiple sequential analysis steps coherently, (2) manage large quantities of raw data, and (3) work across scientific domains.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BixBench3, a benchmark to systematically evaluate how well AI agents can execute end-to-end computational biology studies from raw data to publishable results.
AI.motivation: While AI models are increasingly used in biology, there has been no systematic way to assess whether AI agents can autonomously perform entire computational biology workflows, from raw data processing to scientific outputs, at the scale and complexity of real research papers.
AI.method: The authors build BixBench3, a benchmark composed of 20 tasks derived from real published biological studies. Each task mimics a scientist delegating work to an AI agent: the scientist defines the research question and high-level methods, and the agent receives this objective plus raw experimental data. The agent must implement all analysis steps to generate intermediate and final artifacts (e.g., peak call matrices, differential expression tables). These outputs are automatically graded by comparing them programmatically to the corresponding artifacts from the original studies. Thirteen frontier LLM-based agents are evaluated on their ability to complete 138 unique artifacts, and their performance, resource usage, and sensitivity to data size and workflow length are measured.
AI.result: Across the 20 tasks and 138 artifacts, the 13 evaluated agents show wide variation in performance, with benchmark scores ranging from 0.00 (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite) to 0.48 (GPT 5.6 Sol). Agents perform substantially worse on tasks involving larger raw datasets (>100 GB) and on workflows requiring more sequential analysis steps (3 or more). Resource usage is high: on average, each task attempt uses 6.8 hours of runtime, 102 million tokens, and about $43, with some runs reaching 24 hours, over 1 billion tokens, and $525. Interestingly, better-performing agents tend to be more efficient, using fewer tokens and costing less than weaker agents.
AI.conclusion: BixBench3 shows that current LLM-based agents are far from reliably executing full computational biology studies, especially when facing large datasets and multi-step analysis pipelines. The benchmark exposes major limitations in agents' abilities to maintain coherent multi-step reasoning, handle large-scale biological data, and generalize across scientific tasks and domains. At the same time, it provides a structured way to compare models and highlights that higher quality models can be both more accurate and more cost-efficient, guiding future development of AI agents for scientific research.

title: VietAIDetector: An Open-Source Zero-Shot Detector for Vietnamese AI-Generated Text
summary: In recent years, distinguishing between AI-generated text and human-written text has remained a challenge. In this paper, we introduce VietAIDetector, an open-source tool designed specifically for detecting Vietnamese AI-generated text. It allows users to interact through a Gradio web interface with inputs ranging from raw Vietnamese text to common text file formats, including scanned documents and exceptionally long texts that exceed the context size of the employed Large Language Models (LLMs). The core component of the tool employs a Zero-Shot approach to detect AI-generated text without requiring domain-specific training data, building upon the previous VietBinoculars and Binoculars research. The tool is built upon a Vietnamese-specific language model and has been evaluated on out-of-domain datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods primarily developed for English. Additionally, users can select optimal detection thresholds based on F1 score, accuracy, or TPR@0.05FPR requirements. The results are presented through the web interface, allowing users to easily review and verify suspicious texts or download them as a PDF report. The tool is publicly available at https://github.com/trieuntu/VietAIDetector

AI.tldr: VietAIDetector is an open-source Vietnamese-focused tool that detects AI-generated text using a zero-shot method and a Vietnamese language model, with a user-friendly Gradio interface and strong performance on out-of-domain data.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-text detectors are mostly designed for English and struggle with Vietnamese, especially for varied formats like scanned docs and very long texts; there is a need for a robust, language-specific, easily usable Vietnamese AI-text detector that works without task-specific training data.
AI.method: The authors build an open-source detection tool around a Vietnamese-specific language model and a Zero-Shot detection approach inspired by VietBinoculars and Binoculars. The system is wrapped in a Gradio web interface that accepts raw Vietnamese text, standard text file formats, scanned documents via OCR, and long texts beyond LLM context windows. The model outputs scores for AI-generated vs human-written text, and the interface lets users select thresholds optimized for F1, accuracy, or TPR@0.05FPR, then visualize and export results as a PDF report.
AI.result: On out-of-domain Vietnamese datasets, VietAIDetector outperforms existing AI-text detection methods that are mainly designed for English, indicating better robustness and accuracy in Vietnamese AI-text detection across diverse text types.
AI.conclusion: VietAIDetector provides an effective, open-source, and practical solution for detecting AI-generated Vietnamese text, outperforming English-centric baselines, handling diverse and long inputs via a web interface, and offering flexible threshold selection and reporting, thereby filling a key gap in AI-text detection for Vietnamese.

title: FinRiskAtlas: Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Large Language Models for Financial Risk Review
summary: Deploying large language models for professional financial review requires more than measuring general financial competence: models must perform the specific review operation required by a workflow and determine whether available evidence is sufficient for a defensible decision. Existing financial benchmarks cover knowledge, reasoning, compliance, and professional tasks, but their evaluation units are often organized around datasets or task formulations rather than the decisions that deployed systems support. We introduce FinRiskAtlas, a Chinese-language benchmark that evaluates financial LLMs along two complementary dimensions: operation execution under fixed evidence states and evidence-state control under evolving review conditions. The static benchmark contains 9,742 instances across 53 task families, including 42 Domain Knowledge families and eleven downstream review operations defined by explicit evaluation contracts. FinRisk-Ask extends this framework through offline replay of 680 pre-action states from 104 de-identified professional trajectories, withholding future evidence during inference and using it only to construct expert-verified evidence targets. Across 33 model configurations, operation-level evaluation yields non-redundant rankings (mean pairwise Spearman correlation 0.42 across downstream operations), and knowledge-based shortlisting can incur up to 18.01 points of regret on individual operations. FinRisk-Ask further shows that entering the Ask branch more frequently does not necessarily improve request targeting or end-to-end evidence acquisition. These results show that broad financial capability scores do not fully capture where models are reliable in professional workflows, motivating evaluation units aligned with the decisions and evidence states that deployed systems must support.

AI.tldr: The paper presents FinRiskAtlas, a Chinese-language benchmark for evaluating large language models in professional financial review workflows, focusing on decision- and evidence-state-centric evaluation rather than generic financial competence.
AI.motivation: Existing financial LLM benchmarks mainly test knowledge, reasoning, and generic professional tasks, but they are not aligned with actual decision units and evidence sufficiency questions in real financial review workflows. Deployed systems must not only know finance but also execute specific review operations and decide whether current evidence is enough to make a defensible decision or whether more information is needed. There is a need for benchmarks that mirror these operational and evidence-state demands, especially for professional Chinese-language financial workflows.
AI.method: The authors design FinRiskAtlas with two evaluation dimensions. First, a static benchmark evaluates operation execution under fixed evidence states, covering 9,742 instances, 53 task families (42 Domain Knowledge families plus 11 downstream review operations), each with explicit evaluation contracts. Second, FinRisk-Ask evaluates evidence-state control via offline replay of 680 pre-action states from 104 de-identified real professional trajectories: models see only current evidence at inference time, while withheld future evidence is used post hoc to define expert-verified evidence targets. They test 33 LLM configurations and compute operation-level metrics and correlations across operations to study ranking redundancy and regret from knowledge-only model selection, as well as behavior in Ask (information-request) branches.
AI.result: Operation-level evaluation across 33 model configurations yields non-redundant rankings, with mean pairwise Spearman correlation of 0.42 across downstream operations, indicating that performance varies substantially by operation. Selecting models based solely on knowledge-based shortlisting can incur up to 18.01 points of regret on individual downstream operations. In the dynamic FinRisk-Ask setting, models that trigger the Ask branch more frequently do not necessarily achieve better request targeting or more effective end-to-end evidence acquisition. These findings show that broad financial capability scores are poor proxies for task- and operation-specific reliability in professional workflows.
AI.conclusion: FinRiskAtlas demonstrates that financial LLM evaluation should be aligned with concrete decisions and evidence states required in professional financial review workflows rather than relying on aggregate financial competence metrics. Operation-level and evidence-state-aware benchmarks reveal substantial variations in model reliability that generic benchmarks miss, showing that knowledge-oriented scores can be misleading for model selection. The work motivates designing and adopting decision- and workflow-aligned evaluation units for deploying financial LLMs in practice, particularly in Chinese-language professional review contexts.

title: ReliableRAG: Combating Misinformation in Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Reliability-Guided Reasoning Chains
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful architecture for Question Answering (QA) by integrating external information into Large Language Models (LLMs). However, false, inaccurate, and misleading information in news and social media poses a serious challenge to real-world RAG systems, especially in multi-hop QA, where complex multi-step reasoning can be misled by even a single deceptive misinformation segment in the retrieved documents. Existing approaches mainly rely on implicit alignment or explicit regulation, but their limited ability to assess fine-grained information reliability makes them vulnerable to deceptive misinformation that is semantically relevant to the question yet factually incorrect, leading to erroneous answers. To address this limitation, we propose ReliableRAG, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first reliability-driven framework that mitigates deceptive misinformation in multi-hop QA through fine-grained evaluation of individual triples. ReliableRAG first extracts information segments from source documents and represents them as structured triples. It then quantifies triple reliability by combining query-triple semantic relevance with triple credibility, retaining only the top-$K$ reliable and non-redundant triples. Based on these refined triples, ReliableRAG autoregressively constructs robust reasoning chains to consolidate trustworthy evidence and filter deceptive misinformation, producing accurate answers faithful to reliable information. Experiments on three multi-hop QA datasets show that ReliableRAG outperforms existing methods, substantially improving the factual reliability and robustness of RAG systems under deceptive misinformation injection.

AI.tldr: A reliability-driven RAG framework (ReliableRAG) filters deceptive misinformation in multi-hop QA by scoring and selecting fine-grained triples before reasoning.
AI.motivation: RAG systems for multi-hop QA are vulnerable to deceptive misinformation in retrieved documents. Existing methods lack fine-grained reliability assessment, so semantically relevant but factually wrong content can mislead reasoning and cause incorrect answers.
AI.method: ReliableRAG extracts information segments from retrieved documents and converts them into structured triples. It assigns each triple a reliability score that combines semantic relevance to the query with an estimate of the triple’s credibility. It then selects the top-K reliable, non-redundant triples and uses them to autoregressively build reasoning chains that emphasize trustworthy evidence and filter out deceptive information when generating answers.
AI.result: On three multi-hop QA datasets with injected deceptive misinformation, ReliableRAG achieves better performance than prior RAG and regulation/alignment-based baselines, improving factual reliability and robustness of QA answers.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained, triple-level reliability estimation and selection prior to reasoning significantly strengthens RAG systems against deceptive misinformation in multi-hop QA, leading to more accurate and trustworthy answers than existing approaches.

title: Learning What to Share and What to Personalize: Hierarchical Strategy Co-Evolution for Agent Memory
summary: Memory-augmented agents maintain compact user profiles throughout extended conversations, enabling personalized and consistent responses without the need to process the entire dialogue history. The quality of these user profiles relies on the underlying memory management strategy: at each step, the agent must determine what to retain, compress, or discard. However, existing methods typically employ a static, one-size-fits-all strategy established before training. In practice, the optimal memory decision is inherently user-specific and dynamically evolves alongside policy optimization. To address this, we propose \textbf{HiPS} (\textbf{Hi}erarchical \textbf{P}ersonalized \textbf{S}trategy), a framework that decouples memory management into a globally shared foundation and a user-specific adaptive tier. Specifically, HiPS employs \textbf{Universal Strategy} to extract shared principles from cross-persona trajectories, alongside \textbf{Persona Delta Distillation} to generate tailored rules for users whose behaviors diverge from general patterns. \textbf{Cross-Level Rule Flow} dynamically calibrates their boundary by promoting broadly validated personal rules and demoting contradicted global ones. The architecture establishes a co-evolution loop where a mechanism guarantees that all strategy refinements are anchored to task outcomes. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over memory-augmented baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HiPS, a hierarchical personalized strategy framework for memory management in conversational agents, achieving better personalization and task performance than static memory strategies.
AI.motivation: Memory-augmented conversational agents need to keep compact but useful user profiles over long dialogues. Existing systems use a static, global memory strategy that ignores user-specific differences and the fact that optimal strategies should evolve with the policy and over time. The paper aims to create a dynamic, user-personalized, and outcome-driven memory management mechanism.
AI.method: The authors propose HiPS, which decomposes memory management into two levels: (1) a global Universal Strategy learned from cross-persona trajectories that captures shared memory principles; and (2) a user-specific Persona Delta Distillation component that learns adjustments (deltas) for users whose behavior deviates from the global pattern. A Cross-Level Rule Flow mechanism moves rules between the global and personal levels by promoting widely validated personal rules to global and demoting contradicted global rules, tying all updates to task outcomes and creating a co-evolution loop between memory strategy and policy.
AI.result: Across extensive experiments on memory-augmented conversational tasks, HiPS consistently outperforms baselines that use fixed, non-personalized memory strategies, yielding better task performance and higher-quality user profiles.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical, adaptive, and user-personalized memory management strategies lead to more effective memory-augmented conversational agents than static, one-size-fits-all approaches. By combining a universal global strategy with user-specific deltas and a dynamic rule flow mechanism grounded in task outcomes, HiPS achieves more optimal and evolving memory decisions over time.

title: TOPAS: Workflow-Aware Prefix-State Scheduling for Multi-Agent LLM Serving
summary: Prefix caching introduces a fundamental tradeoff in multi-agent large language model (LLM) serving: retaining a long system-prompt key-value (KV) cache for an agent accelerates future calls, yet it reduces the GPU memory available for batching concurrent requests. In multi-stage workflows, existing schedulers tend to prioritize either immediate prefix locality or overall workflow progress. However, under a shared KV cache budget, optimizing either objective in isolation can prolong tasklevel job completion time (JCT) through downstream delays or frequent prefix replacement. To strike a balance, we here propose TOPAS, a Task-Oriented Prefix-Aware Scheduler that jointly decides which agent prefixes to keep in the cache and which requests to schedule for execution. TOPAS scores candidate post-decision states by trading off the expected reduction in each task's longest remaining service path against the near-term benefit of downstream prefix reuse, accounting for the costs of prefix movement and preemption. A task-level aging mechanism is also incorporated to prevent starvation. We implement TOPAS within the SGLang framework and assess its performance on three synthetic DAGs and two MetaGPT software-development workflows. Compared with the best performing baseline for each workload and metric, TOPAS reduces the mean/p99 JCT by up to 39.8%/49.4% on the synthetic workloads, while lowering mean JCT by 9.8% on MetaGPT-SOP and mean/p99 JCT by 22.0%/26.6% on MetaGPT-TL.

AI.tldr: TOPAS is a scheduler for multi-agent LLM serving that jointly manages prefix KV-cache retention and request scheduling to minimize task-level job completion time under limited GPU memory.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent LLM workflows, keeping long system-prompt KV caches speeds up future calls but consumes GPU memory, limiting batching and increasing contention. Existing schedulers either focus on prefix reuse locality or overall workflow progress, which under a shared KV cache budget can worsen task-level job completion time due to downstream bottlenecks or frequent cache replacement. A better scheduler must explicitly balance cache management with workflow-aware scheduling decisions.
AI.method: The authors design TOPAS, a Task-Oriented Prefix-Aware Scheduler that makes joint decisions about which agent prefixes (KV caches) to retain and which requests to execute. TOPAS evaluates candidate post-decision system states using a scoring function that trades off (1) expected reduction in each task's longest remaining service path across the workflow DAG and (2) the potential near-term benefit from reusing cached prefixes. The scoring incorporates the costs of moving prefixes in/out of cache and preempting work. A task-level aging mechanism is added to avoid starvation. TOPAS is implemented in the SGLang LLM serving framework.
AI.result: On three synthetic DAG workloads and two real MetaGPT software-development workflows, TOPAS outperforms prior schedulers. Relative to the best baseline per workload and metric, TOPAS reduces mean and p99 job completion time (JCT) by up to 39.8% and 49.4% respectively on synthetic workloads, achieves a 9.8% mean JCT reduction on MetaGPT-SOP, and reduces mean/p99 JCT by 22.0%/26.6% on MetaGPT-TL.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing prefix KV-cache retention and task scheduling, while accounting for workflow structure, cache movement costs, and starvation, leads to significantly lower task-level JCT in multi-agent LLM serving. TOPAS demonstrates that task-oriented, prefix-aware scheduling is more effective than heuristics that separately optimize for locality or progress, and can be practically integrated into existing LLM serving frameworks like SGLang.

title: Where vs What: Decomposing Structural and Content Failures in LLM-Generated Structured Outputs
summary: Structured outputs such as JSON and tables are central to modern LLM-based systems, yet generation failures are evaluated monolithically, conflating two distinct error modes: placement errors (correct values at wrong positions) and value errors (wrong values at intended positions). We introduce Structure-Content Decomposition (SCD), a framework that independently measures structural fidelity and content accuracy. Applying SCD to nested JSON and table tasks across six models (7B to frontier), we uncover a consistent phenomenon: structural fidelity degrades earlier and more sharply than content accuracy as complexity increases. At the highest complexity, even DeepSeek-V4-Flash (with reasoning) misplaces 35% of recalled values, while Qwen2.5-7B misplaces 74%. Controlled ablations suggest that this pattern is associated with reliance on semantic shortcuts rather than topological understanding of output structure. Based on these findings, we propose SA-RLVR, converting SCD metrics into verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning via GRPO. SA-RLVR successfully optimizes structural addressing across distinct topologies: it lifts JSON Value Placement Accuracy (VPA) from 26% to 63% while generalizing to held-out schemas; moreover, it consistently drives VPA improvements in the table domain, demonstrating that structure-aware rewards can directly enhance multi-domain structural positioning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Structure-Content Decomposition (SCD) to separately evaluate structural fidelity and content accuracy in LLM-generated structured outputs, shows that structure fails earlier than content as complexity grows, and proposes a reinforcement learning method (SA-RLVR) that uses SCD-based rewards to significantly improve structural placement across JSON and table tasks.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of structured outputs from LLMs treat all errors as the same, failing to distinguish between misplacing correct values and generating wrong values. This conflation hides important failure modes and hinders targeted improvements. The authors want a principled way to disentangle structure-related errors from content-related errors, understand how each scales with complexity, and design training signals that directly optimize structural correctness.
AI.method: They define Structure-Content Decomposition (SCD), which separately measures structural fidelity (are values placed in the right slots/coordinates?) and content accuracy (are the values themselves correct for their intended slots?). They apply SCD to nested JSON and table-generation tasks across six models ranging from 7B to frontier-scale, under varying structural complexities. They run controlled ablations to probe whether models rely on semantic shortcuts vs genuine structural/topological understanding. Building on SCD, they design SA-RLVR, a structure-aware reinforcement learning scheme that converts SCD metrics into verifiable rewards, using GRPO as the RL optimization mechanism, and evaluate it across different schema/topology settings and domains (JSON, tables).
AI.result: Empirically, they observe a robust trend: as structural complexity increases, structural fidelity degrades much earlier and more steeply than content accuracy, even for advanced models with reasoning capabilities. For example, at high complexity DeepSeek-V4-Flash misplaces 35% of recalled values and Qwen2.5-7B misplaces 74%. Ablations link this to reliance on semantic shortcuts over explicit structural reasoning. SA-RLVR, using SCD-based rewards, substantially improves structural placement: JSON Value Placement Accuracy (VPA) increases from 26% to 63%, these gains generalize to unseen JSON schemas, and they also obtain consistent VPA improvements for table tasks, showing cross-topology and cross-domain effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating structured outputs via a single aggregate metric obscures crucial differences between structural and content failures in LLMs. Structure-Content Decomposition reveals that models tend to lose structural fidelity before content accuracy as task complexity grows, indicating weak topological understanding and a dependence on semantic cues. By transforming SCD into verifiable RL rewards (SA-RLVR), the authors show that it is possible to directly optimize structural addressing and significantly improve value placement across diverse structures and domains, suggesting a promising pathway for more robust structured generation systems.

title: ClueWeaver: Reward-Guided Dual-Agent Evidence Reasoning for Compact LLMs on Literary Long Narratives
summary: Humanities and social science research requires close reading of long narrative materials such as novels, scripts, archives, and case reports, yet many users have limited access to costly proprietary long-context models. Compact, locally deployable language models are a practical alternative, but directly feeding them an entire long context remains costly, hard to inspect, and prone to missing sparse evidence. We present ClueWeaver, an evidence-aware dual-agent framework for long-narrative question answering with compact local models. A Finder identifies passages containing answer-critical clues through retrieval-guided segmentation, while an Interpreter derives the answer from the selected evidence, produces rationales with paragraph-ID citations, and applies an internal self-calibration pass for high-risk questions. Both agents are optimized with reward-guided reinforcement learning: Finder rewards emphasize evidence retention and faithful paragraph-ID references, and Interpreter rewards emphasize correctness, grounding, and concise explanations. This decomposition makes evidence selection and reasoning more inspectable than end-to-end prompting. Experiments across multiple long-context narrative question answering and claim verification settings show that ClueWeaver substantially improves local end-to-end language models while providing evidence coverage and paragraph-referenced reasoning traces. Code is available at https://github.com/Ameame1/ClueWeaver.
