AI.tldr: ClueWeaver is a dual‑agent, evidence‑aware framework that lets small, local language models answer questions about long narratives by first finding key passages and then carefully reasoning over them with explicit citations.
AI.motivation: Long-narrative humanities and social science research (novels, archives, case reports) needs close reading over many pages, but most users lack access to expensive long-context LLMs. Small, locally deployable models are more practical, yet naively feeding them entire long texts is inefficient, opaque, and risks missing sparse but crucial evidence. The authors want a method that (1) works well with compact local models, (2) scales to long narratives, and (3) yields inspectable evidence and reasoning rather than a black-box answer.
AI.method: They propose ClueWeaver, a dual-agent framework tailored for long-narrative QA using compact models. A Finder agent first segments the long text and uses retrieval-guided selection to identify passages likely containing answer-critical clues. An Interpreter agent then reads only these selected segments, generates answers with paragraph-ID–level citations, and runs a self-calibration step for high-risk questions. Both agents are trained via reward-guided reinforcement learning: Finder is rewarded for high evidence recall and accurate paragraph references; Interpreter is rewarded for answer correctness, grounding in cited evidence, and concise rationales. This decomposes the task into explicit evidence selection plus reasoning, improving transparency and controllability versus end-to-end prompting.
AI.result: Across several benchmarks in long-context narrative question answering and claim verification, ClueWeaver significantly boosts the performance of compact, local end-to-end models. It achieves better answer accuracy while maintaining strong evidence coverage and producing reasoning traces that are explicitly tied to paragraph IDs. The reported results show consistent gains over baseline approaches that either attempt full-context processing or less-structured retrieval-augmented setups.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that a dual-agent, evidence-aware design combined with reinforcement learning is an effective way to adapt compact local language models to long-narrative tasks. By explicitly separating evidence finding from interpretation, ClueWeaver delivers improved accuracy, better coverage of relevant evidence, and more inspectable, paragraph-referenced rationales compared to monolithic prompting. This suggests a viable, transparent alternative to relying on expensive, proprietary long-context LLMs for humanities and social science applications involving extended narratives.

title: Can your AI agent be cheaper? Investigating the effects of task specifications on token spend in agentic coding tasks
summary: Agentic coding workflows are now widely deployed in real-world systems. With long-horizon reasoning and tool use, token usage has become an important consideration for both cost and efficiency. Two engineers using AI will solve the same problem differently. How the specification of a task shapes an agent's token spend, and whether that spend can be predicted in advance, are open questions. Here, we study the effects of different task specifications on agentic token spend with the Kimi K3 model at three thinking efforts. Across $2,700$ runs, we show that reducing a full task specification to a bare user story raises token spend by $29.7\%$, while run-to-run variance remains unaffected by any prompt changes. We show that prompt-sensitivity is task-dependent, running from $13\%$ to $115\%$. We fit a simple predictor that can price a full distribution of task specifications and thinking effort configurations from a single cheap probe on an unseen task within $36\%$, improving over prior work in predicting token spend. Our work provides initial results quantifying the effects of task specification on agentic token spend and introduces a method that can be used to systematically evaluate the cost of AI coding workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different task specifications affect token usage and its predictability in agentic coding workflows using the Kimi K3 model.
AI.motivation: As agentic coding systems become common in real-world use, token usage directly impacts cost and latency. However, how different ways of specifying the same coding task change token consumption, and whether this can be predicted beforehand, is unclear. The authors aim to systematically quantify these effects to help practitioners plan and optimize AI coding workflows.
AI.method: They run 2,700 experiments using the Kimi K3 model across three levels of “thinking effort” (depth/length of reasoning) and multiple prompt styles, from full task specifications to minimal user stories. They measure total token spend, analyze variance across runs, and quantify prompt-sensitivity per task. They then train a simple predictor model that, using a single low-cost probe on a new task and effort level, estimates the entire distribution of token usage across different task specifications and thinking efforts.
AI.result: They find that compressing a detailed specification into a bare user story increases token spend by 29.7% on average, while run-to-run variance in token usage is essentially unaffected by prompt modifications. Prompt-sensitivity depends heavily on the task, ranging from 13% to 115%. Their predictor can estimate token spend distributions for unseen tasks and configurations within 36% error, surpassing prior work on token usage prediction.
AI.conclusion: Task specification has a quantifiable and often substantial impact on token usage in agentic coding workflows. Simplifying prompts can unexpectedly increase total tokens used, and this sensitivity varies by task but not in terms of variance across runs. A simple probe-based predictor can reasonably forecast token costs for new tasks, enabling more systematic pricing and optimization of AI coding workflows.

title: Virgil: Navigating Explainability for Transformer-based Language Models
summary: Explainability for transformer-based language models is becoming crucial as these systems are deployed in high-stakes applications. As a result, the ecosystem of explainability tools is rapidly evolving, becoming richer, but also more fragmented and harder to navigate. To address this challenge, we present Virgil, an interactive system that lets practitioners and researchers, including non-experts, navigate explainability tools for transformer language models. Supported by a curated knowledge base, the system enables users to discover and compare explainability tools within a unified interface.

AI.tldr: Virgil is an interactive system that helps users navigate and compare explainability tools for transformer-based language models via a curated knowledge base and unified interface.
AI.motivation: The growing use of transformer-based language models in high-stakes applications makes explainability critical. However, the explainability ecosystem is rapidly expanding and fragmented, making it hard for practitioners—especially non-experts—to find, understand, and compare appropriate tools.
AI.method: Design and implementation of Virgil, an interactive system backed by a curated knowledge base of explainability tools. The interface allows users to browse, filter, and compare tools for transformer language models in a unified environment tailored to both practitioners and researchers.
AI.result: Virgil provides a centralized, interactive environment where users can systematically discover and compare explainability tools for transformer-based language models, mitigating fragmentation and lowering the barrier to entry for non-experts.
AI.conclusion: A curated, interactive, and unified system like Virgil can substantially improve how practitioners and researchers access and reason about explainability tools for transformer language models, addressing fragmentation and supporting more informed tool selection and use.

title: Paint What You See: Benchmarking Dexterous Visual Tool Use in Multimodal Agents
summary: Evaluation is shifting from static QA toward agentic settings where models act through external tools. We identify a critical yet underexplored capability within this space - dexterous visual tool use: fine-grained, closed-loop parameterized visual action in which models infer tool parameters from visual evidence, and those parameters directly govern the final result. Existing benchmarks cover web navigation, GUI operation, and software engineering, but rarely target this coupling between visual evidence and execution precision. We propose EASEL, a benchmark evaluating a controlled instance of dexterous visual tool use that adopts reference-guided visual reconstruction as its primary proxy task: the agent incrementally paints a canvas to match a reference image. EASEL additionally includes semantic tasks spanning region annotation, handwriting, and path planning. We further provide EASEL-Data, a 440k-sample two-stage curriculum dataset for trajectory supervision, and EASEL-9B to investigate its effect on this capability. Evaluation of 25 models reveals that current multimodal agents systematically struggle on EASEL. Reconstruction similarity bottlenecks at low levels (0.40-0.54), while trajectory diagnostics expose severe closed-loop instability - models typically saturate early or degrade post-peak. Semantic tasks reveal sharp capability boundaries in precision annotation and path planning. EASEL-9B, trained on EASEL-Data, surpasses the base model by a relative 6.3%, ranking third among all evaluated models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EASEL, a benchmark and dataset for testing models’ ability to perform precise, closed-loop visual tool use via reference-guided image reconstruction and related semantic tasks.
AI.motivation: As evaluation shifts from static question answering to agentic tool-using models, there is a gap in benchmarks that specifically test fine-grained visual control: inferring continuous action parameters from visual evidence where these parameters tightly determine the final outcome. Existing benchmarks emphasize navigation or discrete UI actions, not the precise coupling between perception and parametric execution, so the authors aim to fill this gap.
AI.method: They design EASEL, a benchmark where an agent incrementally paints a canvas to match a reference image, requiring parameterized strokes conditioned on visual comparison. They add semantic subtasks such as region annotation, handwriting, and path planning to probe related skills. They create EASEL-Data, a 440k-sample, two-stage curriculum dataset for trajectory supervision, and train EASEL-9B, a model specialized on this data. They then evaluate 25 multimodal models on EASEL, analyzing reconstruction scores and detailed trajectory diagnostics to assess closed-loop stability and precision.
AI.result: Across 25 multimodal agents, reconstruction performance is low (similarity scores 0.40–0.54), and trajectory analyses show strong closed-loop instability, with agents’ performance saturating early or degrading after an initial peak. Semantic tasks reveal clear limitations in precise annotation and path planning. The EASEL-9B model trained on EASEL-Data improves relative performance by 6.3% over its base model and ranks third among all evaluated models.
AI.conclusion: Dexterous visual tool use—precise, feedback-driven parameter control based on visual input—is currently a major weakness of multimodal agents. EASEL provides a controlled benchmark and large-scale dataset to study this capability and its failure modes. While specialized training on EASEL-Data (EASEL-9B) yields measurable gains, overall results show that current systems are far from robust, stable visual tool users, underscoring the need for further research on closed-loop, fine-grained visual control.

title: EgoArgus: Benchmarking VLMs as Situational Assistants for Modality-Grounded User Supports
summary: VLMs are increasingly positioned as daily assistants that perceive first-person environments, follow user dialogue, and decide how to help. Existing egocentric benchmarks mainly evaluate visual understanding in isolation, leaving open whether models can arbitrate between visual evidence and user-provided language when the two are helpful, irrelevant, or conflicting. We introduce EgoArgus, a human-annotated dataset for evaluating egocentric assistants on understanding and decision tasks in five dialogue-video daily scenarios. Our results demonstrate that it is still challenging for current VLMs as reliable egocentric assistants, which requires identifying which modality is trustworthy and deciding when intervention is warranted. Deeper analysis also shows that existing modality bias mitigation methods are quite restricted to enhance performance, providing insights to aid practioners into the deployment of current VLMs as daily assistants.

AI.tldr: EgoArgus introduces an egocentric dialogue–video benchmark to test whether VLM assistants can correctly balance visual evidence and user language, revealing that current models still struggle, especially with modality conflicts and intervention decisions.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models are being used as daily assistants in first-person settings, where they must interpret both what they see and what users say. Existing benchmarks mainly test visual understanding alone, not the crucial ability to arbitrate between visual information and user instructions, especially when they are misaligned or only partially helpful. The authors want to fill this evaluation gap to understand how reliable VLMs are as egocentric assistants and how modality biases affect their decisions.
AI.method: The authors construct EgoArgus, a human-annotated dataset focused on egocentric assistant behavior in dialogue–video scenarios from daily life. The benchmark defines understanding and decision-making tasks across five types of dialogue-video situations, where visual and linguistic cues can be helpful, irrelevant, or conflicting. They then evaluate current VLMs on this benchmark and test existing methods for mitigating modality bias to see how well these techniques help models choose the right modality and decide on appropriate interventions.
AI.result: Experiments show that current VLMs perform poorly or unreliably when they must choose between or integrate visual evidence and user language in egocentric scenarios. The models often fail to identify which modality is more trustworthy and to determine when they should intervene. Attempts to apply existing modality bias mitigation techniques yield only limited improvements, indicating that these methods are not sufficient for robust egocentric assistance.
AI.conclusion: EgoArgus reveals that present-day VLMs are not yet dependable as egocentric daily assistants, particularly in situations where visual and linguistic information differ in relevance or conflict. The benchmark highlights the need for better approaches to modality arbitration and intervention decision-making, and it shows that current bias mitigation strategies are too narrow to fully address these issues. This provides practical guidance and open challenges for deploying VLM-based assistants in real-world first-person contexts.

title: Distance Is Not Enough: Forget-Retain Alignment Gap Predicts LLM Relearning Robustness
summary: Machine unlearning aims to make a model forget specific data, yet unlearned LLMs often fail to stay unlearned: brief fine-tuning can revive removed knowledge. Existing robustness predictors rely on global weight-space displacement, but distance alone can be misleading when random or destructive updates collapse performance. We argue that relearning robustness depends on update structure: robust unlearning should affect forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones. We introduce the Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG), a training-free predictor that scores an update's forget-retain alignment without running a relearning attack, and separates selective from dense updates more reliably than global distance. Building on the forget-critical, retain-sparing principle, Forget-Retain Pruning (FRP) improves relearning robustness. Our results suggest that weight selectivity better explains robustness than distance alone. Code is available at https://github.com/Yi1-Chen/FRAG.

AI.tldr: The paper studies why machine unlearning for LLMs is not robust and proposes a new metric (FRAG) and a pruning method (FRP) to make unlearning more resistant to relearning attacks by focusing on which weights are changed, not just how much they change.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning for LLMs often fails because removed knowledge can be quickly relearned via brief fine-tuning, and current robustness metrics based on overall weight distance do not reliably predict this vulnerability. The authors want a better explanation and predictor of relearning robustness that accounts for how selectively the unlearning update targets relevant parameters.
AI.method: They conceptually split model parameters into forget-critical and retain-critical weights and argue that robust unlearning should mainly modify the former while preserving the latter. They introduce the Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG), a training-free predictor that evaluates how well an update is aligned with this forget/retain distinction, going beyond simple global distance. They also propose Forget-Retain Pruning (FRP), a technique that prunes or adjusts weights based on this principle to improve robustness against relearning attacks.
AI.result: FRAG can distinguish selective unlearning updates from dense or destructive ones more accurately than global weight-space distance and predicts relearning robustness without needing to run full attacks. Using FRP leads to models that are more robust to attempts to quickly relearn the unlearned information, indicating that targeting forget-critical and sparing retain-critical weights is effective.
AI.conclusion: Relearning robustness in machine unlearning is better explained by the structural selectivity of parameter updates—specifically their alignment with forget-critical vs. retain-critical weights—rather than by the magnitude of overall weight changes. The proposed FRAG metric and FRP method operationalize this insight and yield more reliably unlearned models.

title: Controllable Affective Generation via Latent Vector Steering
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often produce emotionally flattened responses after alignment, limiting their effectiveness in affect-sensitive applications. In this paper, we propose EmoVec, a lightweight framework for controllable affective generation via latent vector steering. EmoVec extracts emotion-specific directions from paired neutral and emotion-conditioned responses using contrastive activation addition, and further refines them through task-specific debiasing and principal subspace removal. During inference, these vectors are injected into the final residual stream with static or scenario-adaptive scaling, enabling continuous control over emotional intensity without updating model weights. Experiments across three LLMs and eight emotions show that EmoVec consistently improves emotional salience while largely preserving semantic content, fluency, and coherence. Ablation studies and human evaluation further confirm the effectiveness of vector purification and adaptive scaling, establishing EmoVec as a practical inference-time method for affective control in deployed LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EmoVec, a lightweight method to control the emotional tone of LLM outputs by steering internal activation vectors, improving emotional expressiveness without retraining the model.
AI.motivation: Aligned LLMs tend to generate emotionally flat responses, which reduces their usefulness for applications that require nuanced affect, such as empathetic dialogue, mental-health support chatbots, creative writing, or affect-aware tutoring. Existing emotion control methods often require fine-tuning, are model-specific, or sacrifice fluency and semantics. The authors are motivated to design a practical, inference-time technique that can enhance and control emotional expressiveness while preserving the original content and coherence, and that can work across different LLMs and emotions.
AI.method: The authors propose EmoVec, which operates by discovering and injecting "emotion vectors" in the LLM’s latent space. First, they collect paired responses: one neutral and one with a target emotion, for the same prompts. They then use contrastive activation addition to compute emotion-specific directions—essentially differences in residual stream activations between emotional and neutral outputs. These raw directions are purified via task-specific debiasing and principal subspace removal to reduce entanglement with non-emotional factors. At inference, without changing the LLM weights, they add these emotion vectors into the final residual stream, using either fixed (static) scaling or context-aware (scenario-adaptive) scaling to control emotional intensity continuously. The framework is evaluated on multiple base LLMs and for eight distinct emotions.
AI.result: Across three different LLM backbones and eight target emotions, EmoVec increases the perceived emotional salience of generated text while mostly preserving the original semantic content, fluency, and coherence. Quantitative metrics and qualitative analyses show that the method effectively amplifies or adjusts emotional tone. Ablation studies indicate that vector purification (debiasing and principal subspace removal) and adaptive scaling significantly contribute to performance, avoiding over-saturation or semantic drift. Human evaluations align with automatic metrics, confirming that outputs are both more affective and still understandable/appropriate.
AI.conclusion: EmoVec is an effective and practical inference-time framework for controllable affective text generation in LLMs. By steering carefully purified emotion vectors in the residual stream, it allows fine-grained control over emotional intensity across multiple emotions and models without any parameter updates. The method improves emotional expressiveness while preserving core semantic content and fluency, and its modular design makes it suitable for deployment in real-world affect-sensitive systems.

title: Training Alignment Auditors via Reinforcement Learning
comment: 82 pages, 15 figures. Code, prompts, and evaluation data are available at https://github.com/paulrosu11/training-auditing-agents-public
summary: Alignment auditing of frontier models increasingly relies on LLM auditors to surface undesirable behaviors at scale, but current automated auditors can struggle with coherent investigation and audit realism. In this work, we improve LLM auditors with reinforcement learning. In our best training environment, the policy investigates target models that potentially possess hidden behaviors planted via their system prompt. An LLM judge, which knows whether the target has a hidden behavior, holistically compares the policy's investigation to a reference investigation to determine the reward. With systematic ablations, we find that pairwise rewards yield more robust training compared to pointwise rewards, and that adding targets without planted behaviors helps maintain a low false positive rate. Training improves investigation quality against targets with planted behaviors, the rate of concerning behaviors surfaced in unmodified production models, and audit realism, while false-positive rates stay below 1%. Furthermore, auditing capabilities generalize across scaffolds: performance on AuditBench's adversarially fine-tuned targets substantially improves [Sheshadri et al., 2026].

AI.tldr: They train LLM-based alignment auditors with reinforcement learning to better uncover hidden unsafe behaviors in frontier models, improving investigation quality and realism while keeping false positives under 1%.
AI.motivation: Automated alignment audits increasingly depend on LLMs to probe other models at scale, but current LLM auditors often conduct shallow, incoherent investigations and fail to mimic realistic red-teaming, limiting their usefulness for detecting subtle or hidden unsafe behaviors.
AI.method: They formulate auditing as a reinforcement learning problem where a policy (the auditor) interacts with target models that may have hidden behaviors implanted via their system prompts. An LLM judge, informed about the ground-truth presence of hidden behaviors, compares each policy investigation trajectory against a reference investigation and assigns rewards, with a focus on pairwise (relative) rewards instead of pointwise scoring. They systematically ablate reward design and target selection, including targets without hidden behaviors, to study training stability, generalization, and false-positive control.
AI.result: Using their RL setup, auditors become better at investigating models with planted hidden behaviors, surface more genuinely concerning behaviors from real, unmodified production models, and generate audits judged as more realistic overall. Pairwise reward schemes outperform pointwise rewards in robustness, and incorporating clean targets (no hidden behavior) is crucial for keeping false positives below 1%. The improved auditor also transfers well across different scaffolding setups, significantly boosting performance on AuditBench adversarially fine-tuned targets.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning can substantially enhance LLM-based alignment auditors, leading to deeper, more realistic investigations that uncover more problematic behaviors without substantially increasing false positives. Careful reward shaping—especially using pairwise comparisons and a mix of contaminated and clean targets—is key, and the resulting auditors generalize beyond their training setup to standardized benchmarks like AuditBench.

title: Generative vs. Encoder Large Language Models for ASR Evaluation: A Comparative Study
summary: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) is typically evaluated using Word Error Rate (WER), which poorly reflects semantic similarity. While embedding-based metrics correlate better with human judgments, the respective roles of encoder and decoder-based Large Language Models (LLMs) remain underexplored. This paper presents a comparative study of both families for ASR evaluation. We analyze BERTScore and SemDist across different LLMs, layers, and pooling strategies, showing that both metrics can achieve strong correlation with human judgments when properly configured. For decoder models, we investigate generative LLMs in two settings: pairwise hypothesis selection via prompting and direct qualitative error classification. Our results show that encoder-based metrics remain highly competitive, while generative LLMs perform strongly in hypothesis comparison and improve the interpretability of ASR evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper compares encoder- and decoder-based large language model metrics for ASR evaluation, showing that properly configured embedding-based scores correlate well with human judgments, and that generative LLMs add strong hypothesis comparison and interpretability benefits.
AI.motivation: Conventional ASR evaluation using Word Error Rate fails to capture semantic similarity between transcripts, motivating the use of embedding-based and LLM-based metrics whose relative strengths are not yet well understood.
AI.method: The authors systematically study embedding-based metrics (BERTScore, SemDist) across various encoder and decoder LLMs, exploring different layers and pooling strategies, and evaluate generative LLMs in two modes: (1) prompting them to choose the better hypothesis among alternatives, and (2) using them to qualitatively classify ASR errors.
AI.result: Both BERTScore and SemDist, when appropriately configured with the right model layers and pooling, show high correlation with human judgments; encoder-based approaches remain very competitive, while generative LLMs excel at pairwise hypothesis selection and provide rich qualitative error analyses.
AI.conclusion: Embedding-based encoder metrics can serve as strong, reliable ASR evaluation tools when carefully tuned, and generative LLMs are particularly valuable for comparative judgments between hypotheses and for making ASR evaluation more interpretable through explicit error categorization.

title: PonsRAG: A Pons-Inspired RAG Bridging Cognitive Islands for Coordinated Long Narrative Reasoning
summary: Long Narrative Reasoning is an essential capability for processing and reasoning over complex narratives. While retrieval-augmented generation provides a promising framework, existing methods still face two critical challenges: cognitive islanding and cross-layer evidence disconnection. To address these issues, we propose PonsRAG, a coordinated RAG framework inspired by the biological pons. PonsRAG consists of two key components: Triple-Layer Indexing, which organizes documents into a connected knowledge structure to bridge cognitive islands, and Coordinated Reasoning, which retrieves evidence across distinct layers and integrates cross-layer information into a unified context. We evaluate PonsRAG on four long-context narrative benchmarks, and experimental results show that it outperforms the strongest baseline, achieving a 11.56% relative improvement in average accuracy on multi-choice tasks.

AI.tldr: PonsRAG is a coordinated retrieval-augmented generation framework for long narrative reasoning that builds a triple-layer index and coordinated cross-layer reasoning, significantly improving accuracy on long-context narrative benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG methods struggle with long narrative reasoning due to two issues: cognitive islanding, where relevant pieces of information stay isolated, and cross-layer evidence disconnection, where evidence residing in different representational layers (e.g., passages, events, entities) is not effectively linked for reasoning.
AI.method: The authors propose PonsRAG, a biologically inspired framework with two main components. Triple-Layer Indexing structures the corpus into three interconnected layers, forming a connected knowledge graph-like structure that links related narrative pieces and reduces isolation. Coordinated Reasoning then retrieves evidence from these distinct layers in a coordinated manner and integrates them into a unified context for generation, enabling the model to reason across narrative levels rather than from a flat set of passages.
AI.result: On four long-context narrative benchmarks, including multi-choice tasks, PonsRAG consistently outperforms strong RAG baselines. It yields an 11.56% relative improvement in average accuracy on multi-choice tasks, indicating better capability in handling complex, long narrative reasoning problems.
AI.conclusion: Structuring narrative documents into a triple-layer index and coordinating cross-layer retrieval and reasoning can substantially mitigate cognitive islanding and evidence disconnection in RAG systems. PonsRAG demonstrates that such a biologically inspired coordination mechanism leads to more effective long narrative reasoning and measurable performance gains over existing methods.

title: Cross-Dataset Stability of Expert-Informed Skill Prompting and Fine-Tuning for Chinese Metaphor Identification
summary: Metaphor-identification performance can change markedly across datasets that differ in text distribution and annotation policy. We examine whether a fixed expert-informed procedure produces a more even cross-dataset profile than task-specific parameter adaptation. Four prespecified conditions are compared for Chinese sentence-level metaphor identification: BERT fine-tuning (BERT-FT), QLoRA-based large language model fine-tuning (LLM-FT), direct zero-shot LLM prompting (LLM-ZS), and zero-shot prompting with a frozen procedural Skill (Skill-ZS). The Skill operationalizes established criteria involving contextual meaning, basic meaning, contrast, and comparison. Evaluation covers CMRE Test and two external datasets, CCIME and CMC. Fine-tuned scores are means over three seeds, whereas each zero-shot score comes from one deterministic configuration. Fine-tuning remains strongest on the native test set: BERT-FT reaches 91.76 Macro-F1. LLM-FT has the highest external mean (83.52), while Skill-ZS is close at 82.92 and has both the highest external floor (82.64) and the smallest observed range across all three datasets (4.08 points). In the matched zero-shot comparison, adding the Skill reduces metaphorical predictions on every dataset. This sharply lowers false positives on CCIME but increases false negatives on CMRE Test and CMC. The results position expert-informed Skill prompting as a complementary route to more even observed cross-dataset performance, while fine-tuning retains its advantage in native-data accuracy. To our knowledge, this is the first study to compare an expert-informed procedural Skill with task-specific fine-tuning in the same cross-dataset evaluation of Chinese sentence-level metaphor identification.

AI.tldr: The paper compares expert-informed procedural prompting and model fine-tuning for Chinese sentence-level metaphor identification across multiple datasets, finding that fine-tuning excels on in-domain data while the procedural Skill yields more stable cross-dataset performance.
AI.motivation: Metaphor detection systems often show large performance drops when applied to new datasets with different text distributions and annotation policies. The authors want to know whether using an expert-designed, fixed decision procedure (a "Skill" based on linguistic metaphor criteria) can provide more consistent performance across datasets than standard task-specific fine-tuning approaches.
AI.method: They evaluate four pre-specified conditions on Chinese sentence-level metaphor identification: (1) BERT fine-tuning (BERT-FT), (2) QLoRA-based fine-tuning of a large language model (LLM-FT), (3) direct zero-shot prompting of an LLM (LLM-ZS), and (4) zero-shot prompting of an LLM using a frozen, expert-informed procedural Skill (Skill-ZS) that encodes criteria about contextual vs. basic meaning, contrast, and comparison. Models are trained on CMRE and tested on its Test set plus two external datasets, CCIME and CMC. Fine-tuned models are averaged over three random seeds; zero-shot settings use a single deterministic configuration. They compare Macro-F1 scores, cross-dataset means, floors, and performance ranges, and analyze error trade-offs (false positives vs. false negatives).
AI.result: On the native CMRE Test set, fine-tuning performs best: BERT-FT achieves 91.76 Macro-F1. Across external datasets, LLM-FT has the highest average Macro-F1 (83.52), closely followed by the Skill-ZS condition (82.92). The Skill-ZS setting attains the highest external floor (82.64) and the smallest performance spread across all three datasets (a 4.08-point range), indicating more even cross-dataset behavior. When comparing zero-shot methods directly, adding the Skill reduces the proportion of metaphorical predictions on every dataset, which sharply cuts false positives on CCIME but increases false negatives on CMRE Test and CMC.
AI.conclusion: Expert-informed procedural Skill prompting, when used in zero-shot LLM prompting, offers a complementary approach to task-specific fine-tuning by providing more stable performance across different metaphor datasets, even if it does not surpass fine-tuning on in-domain accuracy. Fine-tuning remains the best option for maximizing performance on the training-domain test set, but the Skill-based method improves robustness and consistency under cross-dataset evaluation. The study is presented as the first to directly compare such an expert-informed Skill with fine-tuned models for Chinese sentence-level metaphor identification across multiple datasets.

title: CaSKG: Counterfactual-Causal Skill Graphs for Scalable Agent Skill Retrieval
summary: Reusable skill libraries allow large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedural knowledge across tasks, but they also turn memory access into a challenging retrieval problem. Full-library prompting preserves coverage at high context cost, vector retrieval returns compact neighborhoods but treats skills as independent text, and graph-based retrieval can recover workflow context only when the edges that carry relevance are reliable. We propose CaSKG, a counterfactual-causal skill graph framework that calibrates procedural relations before retrieval. CaSKG first builds a high-recall directed candidate graph from semantic, lexical, input/output, and structural evidence, with repair evidence and an optional LLM judge further refining candidate scores. It then applies direction-conditioned textual counterfactual probes that remove, substitute, and reorder skill pairs, aggregates the evidence with Bayesian smoothing, and publishes a state-filtered weighted graph for task-conditioned expansion. The graph is constructed offline and used without changing the downstream agent policy or task interface. Across six LLM backbones on ALFWorld ID-140 and ScienceWorld U211, CaSKG achieves the highest task score in all twelve combinations of model and benchmark. Relative to Graph-of-Skills (GoS), it improves the six-model macro-average ScienceWorld score from 72.62 to 80.50 and ALFWorld success from 80.01\% to 86.79\%, while reducing mean environment steps on both benchmarks. Qualitative and ablation analyses further show that calibrated edges help retrieval preserve prerequisites, state-changing actions, verification routines, and final completion steps. These results position edge-confidence calibration as an effective route to compact and executable skill retrieval at scale\footnote{Code is available at: https://github.com/ZhiyuanLi218/Caskg }.

AI.tldr: CaSKG introduces a counterfactual-causal skill graph to improve retrieval from reusable skill libraries for LLM agents, significantly boosting task performance and efficiency over prior graph-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for retrieving skills from large reusable libraries face trade-offs: full-library prompting is expensive, vector retrieval ignores procedural structure, and prior graph-based retrieval depends on noisy or unreliable edges. There is a need for a retrieval mechanism that preserves procedural dependencies (like prerequisites and verification steps) while remaining compact and scalable.
AI.method: CaSKG constructs a high-recall candidate directed graph of skills using multiple evidence sources (semantic, lexical, input/output, structural, plus repair signals and an optional LLM judge). It then runs direction-aware textual counterfactual probes that remove, substitute, or reorder skill pairs to estimate how one skill causally depends on another. These signals are combined with Bayesian smoothing to calibrate edge weights. The result is a state-filtered weighted skill graph that can be used at inference time for task-conditioned expansion, without modifying the downstream agent policy or interface.
AI.result: Across six LLM backbones on ALFWorld ID-140 and ScienceWorld U211 benchmarks, CaSKG yields the best task scores in all twelve model–benchmark combinations. Compared to Graph-of-Skills, it raises macro-average ScienceWorld scores from 72.62 to 80.50, ALFWorld success from 80.01% to 86.79%, and also reduces mean environment steps on both benchmarks. Qualitative and ablation studies show that calibrated edges preserve important procedural relations such as prerequisites, state-changing actions, verification routines, and final completion steps.
AI.conclusion: Edge-confidence calibration via counterfactual-causal probing enables more accurate and compact skill retrieval for LLM agents, leading to higher task success and greater efficiency. CaSKG demonstrates that carefully constructing and calibrating a skill graph offline can significantly improve downstream performance without altering the agent’s policy or task interface, highlighting edge calibration as a promising direction for scalable skill reuse.

title: GRIP: Granular Reward-Guided Parameter Interpolation for Efficient Reasoning
summary: Reasoning-oriented large language models often achieve strong problem-solving performance by generating long chains of thought, but this behavior substantially increases inference cost and latency. In contrast, instruction-tuned models tend to answer more concisely, yet often lack comparable reasoning ability. This accuracy-efficiency mismatch motivates a lightweight approach that combines the strengths of both models without full model retraining. In this paper, we propose GRIP (Granular Reward-guided Interpolation of Parameters), a reward-guided parameter interpolation framework for efficient reasoning. Given a reasoning model and an instruction model with identical architectures, GRIP assigns learnable interpolation ratios to individual modules and optimizes only these ratios while keeping both source models frozen. The interpolation ratios are trained with a reward signal that favors responses that are both correct and concise. Experiments show that GRIP achieves a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off than fixed or search-based merging baselines and further reveals module-wise fusion patterns associated with efficient reasoning.

AI.tldr: A method to efficiently combine a strong reasoning LLM and a concise instruction-tuned LLM by only learning interpolation ratios between their modules, improving the accuracy–efficiency trade-off without retraining full models.
AI.motivation: Reasoning-focused LLMs require long chains of thought, leading to high inference cost and latency, while instruction-tuned models are cheaper but weaker at reasoning. There is a need for a simple way to get the benefits of both—strong reasoning and concise answers—without expensive full model retraining or sacrificing efficiency.
AI.method: Start with two models of identical architecture: a reasoning model and an instruction-tuned model. Introduce learnable interpolation ratios for each corresponding module of the two models. During training, keep both base models frozen and optimize only these interpolation ratios using a reward signal. The reward encourages responses that are simultaneously correct and concise, so the learned module-wise fusion balances reasoning depth with brevity.
AI.result: The proposed GRIP framework outperforms fixed or search-based model merging techniques on the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency (e.g., shorter outputs, lower cost/latency for comparable or better accuracy). Analysis of the learned interpolation ratios uncovers meaningful module-wise fusion patterns that correlate with efficient reasoning behavior.
AI.conclusion: GRIP provides an efficient, training-light way to fuse a reasoning LLM with an instruction-tuned LLM, yielding models that maintain strong reasoning while reducing chain-of-thought length and inference cost. It also offers insight into which modules contribute most to efficient reasoning via the learned interpolation patterns.

title: Agentic Game Development as a Verifiable Trajectory Data Engine for Scaling World Models
summary: A common strategy for scaling world models is to train on more crawled video with more compute. We argue that this strategy is inefficient: scaling world models also requires a recursive data engine that offers grounded reward signals. The success of code agents illustrates why this matters. As code is executable, compilers and runtimes can provide high-quality rewards for Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training of LLMs. By contrast, spatial generation still relies largely on fuzzy proxies such as CLIP scores. These signals are fuzzy and biased, making them hard to support RL post-training. Compared with these, game development provides a missing reward environment for spatial world models. A scene encoded by a game engine is an executable world specification: the engine can efficiently check collision, physics, navigability and bounded playability, while the developer provides the global verification signal by judging whether the scene should be accepted. Game development also provides real-world long-horizon trajectory data for RL post-training. We therefore propose Reinforcement Learning with Human-Engine Verification (RLHEV), a post-training paradigm that combines dense engine signals with implicit human acceptance feedback from the development process.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RL with Human-Engine Verification (RLHEV), using game engines plus human acceptance as grounded reward signals to more efficiently scale spatial world models, analogous to how executability and compilers benefit code agents.
AI.motivation: Scaling world models by simply adding more crawled video and compute is inefficient and lacks grounded reward signals suitable for RL post-training. While code agents benefit from executable code and compiler/runtime feedback that provide clear, dense rewards, spatial generation models currently depend on fuzzy, biased proxies like CLIP scores. There is a need for an environment that offers executable, grounded, and rich feedback for spatial world models to enable effective RL post-training and better scaling.
AI.method: The authors reframe game development as a rich reward environment for spatial world models. They propose Reinforcement Learning with Human-Engine Verification (RLHEV), a post-training paradigm where game engines serve as executors of scene specifications. The engine computes dense, structured signals (e.g., collision, physics, navigability, playability constraints), while human developers provide an implicit binary or scalar acceptance signal based on whether generated scenes are actually adopted in development. RLHEV combines these dense engine-based rewards with human acceptance feedback to train and refine spatial world models.
AI.result: Within the abstract, detailed empirical results are not provided. Conceptually, the result is the demonstration that game-engine-backed environments can function as an “executable world specification” analogous to code execution environments, offering a practical framework for grounded RL post-training of spatial world models through RLHEV.
AI.conclusion: To efficiently scale spatial world models, it is not enough to increase passive video data and compute; one must also build a recursive data engine with grounded reward signals. Game engines, treated as executable specifications of 3D scenes, provide such signals through physics and playability checks, while developers supply high-level acceptance feedback. The proposed RLHEV paradigm combines these elements, offering a promising route for post-training spatial world models with more reliable and informative rewards than current proxy metrics like CLIP scores.

title: JIT-Agent: Scaling Harness Intelligence via Just-in-Time Harness Evolution
summary: Agent capability is not determined by the model alone. The agent harness, encompassing memory management, planning strategy, action protocol, and tool/skill orchestration, can dominate the contribution of the underlying foundation model. Yet harness design remains manual, task-specific, and fundamentally unscalable. We present JIT-Agent, a harness intelligence model trained to synthesize task-adaptive agent harnesses on the fly for arbitrary off-the-shelf agentic LLMs. We formalize the agent harness as a composable, machine-generatable artifact governed by a fixed four-module protocol, and train JIT-Agent to customize harnesses for a given task at hand, repair harnesses for stable and reliable execution, and self-evolve by distilling performance signals from an expanding archive of prior harness configurations. Equipped with JIT-Agent as a harness helper, DeepSeek-V4-Flash surpasses GPT-5.6 on DeepSearchQA (+9.1) and OdysseyBench (+4.3), while the already strong GLM-5.2 gains up to +20.2 points. Across controlled evaluations, JIT-Agent-generated harnesses are performance-competitive with mature agent runtimes such as OpenCode and Claude Code and consistently improve multi-scale model families of DeepSeek V4, Mimo-V2.5, and Qwen3.6. To our knowledge, JIT-Agent is the first model purpose-built for just-in-time harness generation, establishing harness intelligence as a trainable, transferable, and compounding dimension of agent capability orthogonal to model scaling.

AI.tldr: JIT-Agent is a model that automatically generates and adapts agent harnesses (memory, planning, tools, control logic) for LLM agents, greatly boosting performance without changing the base model.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents rely heavily on manually designed, task-specific harnesses (memory systems, planners, tool protocols, etc.). These are labor-intensive, don’t transfer well across tasks, and do not scale. Moreover, empirical evidence shows that such harnesses can dominate overall agent capability, sometimes more than the underlying foundation model. The authors aim to make this harness intelligence itself trainable and generalizable, so that agent behavior can be optimized automatically and adaptively rather than via ad‑hoc engineering.
AI.method: They formalize an “agent harness” as a composable artifact governed by a fixed four‑module protocol (covering memory management, planning, action protocol, and tool/skill orchestration). They then train a specialized model, JIT-Agent, to: (1) synthesize task‑adaptive harnesses on the fly for arbitrary off‑the‑shelf agentic LLMs; (2) repair harnesses for stable, reliable execution; and (3) self‑evolve by distilling performance signals from an expanding archive of prior harness configurations. The model learns to output concrete harness configurations adhering to the four‑module schema for a given task and target LLM and iteratively improves using outcomes from previous runs.
AI.result: When used as a “harness helper” around different LLMs, JIT-Agent significantly increases performance. For example, DeepSeek‑V4‑Flash equipped with JIT-Agent outperforms GPT‑5.6 on DeepSearchQA by +9.1 points and on OdysseyBench by +4.3 points. GLM‑5.2, already a strong model, gains up to +20.2 points. In controlled benchmarks, JIT-Agent‑generated harnesses are competitive with established agent runtimes like OpenCode and Claude Code, and systematically improve several model families (DeepSeek V4, Mimo‑V2.5, Qwen3.6).
AI.conclusion: JIT-Agent demonstrates that the “harness” around an LLM—its memory, planning, tool use, and control logic—can be modeled as a trainable, generative artifact rather than static hand‑engineered code. The work establishes “harness intelligence” as a distinct, transferable, and compounding dimension of agent capability that is largely orthogonal to scaling the base language model itself. This opens a path toward automatically customized and continually self‑improving agent runtimes for diverse tasks and models.

title: Using profiles of cognitive capability to assess AI suitability for workplace tasks
summary: Organisations deploying AI face a scoping problem: which tasks can be automated, which should remain with humans, and which are best shared between the two. Aggregate benchmark scores provide little insight into where systems will succeed or fail in practice, while human judgements of model capabilities quickly become outdated. We introduce a pipeline that profiles agents and tasks using a shared set of core cognitive capabilities. Cognitive capability profiling infers an agent's capabilities from performance on a benchmark battery annotated for the cognitive demands of each item. Task requirements weighting elicits from domain experts the relative importance of these same capabilities for their work. As both use a common set of cognitive dimensions, they can be updated independently as models and roles change, and combined to estimate AI suitability at the level of a domain, organisation, role, or individual duty. We validate capability recovery on synthetic agents, profile six AI systems, and elicit task requirements from 410 employees across six occupational domains. AI systems differed more across cognitive dimensions than across model families, while workplace activities converged on a shared cognitive core. The resulting scores provide a comparative scoping tool for identifying promising candidates for piloting and areas where current systems are unlikely to be well suited. We discuss extending the framework to profile human workers alongside AI systems, moving from AI suitability towards human-machine task allocation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a cognitive capability profiling framework to decide which workplace tasks are suitable for AI, which for humans, and which should be shared.
AI.motivation: Existing AI evaluation methods, such as aggregate benchmark scores and static human judgments, do not offer actionable, up‑to‑date guidance on where AI systems will succeed or fail in real organisational tasks. Organisations therefore struggle to scope AI deployment: they lack a principled way to match specific AI systems to specific work activities. The paper aims to create a systematic, adaptable method to align AI capabilities with the cognitive demands of jobs.
AI.method: The authors build a two-sided profiling pipeline based on a shared set of core cognitive capabilities. On the AI side, they annotate items in a benchmark battery with the cognitive demands they require, then use AI agents’ performance on those items to infer each agent’s latent cognitive capability profile. On the task side, they collect task requirements weightings from domain experts, who rate the importance of each cognitive capability for their own roles and activities. Because both sides use the same cognitive dimensions, they can be independently updated and then mathematically combined to estimate AI suitability for specific domains, organisations, roles, or duties. They validate capability recovery on synthetic agents, profile six real AI systems, and survey 410 employees across six occupational domains to obtain human task profiles.
AI.result: The pipeline successfully recovers known capabilities for synthetic agents, indicating the method can infer latent cognitive profiles from annotated benchmarks. When applied to six real AI systems, the authors find that systems vary more along cognitive dimensions (e.g., reasoning, memory-like abilities, language use) than along high-level model families. Human workplace activities across six occupational domains show convergence on a shared core of cognitive capabilities, despite surface-level job differences. Combining AI and task profiles yields quantitative suitability scores that distinguish tasks where current AI is likely promising from those where it is currently weak.
AI.conclusion: The proposed cognitive capability profiling framework provides a comparative scoping tool for AI deployment, enabling organisations to identify where specific AI systems are likely to be useful and where human work should remain central. Because both AI and task profiles are expressed in the same cognitive space and can be updated independently, the approach is adaptable as models and job roles evolve. The authors suggest extending the framework to profile human workers alongside AI systems, supporting more nuanced human–machine task allocation rather than a simple automation-versus-human dichotomy.

title: From Specialization to Generalization: Instruction-tuned LLMs for Robust Harmful Content Mitigation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive performance across a wide range of general NLP tasks; however, their effectiveness in sensitive domains, such as hate speech detection, remains less clear. Prior studies comparing prompted LLMs with state-of-the-art encoder-based models (e.g., BERT variants (Roy et al., 2023; Dönmez et al., 2024)) have shown only marginal gains, suggesting that LLMs may not excel in hate speech detection or mitigation. In this work, we revisit this question through the lens of instruction tuning. By thoroughly unifying 36 English hate speech datasets spanning multiple labeling schemes, we fine-tune a generalist LLM, based on Qwen3 (Qwen Team, 2025), specifically for hate speech mitigation. Our results demonstrate not only state-of-the-art performance on in-domain benchmarks but also substantial improvements in cross-domain and cross-lingual generalization--areas where encoder-based specialist classifiers often struggle.

AI.tldr: They instruction-tune a Qwen3-based LLM on a unified collection of 36 hate speech datasets and show it outperforms prior models, especially in cross-domain and cross-lingual settings.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs perform well on general NLP tasks, their advantage in sensitive areas like hate speech detection is unclear. Prior work using prompted LLMs finds only small gains over strong encoder-based models, leading to doubts that LLMs are useful for hate speech mitigation. The authors want to revisit this question by better aligning LLMs to the task via instruction tuning and using a broad, unified dataset to test robustness and generalization.
AI.method: They first unify 36 English hate speech datasets that use diverse labeling schemes, creating a consistent instruction-style framework for hate speech mitigation. Then they fine-tune a generalist Qwen3-based LLM with instruction tuning on this unified corpus, targeting both detection and mitigation behavior. They evaluate the resulting model on standard in-domain benchmarks and also on out-of-domain and cross-lingual test sets, comparing to state-of-the-art encoder-based specialist models and prompted general LLMs.
AI.result: The instruction-tuned Qwen3-based model achieves state-of-the-art performance on in-domain hate speech benchmarks. More importantly, it shows strong cross-domain and cross-lingual generalization, substantially outperforming encoder-based classifiers in these settings where such specialist models typically underperform.
AI.conclusion: When appropriately instruction-tuned on a large, unified multi-dataset corpus, a generalist LLM can become a highly effective hate speech mitigation model. This challenges prior conclusions that LLMs offer only marginal benefits for hate speech detection and indicates that instruction tuning and dataset unification are key to unlocking their advantages, especially for robustness and transfer across domains and languages.

title: Narcissus: Program Synthesis Using Context-Aware LLM Approximations
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at programming, but not when the task fixes the target language: prompted with a grammar rare in their training data, their programs usually break the grammar or fail the given specification. Enumerative synthesizers search the space of syntactically correct programs systematically guided by LLMs; the state of the art guides them by approximating LLM proposals into rule frequencies, which loses where each construct belongs and prunes every rule the proposals miss, exactly when the proposals are wrong. We present Narcissus, a synthesizer that keeps the proposals as syntax trees and scores each expansion of a candidate program in its context: does a proposal with the same surrounding structure continue the same way, and does the expansion rebuild a fragment the proposals repeat? A regularization term keeps every rule reachable, so wrong proposals delay the solution but cannot hide it. Across five domains and two search backends, Narcissus beats static guidance at every budget and consistently outperforms re-prompting the LLM to fix its own proposals; it reaches proposal-like programs an order of magnitude sooner and solves $40\%$ of ARC tasks where the raw proposals solve $13\%$, all without a single LLM call during search.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Narcissus, a program synthesizer that uses LLM-generated syntax trees directly for search guidance, achieving faster and more robust synthesis in low-resource grammars than prior LLM-guided methods or raw LLM generation.
AI.motivation: LLMs are strong at code generation in familiar languages but struggle when constrained to rare or synthetic grammars, often violating syntax or missing specifications. Existing LLM-guided enumerative synthesizers convert LLM program samples into rule frequencies, which discards structural information, over-prunes the search space, and fails badly when LLM proposals are wrong. There is a need for a synthesis method that benefits from LLM priors while remaining sound and complete over the grammar, and that works efficiently even when LLM proposals are noisy or low-quality.
AI.method: Narcissus first asks an LLM for program proposals in the target DSL and parses them into syntax trees. During enumerative search, each candidate program expansion is scored using two structure-aware signals: (1) contextual consistency—whether proposals with a similar surrounding syntactic context continue in the same way; and (2) fragment reconstruction—whether the expansion helps rebuild subtrees frequently seen in proposals. A regularization term ensures every production rule remains reachable, preventing the guidance from pruning away the true solution even if proposals are misleading. The approach is plugged into two different search backends and evaluated across five domains, all without additional LLM calls during search.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks and two underlying search algorithms, Narcissus consistently outperforms static rule-frequency guidance and LLM re-prompting strategies. It reaches programs similar to the LLM’s own proposals up to an order of magnitude faster. On ARC tasks, the raw LLM proposals solve 13% of problems, whereas Narcissus solves 40% while using only the initial batch of proposals and no further LLM interaction during the search phase.
AI.conclusion: Structure-aware use of LLM proposals—treating them as full syntax trees and scoring search states in context, while retaining completeness via regularization—substantially improves enumerative program synthesis under fixed grammars. Narcissus demonstrates that LLMs can provide powerful one-shot priors for search without being in the loop, achieving higher success rates and faster convergence than both static rule-based guidance and iterative LLM prompting.

title: AWM: Answerable Working Memory for Long-Document VQA Agents
summary: Long-document visual question answering increasingly relies on VLM agents that retrieve candidate pages, inspect page images, write findings to working memory, and synthesize answers. Working memory should carry answer-supporting evidence across page inspections for later grounded answering, yet existing evaluation mainly checks final-answer correctness and evidence-page access. This creates a memory-quality blind spot: an agent may reach the right page and answer correctly while leaving behind memory too generic or incomplete to support answering once page context is removed. We introduce \emph{memory-only answerability}, a diagnostic that asks whether a reader can answer from the question and terminal working memory alone. Building on this diagnostic, \emph{Answerable Working Memory} (AWM) treats terminal working memory as an answerable evidence artifact, and AWM-GRPO incorporates this signal into the GRPO reward while preserving final-answer priority. Under GRPO, this reward assigns higher advantages to answer-correct trajectories whose terminal working memory remains answerable. On \textsc{MMLongBench-Doc}, even when gold evidence pages are provided, 42.5\% of correct answers still cannot be answered from terminal working memory alone. AWM-GRPO improves final-answer accuracy over the RAG baseline by 8.1 and 11.9 points on \textsc{MMLongBench-Doc} and \textsc{LongDocURL} and reduces the memory-missing-correct rate by 2.7 points over answer-only GRPO.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new diagnostic and training signal that ensures a VLM agent’s working memory alone is sufficient to answer questions in long-document visual QA, improving both accuracy and memory quality.
AI.motivation: Existing long-document visual QA systems with VLM agents focus on reaching the right pages and giving correct final answers, but they ignore whether the agent’s working memory actually contains sufficient, specific evidence to support those answers once the original page context is gone. This creates a blind spot where models can appear to perform well while having poor or incomplete internal evidence representations, which hurts robustness and interpretability. The authors want an evaluation and learning signal that explicitly rewards high-quality, answerable working memory, not just final-answer correctness.
AI.method: They introduce the concept of memory-only answerability: checking if a reader could answer a question using only the final working memory plus the question, with no access to the original pages. Based on this, they define Answerable Working Memory (AWM), treating the terminal working memory as an evidence artifact that should itself enable answering. They then design AWM-GRPO, a variant of GRPO (a reinforcement learning/optimization method) that augments the reward: trajectories with correct final answers get higher advantages when their terminal working memory is also answerable, while still prioritizing final-answer correctness. This is applied to VLM agents that retrieve document pages, inspect their images, write notes into memory, and then synthesize answers.
AI.result: Empirically, on the MMLongBench-Doc benchmark, they find that even when the model is given the gold evidence pages, 42.5% of correct answers are not recoverable from the final working memory alone, showing a large memory-quality gap. Using AWM-GRPO, they significantly improve performance over a standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) baseline: final-answer accuracy improves by 8.1 points on MMLongBench-Doc and 11.9 points on LongDocURL. Compared with using GRPO that rewards only final answers, AWM-GRPO also reduces the rate at which correct answers have missing or insufficient memory by 2.7 points.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating and training VLM agents solely based on final-answer correctness and evidence-page access is insufficient because it overlooks the quality of the agent’s working memory. The proposed memory-only answerability diagnostic and AWM-GRPO training framework explicitly encourage working memories that are themselves answerable evidence artifacts. This leads to better long-document visual QA performance and more faithful, complete internal representations of evidence, making agents more robust and interpretable in multi-step reasoning over long documents.

title: ToST: A Tree-of-Thought Socratic Teaching Framework for Multi-Path Guidance and Parallel Thinking
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong problem-solving abilities, positioning them as promising agents for Socratic teaching to guide students through step-by-step heuristic questioning. However, existing approaches typically adopt a one-problem-one-solution paradigm, restricting the teaching guidance to a single linear reasoning path. This design limits instructional flexibility, weakens error recovery, and restricts students' ability to engage in parallel thinking to explore multiple valid solutions. To overcome these, we propose ToST, a Tree-of-Thought Socratic Teaching framework that explicitly supports multi-path guidance under a one-problem-multiple-solutions paradigm. ToST employs Parallel Sowing, a parallel-thinking-oriented questioning strategy to encourage students to approach problems from diverse perspectives, and a Multi-Path Adaptive Guidance mechanism to provide more robust and non-linear instructions across alternative solution trajectories. Concurrently, to fill the void in systematically evaluating such non-linear instructional capabilities, we advance the task of multi-path Socratic guidance by establishing MPSG-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark that includes a dataset of 31K multi-path teaching dialogues and a five-dimensional evaluation framework grounded in the SOLO (Structure of Observed Learning Outcomes) theory to assess parallel-thinking guidance. Experimental results demonstrate that ToST significantly enhances guidance success rates while empowering students to navigate and explore multiple solution paths more effectively under both automatic and human metrics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ToST, a Tree-of-Thought Socratic Teaching framework and a new benchmark (MPSG-Bench) to enable and evaluate multi-path, non-linear Socratic guidance with LLMs, significantly improving guidance success and parallel-thinking support.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based Socratic tutoring systems mostly follow a one-problem-one-solution, linear reasoning path. This limits flexibility, makes error recovery fragile, and prevents students from exploring multiple valid solution strategies in parallel. There is also a lack of systematic benchmarks to evaluate non-linear, multi-path instructional capabilities of LLM tutors.
AI.method: The authors propose ToST (Tree-of-Thought Socratic Teaching), which organizes teaching as a tree of solution trajectories instead of a single linear chain. It has two main components: (1) Parallel Sowing, a questioning strategy that deliberately elicits multiple perspectives and potential solution paths in parallel; and (2) Multi-Path Adaptive Guidance, which dynamically steers the student along different branches, allowing robust error handling and non-linear instruction. In addition, they construct MPSG-Bench, a benchmark consisting of 31K multi-path teaching dialogues and an evaluation framework with five dimensions, grounded in SOLO theory, to assess parallel-thinking Socratic guidance.
AI.result: Experiments on the MPSG-Bench benchmark show that ToST substantially improves guidance success rates compared with baselines and better supports students in exploring and navigating multiple solution paths. Both automatic metrics and human evaluations confirm ToST’s superiority for multi-path, parallel-thinking Socratic tutoring.
AI.conclusion: Modeling Socratic teaching as a tree-of-thought process, rather than a single linear path, yields more flexible, resilient, and cognitively rich instructional interactions. ToST demonstrates that LLM tutors can effectively provide multi-path guidance, and MPSG-Bench offers a standardized way to evaluate such non-linear teaching capabilities, paving the way for more advanced, parallel-thinking-oriented educational agents.

title: AutoVerifier: Residual-Guided Non-Parametric Optimization for Reference-Based Answer Verification
comment: 8 pages of main text, 5 figures, with appendices
summary: Reference-based verifiers are important for evaluating reasoning models and providing accurate outcome rewards in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. To improve verification accuracy, prior work has explored rule-based, model-based, and tool-augmented verifiers for checking answer equivalence across diverse answer forms. However, the equivalence of answer forms such as $1+3.14$ and $1+π$ may depend on the question and scoring criterion. We frame such implicit assumptions as verifier inductive biases. To address this challenge, we propose AutoVerifier, a residual-guided non-parametric optimization method that learns these biases from recurring verifier errors. Specifically, AutoVerifier records these biases in rule cards and promotes them to code modules or prompt guidance only after replay validation detects no direct regressions, keeping accepted updates auditable, editable, and reusable. Experiments on four verifier benchmarks demonstrate that AutoVerifier outperforms state-of-the-art verifiers by a large margin.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AutoVerifier, a system that automatically learns and integrates inductive biases to improve reference-based verifiers for reasoning models.
AI.motivation: Existing reference-based verifiers struggle with answer-equivalence cases where correctness depends on task-specific assumptions (e.g., scoring criteria), and existing rule/model/tool-based approaches hard-code or overlook these implicit biases, causing recurring verification errors.
AI.method: They propose AutoVerifier, a residual-guided non-parametric optimization pipeline that monitors verifier errors, extracts recurring patterns as "rule cards" (human-readable bias candidates), and selectively promotes them—after replay-based regression checks—to executable code modules or prompt instructions, ensuring updates are auditable, editable, and reusable.
AI.result: On four benchmarks for verifier evaluation, AutoVerifier significantly improves verification accuracy and surpasses prior state-of-the-art verifiers by a large margin.
AI.conclusion: Learning and managing verifier inductive biases via a structured, residual-guided update mechanism (rule cards → validated code/prompt changes) yields more accurate and maintainable reference-based verifiers, enabling better evaluation and reward signals for reasoning models.

title: LocalLSTC: A Long Short-Term Control Architecture for Locally Deployed GUI Agents
summary: Modern GUI-agent frameworks achieve strong desktop task performance with frontier API models, yet persistent control information often remains implicit in growing interaction trajectories. At each step, the planner reconstructs the active task stage, accumulated evidence, and runtime feedback before deciding the next action. This dependence becomes more pronounced under weaker local reasoning backbones. Across four representative state-of-the-art frameworks, replacing GPT-5 with Qwen3.5-9B reduces average OSWorld SR-100 from 60.9\% to 37.7\%. Trajectory annotation further identifies at least one control failure in 91.6\% of failed trajectories. To address this problem, we introduce LocalLSTC, a training-free architecture that organizes control by temporal scope, maintaining persistent cross-step state to guide short-term execution commitments. Long-Term Control maintains the active subgoal, subgoal-aligned evidence, and runtime feedback across interactions, while Short-Term Execution realizes bounded commitments for the current step. Long-to-Short Planning forms each commitment from persistent state, and Short-to-Long Control integrates execution outcomes back into that state for progress assessment, recovery, and termination. With Qwen3.6-27B, LocalLSTC reaches 64.7\% SR-100 on OSWorld and 65.3\% on WindowsAgentArena, outperforming the strongest prior local results on both benchmarks. Ablations further support contributions from mechanisms on both sides of execution. These findings identify temporal organization of control information as a distinct architectural dimension for locally deployed GUI agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LocalLSTC, a training-free control architecture for GUI agents that explicitly manages long- and short-term control state, significantly improving performance of locally deployed models on desktop benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing GUI-agent frameworks rely heavily on powerful API models (e.g., GPT-5) to implicitly reconstruct task state at every step from long interaction histories. When these are replaced with weaker or local models, performance drops sharply, and analysis shows most failures are due to control issues rather than basic capabilities. The authors aim to reduce this dependence on very strong models by explicitly structuring persistent control information across time.
AI.method: They propose LocalLSTC, which organizes agent control by temporal scope using a training-free, modular architecture. Long-Term Control persistently tracks the current subgoal, its supporting evidence, and runtime feedback across steps. Short-Term Execution focuses on bounded, step-level action commitments. A Long-to-Short Planning mechanism converts persistent long-term state into concrete short-term execution plans, while Short-to-Long Control feeds execution outcomes back into the long-term state for progress checking, recovery decisions, and termination conditions. They integrate this with off-the-shelf local models (e.g., Qwen) and perform ablation studies on different components.
AI.result: Replacing GPT-5 with a smaller local model (Qwen3.5-9B) in four SOTA GUI-agent frameworks drops OSWorld SR-100 from 60.9% to 37.7%, and trajectory analysis reveals at least one control failure in 91.6% of failed runs. With the proposed LocalLSTC architecture and Qwen3.6-27B, performance reaches 64.7% SR-100 on OSWorld and 65.3% on WindowsAgentArena, surpassing the best prior results achieved with local models on both benchmarks. Ablations confirm that both long-term and short-term control mechanisms materially contribute to the gains.
AI.conclusion: Explicit temporal organization of control information—separating long-term task state from short-term execution commitments and tightly coupling them through planning and feedback—is a key architectural dimension for GUI agents, especially when using weaker or local models. LocalLSTC demonstrates that a training-free, control-focused design can substantially mitigate the reliance on frontier API models and improve robustness and performance in desktop task automation.

title: Unmatched Does Not Mean False: Incomplete Reference Sets Can Reverse Calibration Rankings in Open-Ended Theory-of-Mind Tracking
comment: Main paper: 9 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Supplementary material: 23 pages
summary: Open-ended Theory-of-Mind (ToM) trackers emit valid beliefs absent from finite references. A finite-reference-plus-matcher pipeline marks unmatched outputs false, creating proxy labels that can reverse proper-score model selection on fixed outputs. Holding 259 beliefs and paired scores fixed, reference recoding lowers weighted prevalence from 0.783 to 0.295 and reverses strictly proper Brier risk: a frozen source-prior rule leads native confidence by 0.227 under reference labels and trails by 0.152 under blinded adjudication, in all six authored scenarios. A reference-only Platt recalibrator reverses further. An ICE-specific reversal appears in a released 301-question NQ-open DPR-BERT pipeline: its average-confidence baseline improves instance-level calibration error by 0.045 under exact match but worsens it by 0.074 under human correctness, with both intervals excluding zero. On independently authored OpenToM narratives, 90-96% of audited unmatched beliefs are literally true and the paired direction again reverses. An exact decomposition attributes the distortion to omitted truths, and a closed-form criterion correctly classifies comparisons from twelve released systems. Frozen-audit retrospective replay shows 50 attempted annotations recover ranking direction with probability at least 0.996. TriSource-Restore anchors full-frame reference labels and frozen automatic judgments to a probability-sampled human pilot, maintains at least nominal coverage, narrows intervals, and repairs confidence subject to a base-rate deployment gate.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that common evaluation methods for open-ended Theory-of-Mind (ToM) models are badly distorted by incomplete reference answers, which can even reverse which system looks better; the authors analyze why this happens and propose a method (TriSource-Restore) to fix the labels and restore correct rankings.
