AI.motivation: Open-ended ToM models generate many different, often valid, beliefs about mental states, but standard evaluation pipelines rely on finite reference sets plus automatic matchers. Any correct belief not in the reference set gets labeled false, which can bias metrics, miscalibrate models, and even invert which system seems superior. The authors want to understand and quantify how much this finite-reference bias can distort calibration and model selection, and to design an evaluation procedure that preserves proper scoring and valid confidence estimation.
AI.method: 1) Construct controlled ToM scenarios with 259 beliefs and paired model confidence scores, and compare evaluations using reference-based automatic labeling versus blinded human adjudication. 2) Analyze how recoding reference labels changes estimated prevalence and Brier risk, including the effects of Platt recalibration based only on references. 3) Examine a real ICE-specific pipeline (NQ-open DPR-BERT) and compare calibration under exact-match labels versus human-correctness labels. 4) Audit unmatched beliefs in independently authored OpenToM narratives to estimate how often they are actually true. 5) Provide a mathematical decomposition attributing distortion to omitted truths and derive a closed-form criterion that predicts when system comparisons will flip; test it on 12 released systems. 6) Use frozen-audit retrospective replay to show how many human annotations are needed to reliably recover the correct ranking. 7) Propose TriSource-Restore, which anchors references and automatic judgments to a probability-sampled human pilot, and evaluate its coverage, interval width, and confidence repair properties under a deployment gate based on base rates.
AI.result: 1) Re-encoding references on the 259-belief set drops estimated prevalence from 0.783 to 0.295, and completely reverses Brier-risk ordering: a frozen source-prior rule appears better than native confidence under reference labels, but worse under blinded human labels, consistently across six scenarios. 2) A Platt recalibrator trained only on reference labels introduces an additional reversal, further miscalibrating the system. 3) In the NQ-open DPR-BERT ICE pipeline, a simple average-confidence baseline seems to improve instance-level calibration error by 0.045 under exact-match references but actually worsens it by 0.074 under human correctness, both statistically significant. 4) On OpenToM narratives, 90–96% of unmatched beliefs are literally true, and the direction of comparative evaluation again flips when using human judgment instead of reference-only labels. 5) Theoretical decomposition shows the distortion is driven by omitted truths in the reference set, and the closed-form criterion correctly predicts comparison outcomes across 12 existing systems. 6) Retrospective replay indicates that as few as 50 targeted human annotations are enough to recover the true ranking direction with probability ≥ 0.996. 7) TriSource-Restore, combining probability-sampled human pilots with frozen references and automatic rules, maintains (at least) nominal statistical coverage, produces tighter confidence intervals, and corrects confidence estimates when gated by base-rate information.
AI.conclusion: Finite reference sets plus automatic matchers are fundamentally unreliable for evaluating open-ended ToM models: they systematically undercount true beliefs, break the properness of standard scoring rules, and can reverse which model looks better and how calibrated it appears. These distortions are not minor noise but are mathematically attributable to omitted truths and are empirically large enough to flip conclusions on real systems. However, by strategically incorporating a small, probability-sampled human pilot and anchoring both references and automatic judgments (TriSource-Restore), it is possible to restore proper evaluation, preserve coverage, narrow uncertainty intervals, and obtain trustworthy calibration and model rankings, even in open-ended belief-tracking settings.

title: Choose Your Game Wisely: Measuring Game-Theoretic Structures in Real-World Vehicle Interactions
summary: Game-theoretic models provide principled frameworks for modeling vehicle interactions, but their underlying temporal assumptions have not been systematically examined against real-world driving behavior. In particular, it remains unclear how simultaneous, sequential, and asymmetric interaction structures can be measured from vehicle trajectories. This paper develops a trajectory-based interaction measurement framework to identify interaction events and quantify behavioral change onset, temporal organization, post-onset response dynamics, and ordering stability. The framework uses behavioral deviations to verify candidate interactions. We evaluate the framework on six real-world trajectory datasets, including INTERACTION, highD, inD, rounD, Waymo Open Motion, and nuPlan, covering diverse road geometries, traffic environments, and interaction types. The results show that concurrent and sequential behavioral changes both constitute substantial proportions of observed following, merging, and conflicting interactions. Among sequential interactions, stable ordering is more prevalent than alternating ordering, indicating that persistent asymmetric roles are a common interaction structure. Importantly, temporal precedence does not necessarily coincide with a measurable behavioral response, indicating that temporal ordering alone may not be sufficient to characterize behavioral dependence. These findings show that real-world interactions exhibit concurrent, sequential, and persistently ordered temporal structures. Different game-theoretic formulations are therefore better regarded as complementary modeling abstractions for different interaction regimes rather than as a universal structure governing all vehicle interactions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a trajectory-based framework to empirically measure how vehicles interact over time and compares different temporal game-theoretic structures (simultaneous, sequential, asymmetric) using real-world driving data.
AI.motivation: Game-theoretic models are widely used to represent vehicle interactions, but they make different assumptions about the temporal structure of decisions (simultaneous vs. sequential vs. asymmetric). It is unclear which of these assumptions match real-world driving behavior and how to empirically detect these temporal structures from trajectory data.
AI.method: The authors design a trajectory-based interaction measurement framework that: (1) identifies candidate interaction events from multi-vehicle trajectory data; (2) detects the onset of behavioral change for each agent; (3) quantifies the temporal organization between agents’ behavioral changes (concurrent vs. sequential, symmetric vs. asymmetric); (4) analyzes post-onset response dynamics; and (5) measures ordering stability (whether one agent persistently leads/responds). Behavioral deviations from a baseline are used to verify that an interaction is genuine. The framework is applied to six large real-world trajectory datasets (INTERACTION, highD, inD, rounD, Waymo Open Motion, nuPlan).
AI.result: Across following, merging, and conflicting interactions in six datasets, the framework finds that both concurrent and sequential behavioral changes occur frequently. Within sequential interactions, cases where one vehicle persistently takes the leading or responding role (stable ordering) are more common than situations where the roles alternate. Furthermore, the temporal order in which vehicles appear to act does not always align with when a measurable behavioral response occurs, so simple temporal precedence fails to fully capture behavioral dependence between vehicles.
AI.conclusion: Real-world vehicle interactions cannot be cleanly captured by a single temporal game-theoretic structure. Instead they exhibit a mix of concurrent, sequential, and persistently asymmetric (ordered) interaction patterns. As a result, different game-theoretic formulations (simultaneous-move, sequential-move, asymmetric-role models) should be seen as complementary tools appropriate to different interaction regimes, rather than as one universally valid description of driver behavior.

title: Reconstructing the Right Episode: Evaluating Interleaved Conversational Memory Beyond Long Context
comment: 19 pages, 6 figures, 30 tables. Accepted to the Main Conference of EMNLP 2026
summary: Conversations with chat assistants increasingly span many topics in a single long-running thread, challenging memory systems. Existing long-context and memory benchmarks often expose session or topic boundaries, or probe direct personal-memory questions. These settings understate a harder assistant-memory regime: a flat mixed-topic thread where the system must infer which earlier episode makes a later task decision valid. We introduce SCALE-QA, a constraint-grounded task QA benchmark for flat unsegmented threads targeting episode integrity failure. The dataset contains 3,000 audited questions across 10 domains, uses deterministic four-way multiple-choice grading, and includes a deterministic runtime builder; experiments use all 3,000 questions through 128k and a stratified 400-question diagnostic at 1M. SCALE-QA questions are ordinary task-oriented requests whose correct answer depends on causally related evidence introduced earlier in the conversation. We also propose Temporal-Semantic Interleaved Memory Reconstruction (TSIM), which segments the turn stream into coherent episodes and indexes them through a hierarchical multi-view memory stack with deterministic episode-level summary and cluster-routing views. Experiments show that SCALE-QA challenges strong RAG baselines and long-context LLMs alike; across three open-source and proprietary LLM backends, TSIM achieves the highest accuracy in every backend setting, gaining 5.6-17.6 accuracy points over the strongest corresponding baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SCALE-QA, a benchmark for evaluating chat assistants’ memory in long, mixed-topic conversations, and TSIM, a new memory-reconstruction method that significantly improves accuracy over strong baselines.
AI.motivation: Real chat assistant conversations often involve long, flat, mixed-topic threads without explicit session boundaries, making it hard for systems to reliably recall which past information is relevant to answer later queries. Existing benchmarks simplify the problem by giving clear topic/session boundaries or by probing memory with direct questions, which underestimates the difficulty of maintaining robust assistant memory in realistic conditions. The authors aim to create a benchmark and method that better capture and tackle this harder, more realistic memory regime, particularly focusing on failures where the assistant loses episode integrity and ties a decision to the wrong past context.
AI.method: 1) Benchmark (SCALE-QA): They construct a constraint-grounded QA dataset of 3,000 questions across 10 domains in flat, unsegmented multi-topic threads. Each question is an ordinary task-oriented user request whose correct answer depends on causally related evidence appearing earlier in the conversation. Questions are graded via deterministic four-way multiple choice, supported by a deterministic runtime builder to control the conversational setup. They also define a 400-question stratified diagnostic subset for 1M-token context experiments. 2) Method (TSIM): They propose Temporal-Semantic Interleaved Memory Reconstruction, which automatically segments the conversation into coherent episodes based on temporal and semantic signals. These episodes are organized in a hierarchical multi-view memory stack that includes deterministic episode-level summaries and cluster-routing views, enabling efficient retrieval of the most relevant episode(s) when answering a new question. They evaluate TSIM against strong retrieval-augmented generation baselines and long-context LLMs on SCALE-QA with multiple open-source and proprietary LLM backends.
AI.result: On the SCALE-QA benchmark—including the full 3,000-question set up to 128k context length and the 400-question diagnostic up to 1M tokens—both strong RAG baselines and long-context LLMs struggle, confirming the difficulty of the setting. Across three different LLM backends (both open-source and proprietary), the proposed TSIM memory system consistently achieves the top performance, delivering gains of 5.6 to 17.6 absolute accuracy points over the strongest baseline in each backend configuration.
AI.conclusion: SCALE-QA exposes a more realistic and challenging regime for conversational memory—flat, mixed-topic threads where correct answers hinge on preserving episode integrity rather than responding to explicit memory probes. In this setting, existing long-context models and RAG-based memory systems show significant weaknesses. The proposed TSIM method, which reconstructs and hierarchically indexes episodes via temporal-semantic cues and deterministic summaries, substantially improves performance across multiple LLM backends. This suggests that structured, episode-oriented memory reconstruction is a promising direction for building more reliable long-horizon conversational assistants and highlights SCALE-QA as a robust benchmark for future work in this area.

title: Repair or Resample? Rethinking Failure Debugging in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
summary: As large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MASs) are increasingly applied to long-horizon complex tasks, their reliability has emerged as the core bottleneck hindering their real-world deployment. Existing MAS debugging and repair methods typically rely on rerunning and resampling the entire execution trajectory. However, a fundamental question remains to be answered: do these methods causally repair MAS failures or merely stochastically repair by leveraging the randomness of LLM sampling? To evaluate the effectiveness of MAS repair methods, we introduce SymTrace, a controlled evaluation framework that records the MAS execution trajectory and establishes intervention anchors. During replay, it effectively reconstructs the execution before the anchor using recorded logs and only regenerates the downstream trajectory, thereby enabling the reliable reproduction of MAS failures. We further construct the dataset SymFail, comprising 536 human-annotated failure trajectories with graph-linked locations, categories, and trace evidence. Based on these foundations, we conduct a large-scale empirical study across three mainstream MAS frameworks. Our findings reveal that existing unguided rerun methods are highly unreliable, exhibiting low failure reproduction and repair rates (only 67.97% and 6.90%, respectively). Building upon these findings, we further explore the effectiveness of a symptom-driven intervention method, which successfully repairs 20.15% of the failed cases (a 191.89% improvement to state-of-the-art repair methods). This study aims to provide actionable insights for MAS debugging and repair research, paving the way for the robust deployment of multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SymTrace, a controlled evaluation framework and the SymFail dataset to rigorously test whether multi-agent system (MAS) repair methods causally fix failures or just rely on random LLM sampling, and shows that current unguided reruns are unreliable while symptom-driven interventions substantially improve repair rates.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems are being used for long, complex tasks, but their reliability is a major bottleneck for real-world use. Existing debugging/repair approaches mostly rerun or resample entire trajectories, without clarifying whether they genuinely fix the underlying causes of failures or simply get lucky due to randomness. There is a need for a controlled, reproducible way to evaluate and compare MAS repair methods, including precise failure annotations and traceability.
AI.method: The authors propose SymTrace, an evaluation framework that logs complete MAS execution trajectories and defines intervention anchors (specific points in the trajectory). During replay, SymTrace reconstructs the trajectory up to the anchor from logs and only regenerates downstream steps, allowing controlled interventions and reproducible failures. They also build SymFail, a dataset of 536 human-annotated MAS failure trajectories that include graph-linked failure locations, categories, and trace evidence. Using these tools, they run a large-scale empirical study on three mainstream MAS frameworks to compare unguided rerun methods and a symptom-driven intervention strategy.
AI.result: The empirical study finds that current unguided rerun-based repair methods have low reliability: they can only reproduce failures 67.97% of the time and achieve a repair rate of just 6.90%. In contrast, a symptom-driven intervention approach—where interventions are guided by observed failure symptoms—achieves a repair rate of 20.15%, representing a 191.89% improvement over state-of-the-art repair methods within the evaluated settings.
AI.conclusion: Current MAS debugging and repair techniques that rely on unguided reruns are insufficiently reliable and often do not causally repair failures. SymTrace and the SymFail dataset provide a controlled, reproducible foundation to rigorously evaluate MAS repair methods. Symptom-driven interventions demonstrate significantly higher effectiveness, suggesting that more structured, causally informed debugging strategies are necessary for robust, real-world deployment of LLM-based multi-agent systems.

title: Think-Probe-Respond: Improving Large Language Models as Judges of Research Idea Novelty
summary: Automated novelty judgment can accelerate scientific discovery by enabling efficient evaluation, refinement, and comparison of research ideas. While large language models are increasingly adopted for this task, we investigate a previously overlooked limitation in their judgment capabilities: despite generating reasoning rationales that closely mirror those of human experts, their final novelty judgments often diverge substantially. We demonstrate that this miscalibration stems from a systematic bias towards judging ideas as "medium novel". To mitigate this, we propose Think-Probe-Respond (TPR), a lightweight approach that probes latent novelty judgments from hidden states during the reasoning phase and uses the probed judgments to condition the final response. Across strong baselines, TPR improves novelty judgment performance by 22.30% and successfully mitigates the prevalent "medium novelty" bias.

AI.tldr: They identify and reduce a systematic “medium novelty” bias in LLM-based novelty judgments using a probing-based method (TPR) that reads latent novelty signals from hidden states during reasoning.
AI.motivation: Automating novelty assessment could speed up scientific progress by quickly screening and ranking research ideas, but current LLMs, though they can articulate human-like reasoning, still give poorly calibrated and often incorrect novelty labels. In particular, there is an overlooked bias where models default to judging ideas as having medium novelty, which undermines their usefulness in distinguishing truly novel from incremental work.
AI.method: They empirically analyze LLM novelty judgments and show a systematic tendency toward ‘medium novelty’ decisions, even when the chain-of-thought matches human experts. They then introduce Think-Probe-Respond (TPR), where the model first reasons about the idea (Think), then a probe reads out latent novelty judgments from intermediate hidden states (Probe), and finally the model conditions its final answer on these probed signals (Respond). TPR is lightweight and can be layered on top of existing strong LLM baselines.
AI.result: Using multiple strong baselines, TPR increases the accuracy or quality of novelty judgments by 22.30% compared to the best existing approaches and significantly reduces the frequency of biased “medium novelty” outputs, leading to judgments that better align with ground truth or expert evaluations.
AI.conclusion: LLMs’ novelty judgments can be systematically biased toward medium novelty, even when their explicit reasoning appears sound, revealing a miscalibration between rationale and decision. By probing latent signals in hidden states and feeding them back into the decision, TPR substantially improves both performance and calibration, making LLM-based automated novelty assessment more reliable for supporting scientific discovery.

title: Formal, Executable and Explainable Runtime Monitoring of Spoken Air Traffic Control Operational Procedures
summary: Air traffic control procedures are executed through spoken exchanges between controllers and pilots. These interactions are essential to the safety of air transportation: failures in their execution can create severe operational hazards, as evidenced by past fatal accidents. Assessing whether an instruction has been followed requires relating what was said to the aircraft concerned, its state, and the obligations that pilots must meet. We present a runtime verification framework that monitors such procedures by checking controller-pilot exchanges, surveillance data, and onboard observations. The framework parses radio communications into events linked to the entities they concern and merges them with surveillance and onboard observations into a time-stamped trace. The ICAO-derived obligations as formalized as temporal formulas with explicit time bounds and evaluated over execution traces. Every violation is reported along with the breached obligations and the observations that support the verdict. With real traffic, the complete pipeline reaches an F1 of 0.85 against blind human-annotated violations; in 1,495 synthetic situations derived from two public corpora, the monitor logic returns the expected verdict in every case. In two historical accidents reconstructed from official investigation reports, the monitor identifies the same procedural deviations documented by the investigators.

AI.tldr: They build a runtime verification system that listens to controller–pilot speech, links it with radar and onboard data, encodes air traffic control rules as temporal logic with time bounds, and automatically flags procedural violations with traceable evidence, achieving high accuracy on real, synthetic, and historical-accident data.
AI.motivation: Spoken air traffic control procedures are safety‑critical, and failures in correctly following or enforcing these procedures have caused fatal accidents. Today, checking whether pilots follow instructions is largely manual and post‑hoc. There is a need for an automated, systematic way to continuously monitor whether ATC procedures are being followed by relating speech exchanges to the aircraft state and formal obligations, in order to detect deviations and hazards early and objectively.
AI.method: They design a runtime verification pipeline that: (1) parses radio communications between controllers and pilots into structured events tied to specific aircraft and states; (2) merges these events with surveillance and onboard observations into a unified, time‑stamped execution trace; (3) formalizes ICAO‑based procedural obligations as temporal logic formulas with explicit time bounds; and (4) evaluates these formulas over the trace to detect and report violations, including which obligations were breached and what observations support the verdict.
AI.result: On real traffic data, the full pipeline reaches an F1 score of 0.85 when compared against blind human annotations of violations. On 1,495 synthetic scenarios generated from two public corpora, the monitoring logic always produces the expected verdict. When applied to two historical accidents reconstructed from official investigation reports, the system recovers the same procedural deviations that human investigators identified.
AI.conclusion: The proposed runtime verification framework can effectively and reliably monitor air traffic control procedures by combining parsed speech communications with surveillance and onboard data and checking them against formally specified temporal obligations. Its good performance on real, synthetic, and historical‑accident data suggests it is a practical tool for detecting procedural non‑compliance and supporting safety analysis in air traffic operations.

title: Overview of SHROOM-Visions 2026: A Shared Task on Hallucination Detection in Large Vision-Language Models
summary: In 2026, we held the fourth iteration of the SHROOM Shared Task series: SHROOM-Visions (\textbf{S}hared-task on \textbf{H}allucinations and \textbf{R}elated \textbf{O}bservable \textbf{O}vergeneration \textbf{M}istakes in \textbf{Vision} language model\textbf{s}), which is hosted at the UncertaiNLP Workshop co-located with EMNLP 2026. Following the success of the 2024 and 2025 tasks, this time we aim to tackle hallucinations through a model-agnostic detection task focused on large vision-language models. Building on the recently introduced SHEEP dataset, designed for long-term evaluation across model generations, the task invites participants to detect and classify fine-grained hallucination spans in image-conditioned text generation (VQA, image captioning, etc.). The evaluation uses a five-class taxonomy of hallucinations spanning four languages: Chinese, English, French, and Italian. The shared task generated strong interest in the NLP community worldwide, with 27 teams contributing 600+ system submissions. The best systems achieve average scores of 0.58 in character-level correlation, 0.46 in label-conditioned correlation, and 0.51 in intersection-over-union (IoU) across four languages, outperforming the baselines by 30-40 points.

AI.tldr: SHROOM-Visions 2026 is a shared task on detecting fine-grained hallucinations in large vision-language models across four languages, achieving substantial improvements over baselines.
AI.motivation: Hallucinations and overgeneration errors in large vision-language models (VLMs) are a persistent safety and reliability concern, yet they lack standardized, fine-grained, and multilingual evaluation frameworks. Existing work mainly targets text-only models, with limited benchmarks and shared tasks dedicated to systematically detecting and categorizing multimodal hallucinations across languages.
AI.method: The organizers set up a model-agnostic shared task based on the SHEEP dataset, extended to vision-language settings. Participants must automatically detect and classify hallucination spans in image-conditioned text outputs (e.g., VQA, image captioning), using a five-class hallucination taxonomy. The evaluation is span-based, using character-level correlation, label-conditioned correlation, and intersection-over-union (IoU) metrics, covering four languages (Chinese, English, French, Italian).
AI.result: The shared task attracted 27 teams that submitted over 600 systems. Top-performing systems substantially outperformed strong baselines by 30–40 points, reaching around 0.58 character-level correlation, 0.46 label-conditioned correlation, and 0.51 IoU on average across all four languages.
AI.conclusion: The SHROOM-Visions 2026 shared task demonstrates that fine-grained, multilingual hallucination detection in vision-language models is feasible and that current systems can significantly improve over baseline methods. The task, taxonomy, and results provide a standardized benchmark and indicate promising research directions for building more reliable, hallucination-aware VLMs.

title: How Robust Are Automated Fact-Checking Systems? A Cross-Benchmark Evaluation
summary: Automated fact-checking (AFC) systems retrieve evidence and predict claim veracity, yet evaluations omit simple baselines, systems are developed for a single benchmark and cannot be trusted to generalise across domains. No prior work cross-evaluates the full two-stage retrieve-then-verify pipeline across diverse datasets, complementing retrieval-only studies (Thakur et al., 2021) and single-stage benchmarking studies (Calamai et al., 2025). We benchmark nine models, ranging from random and sparse baselines to fine-tuned transformers, zero-shot LLMs, and the two highest-ranked systems from the AVeriTeC 2025 shared task, across four datasets spanning scientific, open-web, and climate domains. Three findings stand out: (1) on ClimateCheck claim-only and fine-tuned models outperform zero-shot LLM and top-performing AVeriTeC 2025 systems, highlighting that noisy evidence can degrade veracity prediction; (2) system rankings are strongly domain- and metric-dependent: the best model on SciFact (macro-F1 0.70) drops to 0.31 on ClimateCheck, while the AVeriTeC 2025 winner and runner-up swap rankings based on evaluation metrics and datasets; (3) replacing retrieved evidence with gold annotations improves veracity accuracy by 14-22 points across models, confirming retrieval remains primary bottleneck. We release code, pre-processed datasets, and all results to support reproducible AFC research.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks end-to-end automated fact-checking pipelines across multiple domains and models, showing that retrieval is still the main bottleneck and that fine-tuned models can outperform zero-shot LLMs when evidence is noisy.
AI.motivation: Existing automated fact-checking systems are usually built and evaluated on a single benchmark, lack simple baselines, and are rarely tested end-to-end across domains. Prior work has focused separately on retrieval or on single-stage benchmarks, so we lack a clear understanding of how full retrieve-then-verify pipelines generalise and where the main bottlenecks lie.
AI.method: The authors evaluate nine AFC models—ranging from random and sparse retrieval baselines to fine-tuned transformer verifiers, zero-shot large language models, and the top two systems from the AVeriTeC 2025 shared task—on four datasets spanning scientific literature, open web content, and climate-related claims. They compare performance under different metrics, domains, and evidence settings, including using retrieved evidence versus gold (human-annotated) evidence, to assess both retrieval and verification components.
AI.result: They find that (1) for the ClimateCheck dataset, claim-only and fine-tuned models outperform zero-shot LLMs and top AVeriTeC systems, suggesting that noisy retrieved evidence can harm veracity prediction; (2) model rankings vary strongly by domain and evaluation metric, with a model achieving macro-F1 0.70 on SciFact but dropping to 0.31 on ClimateCheck, and the AVeriTeC winner and runner-up swapping ranks depending on dataset and metric; and (3) substituting retrieved evidence with gold evidence boosts veracity accuracy by 14–22 percentage points across models, indicating retrieval quality is the key limitation.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end AFC performance is highly domain- and metric-sensitive, and retrieval quality remains the dominant bottleneck in fact-checking pipelines. Fine-tuned models can outperform more complex or zero-shot systems when evidence is noisy, so evaluations should include simple baselines and multiple domains. The authors provide code, processed datasets, and full results to enable more robust, reproducible AFC research and better cross-domain comparisons.

title: Learning New Facts with QLoRA: An Acquisition-Retention Frontier
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning is often assumed to preserve pretrained capabilities because it updates only a small number of parameters. We show that this assumption depends strongly on adapter capacity. We study factual acquisition in a controlled OpenStreetMap-derived benchmark where Qwen3-4B must acquire anonymized geographic associations while retaining unrelated capabilities. Comparing full fine-tuning (FFT) with quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) at ranks 8, 16, 32, and 64, we find that rank induces a clear acquisition--retention frontier. Low-rank QLoRA preserves out-of-domain (OOD) performance but acquires fewer facts, whereas higher ranks improve same-fact paraphrase generalization at an increasing cost in performance on unrelated benchmarks. FFT behaves as a conservative baseline: it retains general capabilities well, but does not reach the highest factual-acquisition regime. Distributional, weight-space, and spectral diagnostics mirror this behavioral trade-off, with higher-rank QLoRA moving farther from the pretrained model. A separate math adaptation experiment shows a weaker frontier, suggesting that the effect is most pronounced when adaptation must install new factual associations rather than reinforce skills already supported by pretraining. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zhngstl/new_facts_forgetting.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how adapter capacity in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (especially QLoRA rank) creates a trade-off between acquiring new factual knowledge and retaining pretrained capabilities.
AI.motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like adapters and LoRA are widely believed to preserve a model’s original abilities because they update only a small subset of parameters. However, this belief is often untested and may depend on how large or expressive the adapters are. The authors want to rigorously examine when and how parameter-efficient fine-tuning starts to overwrite or interfere with existing capabilities, especially when the task requires installing new factual associations rather than just strengthening existing skills.
AI.method: They construct a controlled factual-learning benchmark from OpenStreetMap, where a Qwen3-4B model must learn anonymized geographic associations (new facts) while maintaining performance on unrelated tasks. They compare full fine-tuning (FFT) with QLoRA at different low-rank settings (ranks 8, 16, 32, 64). They measure (a) factual acquisition and paraphrase generalization on the new facts and (b) retention via out-of-domain (OOD) benchmarks that test unrelated capabilities. They also analyze model changes via distributional, weight-space, and spectral diagnostics to see how far the fine-tuned models move from the pretrained checkpoint. Additionally, they run a separate math adaptation experiment to see if the same trade-off appears when tuning on a skill already somewhat present from pretraining.
AI.result: They find a clear acquisition–retention frontier as a function of QLoRA rank. Low-rank QLoRA (e.g., rank 8) preserves OOD performance best but learns fewer new facts and generalizes them less well to paraphrases. Higher-rank QLoRA (up to rank 64) acquires more factual associations and shows better paraphrase generalization, but at the cost of degraded performance on unrelated benchmarks. Full fine-tuning surprisingly behaves as a conservative point on this curve: it retains general capabilities relatively well but never reaches the highest factual-acquisition regime obtained by the highest-rank QLoRA. Diagnostic analyses show that higher-rank QLoRA solutions move farther from the pretrained model in various senses (distributional, weight-space distance, spectral properties). In the math adaptation experiment, the trade-off frontier is much weaker, indicating less interference when fine-tuning reinforces already existing skills rather than encoding brand-new facts.
AI.conclusion: Adapter capacity is a crucial control knob in parameter-efficient fine-tuning: higher-capacity adapters (higher QLoRA rank) can encode more new factual knowledge and better generalize it but increasingly erode pretrained capabilities. Low-rank configurations better preserve original abilities but are limited in factual acquisition. Full fine-tuning is not always the most destructive option; in this setting it retains general skills better than the most aggressive high-rank adapters, though it also cannot match them in factual learning. The strong acquisition–retention frontier appears most clearly when fine-tuning must install novel factual associations, while tasks that reinforce existing skills (like math) show weaker trade-offs. This challenges the blanket assumption that parameter-efficient fine-tuning inherently preserves pretrained capabilities and highlights the need to tune adapter capacity based on whether the goal is to add new facts or refine existing skills.

title: Candidate supply and answer selection shape the value of LLM judging in multi-agent systems
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) sometimes already have the potential to answer correctly, but still report a wrong answer. Explaining this outcome is difficult because generation, communication and final answer-selection rules usually change simultaneously. We conceptualize multi-agent reasoning as an evolutionary pipeline of candidate generation, peer communication and terminal selection, wherein consensus without quality control can exhibit patterns of memetic drift. We study two questions: (1) when an LLM judge provides effective selection pressure by supplying a signal of answer correctness for candidates generated in a multi-agent system, and (2) when using that signal improves the reported answer. To map judge reliability, we analysed 15,336 questions from MMLU-Pro, GPQA, MedXpertQA and MuSR, with Humanity's Last Exam analysed separately. To test these rules, we replayed 81,390 fixed candidate pools drawn from 16,278 questions across five benchmarks. We report three findings. (1) A correct answer is often already present among the generated candidates, but the system can still converge on and report a wrong answer. (2) Judge reliability is not a fixed trait of the model, but varies with the task, the generator and how rare the correct answer is. (3) Combining answer frequency with the judge's evaluation changed only the final answer-selection rule and raised accuracy from 63.82% to 70.82-70.95%, primarily by rescuing correct answers that were outnumbered by popular errors. In the systems studied here, the value of generating more candidates depends on whether those extra samples make correct answers present, frequent or recognisable. By isolating generation, recognition and selection, these findings establish a diagnostic basis for designing multi-agent architectures that protect generated correct answers from being lost.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why multi-agent LLM systems often miss correct answers they already generated and shows how adding an LLM judge–based selection rule can substantially improve final accuracy.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent LLM systems, multiple agents generate and discuss candidate answers before selecting a final one. Empirically, these systems sometimes contain the correct answer among their candidates but still converge on an incorrect response. Because generation, communication, and selection are usually changed together, it is hard to diagnose where reasoning fails and how to fix it. The authors want a principled way to understand when adding an LLM judge as a selection mechanism genuinely improves performance, and under what conditions multi-agent consensus leads to systematic errors (memetic drift).
AI.method: The authors conceptualize multi-agent reasoning as an evolutionary pipeline with three stages: candidate generation, peer communication, and terminal selection. They introduce the notion of memetic drift to describe how consensus without quality control can push the group toward popular but wrong answers. They then: (1) evaluate LLM judge reliability as a selection signal across ~15k questions from several benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, GPQA, MedXpertQA, MuSR, plus separate analysis of Humanity’s Last Exam); (2) construct 81k+ fixed candidate pools from 16k+ questions to "replay" different selection rules on the same underlying generations; and (3) test selection strategies that combine answer frequency (how many agents chose an option) with the judge’s correctness signal, varying generator model, task, and rarity of correct answers to map when judging helps or hurts.
AI.result: The analysis yields three core results: (1) In many multi-agent setups, a correct answer already exists somewhere in the candidate set, yet the system’s selection dynamics still converge to a wrong response. (2) The reliability of an LLM judge is not constant; it depends strongly on the task domain, the generative model used to produce candidates, and especially the relative frequency (rarity) of the correct answer among candidates. (3) A modified selection rule that combines simple answer frequency with the judge’s evaluation—changing only the terminal selection stage, leaving generation and communication fixed—boosts accuracy on the studied benchmarks from 63.82% to about 70.82–70.95%. The gains arise mainly from recovering correct answers that are present but outnumbered by more popular incorrect candidates.
AI.conclusion: By isolating the stages of generation, recognition, and selection, the paper shows that many multi-agent failures stem from selection dynamics rather than lack of knowledge or reasoning capacity. Judge-based signals can act as effective selection pressure, especially to save rare but correct answers from being swamped by common errors, but their utility is task- and model-dependent. The work provides a diagnostic framework for designing multi-agent architectures that explicitly protect existing correct answers from being lost during consensus formation and suggests that adding more agents or candidates only helps if it makes correct answers both present and recognisable to the selection mechanism.

title: When RAG Fails to Equalize: Geo-bias in Factual Question Answering over Public Companies
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely assumed to mitigate factual errors in large language models (LLMs), but it remains unclear whether retrieval uniformly compensates for missing knowledge. We study this question in a controlled factual QA setting over public companies, constructing a benchmark of approximately 2,000 firms across global equity indices. We evaluate six LLMs on four atomic attributes under four conditions: no-context, perfect context, misleading context, and distraction context. We find strong geographic disparities in no-context accuracy, indicating uneven parametric knowledge. While perfect context improves performance, it does not eliminate these gaps: gains are correlated with baseline accuracy, suggesting retrieval effectiveness is coupled to internal representations. Under misleading context, models frequently copy incorrect information. Larger models improve overall performance but do not remove these structural effects. These results challenge the view of RAG as a universal corrective and highlight the interaction between model knowledge, context quality, and entity representation.

AI.tldr: Study shows retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) does not uniformly fix factual errors in LLMs and its effectiveness depends on pre-existing model knowledge and context quality.
AI.motivation: RAG is often assumed to correct LLM factual mistakes by providing external evidence, but it is not well understood whether retrieval can fully compensate for gaps or biases in a model's internal (parametric) knowledge. The authors want to test, in a controlled way, how well RAG works across entities and geographies, and whether it really serves as a universal remedy for hallucinations and missing knowledge.
AI.method: They build a factual QA benchmark on about 2,000 public companies from major global equity indices, focusing on four basic company attributes. They then evaluate six different LLMs under four conditions: (1) no external context, (2) perfect supporting context, (3) misleading but plausible context, and (4) distracting, irrelevant context. This design lets them quantify how much retrieval helps when it’s correct, how susceptible models are to being led astray by wrong context, and how these effects vary by geography and baseline model knowledge.
AI.result: They observe large geographic disparities in model accuracy when no external context is given, meaning LLMs’ internal knowledge is uneven across regions. Providing perfect context improves accuracy overall but does not remove these disparities; the performance gains are strongly correlated with each model’s baseline (no-context) accuracy. This implies that retrieval’s benefit depends on the model’s internal representations of entities. When context is misleading, models often copy the incorrect information rather than relying on internal knowledge. Scaling up to larger models increases overall accuracy but the same structural patterns—geographic gaps, dependence on internal knowledge, and vulnerability to misleading context—remain.
AI.conclusion: RAG should not be treated as a universal fix for LLM factual errors. Its effectiveness is constrained by the model’s underlying knowledge and representations of entities, as well as by the quality and reliability of retrieved context. Larger models help but do not solve structural issues like geographic knowledge gaps or susceptibility to misleading information. The study underscores the need to design RAG systems that explicitly account for model knowledge distribution, context verification, and robustness to incorrect or noisy retrievals.

title: LivingRAG: Augmenting Graph RAG with Experience
summary: Graph-based RAG improves multi-hop question answering by organizing evidence as a knowledge graph. However, most existing RAG systems process each query in isolation and discard useful reasoning from the LLM's response after inference. As a result, later related queries need to retrieve evidence and reason from scratch. We propose LivingRAG, a Graph RAG framework with writable and reusable reasoning experience. LivingRAG adds a writable experience store to a graph-based retrieval backbone, enabling verified experiences to be reused during inference in two ways. Stored graph signals help retrieval find entities and passages that were useful in earlier related queries. Stored summaries provide a reference reasoning pattern for answer generation. We analyze online QA streams and find reusable signals from shared entities, graph neighborhoods, and question templates. Experiments on multi-hop QA benchmarks show that LivingRAG improves accuracy over strong RAG baselines and reduces completion-token use when relevant prior experience is reused.

AI.tldr: LivingRAG is a graph-based RAG framework that stores and reuses verified reasoning experiences to improve multi‑hop QA accuracy and efficiency over time.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based RAG systems treat each query independently and discard the LLM’s intermediate reasoning and successful retrieval patterns. This wastes prior computation and forces the system to re-discover the same multi-hop evidence and reasoning chains for later, related questions. The paper is motivated by the need for a RAG system that can accumulate, structure, and safely reuse prior reasoning so that subsequent queries become more accurate and cheaper to answer, especially in streaming or session-style QA settings.
AI.method: The authors propose LivingRAG, which augments a graph-based retrieval backbone with a writable, persistent “experience store.” During inference, when the system answers a multi-hop QA query, it (1) records graph signals—such as useful entities, their neighborhoods, and passages used as evidence—and (2) stores summaries that capture successful reasoning patterns. These experiences are verified and then written into the store. For future queries, the system reuses these experiences in two ways: (a) the stored graph signals guide retrieval toward entities and passages that worked well for related questions, and (b) the stored summaries are used as reference reasoning templates to steer answer generation. The authors also analyze online QA streams to characterize where reuse is possible, finding repeated entities, overlapping graph neighborhoods, and recurring question templates.
AI.result: On multi-hop QA benchmarks, LivingRAG outperforms strong graph-based RAG baselines in answer accuracy. Additionally, when the incoming questions are related to previously answered ones such that prior experience is relevant, the framework reduces completion-token usage, indicating more efficient generation. The empirical analysis of QA streams further confirms that practical settings contain substantial reusable signals (shared entities, neighborhoods, and templates) that LivingRAG can exploit.
AI.conclusion: LivingRAG demonstrates that making graph-based RAG “living” and stateful—by storing and reusing curated reasoning experiences—can both improve multi-hop QA performance and reduce generation cost in realistic streaming/query-session scenarios. The study suggests that future RAG systems should be designed to accumulate and leverage structured, verified experience rather than treating every query as independent and stateless.

title: Beam Search, Self-Consistency, and the Limits of Inference-Time Scaling for Grammar-Constrained Text-to-SQL in Small Language Models
summary: One common trade-off in the use of large language models involves reducing the size of the model while increasing the amount of computation at inference time, for example by using a wider beam search. In this paper, we examine the constrained case of this "model size vs. inference compute" trade-off, in which the model outputs are constrained by a strict grammar at inference time. Our results demonstrate that the constrained trade-off behaves differently from the unconstrained trade-off. We investigate the task of converting a prose query into an equivalent SQL query (text-to-SQL). Performance is evaluated on the Spider text-to-SQL benchmark, using the Qwen2.5-Instruct model family ranging in size from 0.5B to 7B parameters, all at 4-bit precision. We experiment with two approaches to varying inference compute: (i) beam search with a variable number of beams; and (ii) sample+vote, i.e., sampling several constrained outputs and then voting on their execution results, where the number of samples is varied. On the 1034-example development set, we find that: (a) both beam search and sample+vote improve accuracy, especially on smaller model sizes; (b) the "model size vs.\ inference compute" trade-off is not advantageous in this experiment, because moving to a larger model size typically results in higher accuracy than increasing inference compute on the same model size; (c) beam search outperforms sample+vote at a matched inference budget. This latter result is of particular interest since it contrasts with the findings of the unconstrained trade-off.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how increasing inference-time computation (beam search or sample+vote) trades off against model size, under strict grammar constraints, for text-to-SQL with Qwen2.5 models on Spider.
AI.motivation: Practitioners often want to use smaller LLMs for efficiency but compensate by spending more compute at inference (e.g., wider beam search). Prior work mostly studies this trade-off in unconstrained generation. Many real applications, such as text-to-SQL, need outputs to follow a strict grammar, which may change the nature of this trade-off. The authors want to understand how model size vs. inference compute behaves in such constrained settings and which decoding strategy is more effective.
AI.method: They study a constrained text-to-SQL task: mapping natural language queries to SQL on the Spider benchmark. Outputs must satisfy a strict SQL grammar during decoding. They use Qwen2.5-Instruct models from 0.5B to 7B parameters at 4-bit precision. They vary inference compute in two ways: (1) beam search with different numbers of beams; (2) sample+vote, where multiple grammar-constrained samples are generated and the final prediction is chosen by voting based on execution results. They evaluate performance on the 1034-example Spider development set and compare accuracy across model sizes and compute budgets.
AI.result: (a) Increasing inference compute via either beam search or sample+vote improves accuracy, with larger relative gains for smaller models. (b) Despite these gains, scaling to a larger model is generally more beneficial for accuracy than increasing inference compute at fixed model size, so the model size vs. inference compute trade-off is not favorable in this constrained setting. (c) For a matched inference budget, beam search consistently outperforms sample+vote, in contrast to previous results in unconstrained generation where sampling-based methods can be competitive or superior.
AI.conclusion: In grammar-constrained generation for text-to-SQL, extra inference-time compute helps, but it does not substitute effectively for model size: larger models remain the better route to higher accuracy. Moreover, under a fixed compute budget, beam search is a more effective strategy than sample+vote, diverging from observations in unconstrained settings. These findings suggest that conclusions about model size vs. inference compute and decoding strategies from unconstrained generation do not directly transfer to constrained, structure-aware tasks like text-to-SQL.

title: Quantitative Analysis of $ω$-Regular Robust MDPs
summary:
Robust Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) generalize classical MDPs by allowing uncertainty in transition probabilities and optimizing against their worst-case realization. We consider $(s,a)$-rectangular RMDPs with \emph{linearly defined} uncertainty sets and study parity objectives, which are a canonical representation of $ω$-regular objectives. An uncertainty set is linearly defined if it is described by linear inequalities over the transition distribution together with auxiliary variables, which capture the standard $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ balls as well as general polytopic uncertainty sets.
  The quantitative value is the supremum, over all agent policies, of the satisfaction probability guaranteed against the adversarial environment. Previous work studied the qualitative analysis, namely the almost-sure (resp. positive) problem that asks whether a single agent policy guarantees satisfaction with probability one (resp. positive probability) against every environment policy. In this work, we solve the exact quantitative problem.
  Our contributions are threefold. First, we show that both the agent and the environment admit pure memoryless optimal policies. Second, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for quantitative parity on linearly defined robust Markov chains and use it as a subroutine in a policy-iteration algorithm for RMDPs. The algorithm combines quantitative one-step improvements with qualitative almost-sure improvements. Finally, we report experiments comparing our approach with the explicit reduction to stochastic games.

AI.tldr: The paper studies robust Markov decision processes with linearly defined uncertainty sets and solves the exact quantitative parity objective problem, proving pure memoryless optimal strategies and giving a polynomial-time algorithm plus experiments.
AI.motivation: Classical MDPs assume known transition probabilities, which is unrealistic when there is model uncertainty. Robust MDPs handle such uncertainty, but prior work on parity (ω-regular) objectives in this setting only addressed qualitative questions (almost-sure/positive satisfaction). There is a need to understand and efficiently compute the exact optimal probability of satisfying such objectives under worst-case uncertainty for expressive, practically relevant uncertainty sets.
AI.method: The authors consider (s,a)-rectangular RMDPs whose transition uncertainty sets are specified via linear inequalities, a framework encompassing L1, Linfty, and polytopic uncertainty. They analyze parity objectives and formulate the quantitative value as the supremum satisfaction probability guaranteed against an adversarial environment. They prove structural results (existence of pure memoryless optimal policies for both players), then design a polynomial-time algorithm for quantitative parity on linearly defined robust Markov chains. This algorithm is then embedded as a subroutine in a policy-iteration scheme for RMDPs that combines quantitative one-step improvements with qualitative almost-sure improvements. They also perform empirical comparisons with an alternative approach based on explicit reduction to stochastic games.
AI.result: They establish that optimal policies in this robust parity setting can be chosen pure and memoryless for both agent and environment. They provide a polynomial-time algorithm to solve the quantitative parity problem on robust Markov chains with linearly defined uncertainty. Using this as a building block, they obtain a practical policy-iteration algorithm for general RMDPs. Experimental results indicate advantages of their approach compared to solving the equivalent stochastic game obtained by explicit reduction.
AI.conclusion: The paper fully solves the quantitative parity objective problem for (s,a)-rectangular RMDPs with linearly defined uncertainty sets, both at the level of structural understanding (pure memoryless optimal strategies) and algorithmic solutions (polynomial-time algorithm plus policy iteration). Their approach is general enough to cover common robust uncertainty models and performs competitively in experiments, making it a viable tool for robust verification and synthesis with ω-regular specifications.

title: MoganBert-TR: A Turkish Encoder Foundation Model Trained from Scratch with a CLM-to-MLM Curriculum
comment: 32 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables. Model weights, tokenizer, embedding model and evaluation code: https://huggingface.co/moganai
summary:
Turkish encoder models have adopted modern architectures while leaving the pretraining objective fixed at masked language modelling. This paper introduces MoganBert-TR, a 149M-parameter Turkish encoder foundation model trained from scratch on a language-specifically filtered corpus, together with an embedding model derived from it (MoganBert-Embed).
  MoganBert-TR is trained over 237.3B tokens with a two-stage CLM-to-MLM curriculum: causal language modelling first, masked language modelling for the remainder, with the transition made inside the stable phase of a WSD schedule. In a controlled ablation under an equal step budget, this design outperforms pure MLM by 2.7-3.7x on Turkish MS MARCO retrieval; the measured mechanism is embedding geometry, where a single direction absorbs 28.1% of the variance under pure MLM against 11.9% under the curriculum. Long-context extension and learning-rate decay are then split into two branches after a shared prefix: running the final portion of decay at 1024 context improves the TrGLUE average by 0.49 +/- 0.26 points across five paired seeds (p = 0.013) and beats a model-soup alternative by 0.75 points at ~4.3% additional cost.
  MoganBert-TR attains 78.41 on TrGLUE, the best among the Turkish ModernBERT models compared, and 77.73 on TabiBench, where it leads two of the eight categories with the largest margin on code retrieval (+3.62 points over TabiBERT). MoganBert-Embed, produced through teacher distillation and multi-signal contrastive fine-tuning, ranks first among student models on the MTEB(Turkish) overall average with 68.30 and reaches 99.5% of its 7.57B-parameter teacher's score with a 51x smaller backbone. The accompanying 50,048-token tokenizer outperforms all compared Turkish tokenizers on compression and fertility across two independent test sets. Weights, tokenizer, embedding model and evaluation code: https://huggingface.co/moganai

AI.tldr: The paper presents MoganBert-TR, a new Turkish encoder model trained with a causal-to-masked LM curriculum and long-context training, plus a distilled embedding model, achieving state-of-the-art Turkish benchmarks and efficient embeddings.
AI.motivation: Existing Turkish encoder models use modern architectures but rely solely on masked language modeling objectives and lack optimized training curricula, long-context strategies, and strong open embedding models. The authors aim to improve Turkish language representations, retrieval performance, and tokenizer quality while keeping model size moderate.
AI.method: 1) Train a 149M-parameter Turkish encoder (MoganBert-TR) from scratch on a language-specifically filtered corpus over 237.3B tokens. 2) Use a two-stage curriculum: start with causal language modeling (CLM) and then switch to masked language modeling (MLM) during the stable phase of a warmup-stable-decay (WSD) learning-rate schedule. 3) Perform controlled ablations under equal training-step budgets to compare pure MLM vs CLM→MLM curriculum, and analyze embedding geometry (variance concentration directions). 4) Split training into two branches after a shared prefix to test long-context extension and learning-rate decay: run the final decay phase at 1024-token context vs baselines and model-soup. 5) Distill an embedding model (MoganBert-Embed) from a 7.57B-parameter teacher using teacher distillation and multi-signal contrastive fine-tuning. 6) Design and evaluate a 50,048-token Turkish tokenizer on compression and fertility across two independent test sets. 7) Evaluate on TrGLUE, TabiBench, Turkish MS MARCO retrieval, MTEB(Turkish), and tokenizer metrics.
AI.result: 1) The CLM→MLM curriculum significantly outperforms pure MLM on Turkish MS MARCO retrieval by 2.7–3.7x under the same step budget. Embedding analysis shows that pure MLM leads to a dominant variance direction (28.1% variance) whereas the curriculum reduces this to 11.9%, indicating healthier embedding geometry. 2) Training the final learning-rate decay phase with 1024-token context improves TrGLUE average by 0.49 ± 0.26 points across five paired seeds (p = 0.013) and outperforms a model-soup approach by 0.75 points at ~4.3% extra compute. 3) MoganBert-TR reaches 78.41 on TrGLUE (best among compared Turkish ModernBERT models) and 77.73 on TabiBench, leading two of eight categories, with a +3.62-point gain on code retrieval over TabiBERT. 4) MoganBert-Embed achieves 68.30 on MTEB(Turkish) overall, ranking first among student models and obtaining 99.5% of its 7.57B-parameter teacher’s score with a 51x smaller backbone. 5) The 50,048-token tokenizer outperforms all compared Turkish tokenizers on compression and fertility on two independent test sets.
AI.conclusion: A curriculum that transitions from causal to masked language modeling, paired with long-context training in the late decay phase, substantially improves Turkish encoder representations, retrieval performance, and benchmark scores over pure MLM baselines at modest additional cost. The resulting MoganBert-TR sets new state-of-the-art results on key Turkish benchmarks among comparable models, while the distilled MoganBert-Embed offers near-teacher-level embedding quality with a much smaller model. Additionally, the custom tokenizer delivers superior compression and fertility, making this suite—model weights, tokenizer, and embedding model—a strong, efficient foundation for Turkish NLP tasks.

title: SciMIF: Understanding Multimodal Instruction Following in Scientific Domains
summary: Understanding instruction-following capabilities in scientific domains is essential for effectively leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to advance the development of scientific fields. In this work, we introduce SciMIF, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate the capability of MLLMs in following complex scientific instructions. Specifically, based on an extensive analysis of 22 distinct tasks across 5 representative scientific disciplines, we propose a comprehensive taxonomy comprising 10 constraint groups that captures both general functional requirements and discipline-specific characteristics. Guided by this taxonomy, we develop a high-fidelity instruction injection pipeline to systematically augment existing scientific datasets. We conduct comprehensive experiments on multiple state-of-the-art closed-source and open-source MLLMs. Our findings reveal significant performance disparities across different scientific disciplines, with chemistry posing greater challenges for current MLLMs. Furthermore, we observe that increasing the model scale does not yield corresponding improvements in constraint adherence, and current models still struggle severely with fine-grained constraints and instructions requiring the deep application of disciplinary knowledge. SciMIF fills the current void in evaluating multimodal instruction adherence within scientific domains, laying a crucial foundation for future enhancements of MLLMs in rigorous scientific applications. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/shenye7436/SciMIF .

AI.tldr: SciMIF is a new benchmark to evaluate how well multimodal large language models follow complex, constraint-rich scientific instructions across disciplines.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal LLMs are increasingly applied to scientific problems, but there is no rigorous, systematic way to measure how well they follow detailed scientific instructions, especially those involving discipline-specific constraints and multimodal inputs. Existing benchmarks focus mainly on general tasks or simple instructions and do not expose fine-grained failures in constraint adherence or domain reasoning. This limits our understanding of their reliability for real scientific workflows.
AI.method: The authors first analyze 22 scientific tasks spanning 5 representative disciplines to identify typical instruction patterns and requirements. From this, they build a taxonomy of 10 constraint groups that cover both general functional constraints (e.g., format, steps, structure) and discipline-specific requirements (e.g., chemistry- or physics-specific rules). Using this taxonomy, they design a high-fidelity instruction injection pipeline that augments existing scientific datasets by adding systematically constructed, constraint-rich instructions. They then use the resulting SciMIF benchmark to test multiple state-of-the-art open- and closed-source MLLMs and measure their adherence to these constraints across disciplines and model scales.
AI.result: Experiments show substantial variation in performance across scientific fields, with chemistry emerging as particularly difficult for current MLLMs. Despite increases in model size, adherence to complex and fine-grained constraints does not consistently improve. Models especially underperform on instructions that require detailed constraint tracking and deep, discipline-specific reasoning, highlighting systematic weaknesses beyond mere scaling.
AI.conclusion: SciMIF provides the first focused benchmark for multimodal instruction-following in scientific domains, exposing significant gaps in current MLLMs’ ability to follow complex, constraint-rich scientific instructions, particularly in chemistry and in tasks needing deep domain knowledge. The work establishes a much-needed foundation and clear evaluation protocol for future efforts to improve the reliability and scientific rigor of MLLMs used in research and applied science settings.

title: Localize-Then-Decide Guarantees for LLM Judgments
comment: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026. Code: https://github.com/llm2409/Localize-Then-Decide
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as evaluators to assess output quality and preference alignment, yet providing reliable guarantees of agreement with human judgments remains challenging. Recent work introduces confidence-thresholding methods that provide such guarantees for pairwise comparisons, relying on the assumption that higher estimated confidence implies lower disagreement risk with humans. However, this assumption can break down when the number of candidate responses increases, since distributing probability mass across many alternatives can distort confidence estimates. To address this issue, we propose a Localize-Then-Decide framework. First, conformal prediction localizes a small shortlist that contains the human-preferred response with high probability. Then, a calibrated confidence-based rule selectively chooses a single response from this shortlist or abstains. This design restores the monotonic relationship between confidence and disagreement risk and enables high-probability agreement guarantees. Experiments with multiple candidate sizes across several datasets and judge LLMs demonstrate that our framework consistently achieves higher guarantee success rates and substantially higher coverage than single-stage baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage framework to make large language models more reliable as automatic judges when many candidate responses are compared.
AI.motivation: LLMs are used as automatic evaluators of response quality and preference alignment, but existing confidence-based methods only work reliably for pairwise comparisons. When there are many candidate answers, the link between an LLM’s confidence and its agreement with humans breaks down, so there is no strong guarantee that high-confidence decisions actually match human preferences.
AI.method: They introduce a Localize-Then-Decide framework. In the first stage, they apply conformal prediction to construct a small shortlist of responses that, with high probability, contains the human-preferred answer. In the second stage, they use a calibrated confidence-based decision rule that either selects one response from this shortlist or abstains from making a decision. This two-stage design is meant to restore a monotonic relationship between the model’s confidence and its risk of disagreement with humans, enabling high-probability guarantees about alignment with human judgments.
AI.result: Across multiple datasets, various numbers of candidate responses, and different LLMs acting as judges, the framework consistently achieves higher rates of successfully meeting its agreement guarantees and much higher coverage (i.e., it can confidently decide in more cases) compared with single-stage confidence-thresholding baselines.
AI.conclusion: A two-stage Localize-Then-Decide approach, combining conformal prediction for shortlisting with calibrated confidence rules for final selection or abstention, can provide stronger and more reliable guarantees that LLM-as-a-judge decisions agree with human preferences, especially when evaluating many candidate responses at once.

title: Multi-Granularity Context-Enhanced RAG over Multimodal Knowledge Graphs
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely used to mitigate hallucination issues in large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). In particular, knowledge graph (KG)-based RAG leverages structured knowledge to provide (M)LLMs with high-quality external information. Building on these works, recent studies have explored multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) as knowledge bases for GraphRAG. This enables Graph RAG to integrate knowledge across multiple modalities, thereby further enhancing its performance. However, existing MMKG-based RAG methods generally follow a common pipeline in which different modalities are largely processed independently before being fusion. As a result, textual context is only used to a limited extent during visual information extraction and subsequent multimodal knowledge fusion. This brings a semantic gap between images and text which limits the multimodal GraphRAG performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework for constructing a Context-Enhanced MMKG (CEMMKG) to better support multimodal GraphRAG. The proposed CEMMKG enriches each image with complementary textual context at both local and global scopes. Local context goes beyond the surrounding text by incorporating sentences that are semantically related to the image, while global context provides a summary of the entire passage. We further introduce a multi-granularity design for the local context, allowing it to capture semantically relevant information at different levels of detail. Extensive experiments on the selected vision-centric dataset validate that CEMMKG is effective in leveraging contextual information to improve MMKG-based RAG performance. Moreover, its effectiveness across different MMKG-based RAG methods demonstrates its broad applicability.

AI.tldr: They build a new context-enriched multimodal knowledge graph (CEMMKG) so that RAG over multimodal KGs can better exploit textual context around images and thus perform better on vision-centric tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal KG-based RAG systems process modalities (text, image) mostly independently and fuse them late, which underuses textual context during visual information extraction and multimodal fusion. This causes a semantic gap between images and text and limits multimodal GraphRAG performance.
AI.method: They propose CEMMKG, a framework to construct a context-enhanced multimodal KG. For each image, they attach complementary textual context at two scopes: (1) Local context: not only the immediate surrounding text, but also sentences semantically related to the image, with a multi-granularity design to capture different detail levels; (2) Global context: a summary of the whole passage. They then plug this enriched MMKG into existing MMKG-based RAG/GraphRAG pipelines.
AI.result: On a vision-centric dataset, CEMMKG consistently improves the performance of MMKG-based RAG over baselines that lack such contextual enrichment. The gains hold across different MMKG-based RAG methods, indicating robustness and generality.
AI.conclusion: Enriching MMKGs with carefully designed local and global textual context around images narrows the semantic gap between modalities and significantly boosts multimodal GraphRAG. CEMMKG is an effective and broadly applicable way to enhance MMKG-based RAG systems.

title: Unfolding Scientific Papers into Multi-Turn Generation Trajectories for Continued Pre-Training
summary: A recent line of synthetic-data work reconstructs the thinking behind existing text rather than rewriting the text itself, but it operates on short web passages, recovers only local thoughts, and leaves the structure of whole documents untouched. Scientific papers are written to a clear and largely uniform structure and make a natural substrate for lifting this paradigm to the document level. We present a pipeline that unfolds each paper into a multi-turn generation trajectory in which a teacher model reconstructs the writing process of the whole paper: a writing request, a global plan, and pre-writing deliberation for each section. All section texts and the abstract are kept verbatim from the source paper. We apply the pipeline to quality-filtered arXiv papers and obtain a corpus for continued pre-training (CPT) that is roughly twice the size of the source text. The same reverse construction extends to instruction data and evaluation. Treating real paper text as the answer yields an SFT dataset. Anchoring tasks in held-out papers yields PAW-Bench, an academic-writing benchmark whose tasks carry their own rubrics and checklists. In controlled experiments CPT on our corpus followed by supervised fine-tuning on public datasets improves writing benchmarks broadly while preserving general reasoning and improving long-document reading. The writing gain persists even when every model is fine-tuned on a dedicated writing SFT dataset. Mixing our SFT data into that recipe lifts academic writing further.

AI.tldr: They reconstruct the hidden writing process behind scientific papers to create synthetic trajectories (plans, deliberations) while keeping the original paper text, and show that pretraining and SFT on this expanded corpus improves academic-writing performance and long-document abilities.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic-data work that recovers underlying thoughts from text is limited to short web snippets and only captures local reasoning, leaving whole-document structure and scientific writing largely unaddressed. There is a need for document-level synthetic trajectories that reflect the global planning and section-level deliberation used in real academic writing, to better train models for structured scientific writing and evaluation.
AI.method: They design a pipeline that reverse-engineers the full writing trajectory of scientific papers. For each arXiv paper, a teacher model generates: (1) a high-level writing request, (2) a global plan for the paper, and (3) pre-writing deliberation for each section, while leaving all section texts and abstracts exactly as in the source. This yields multi-turn synthetic trajectories about the paper. They apply it at scale to quality-filtered arXiv to create a continued pre-training (CPT) corpus ~2x the size of the original text. Using the same reverse-construction idea, they also: (a) produce an SFT dataset by treating the real paper text as answers to synthetic instructions, and (b) build PAW-Bench, an academic-writing benchmark where tasks are anchored in held-out papers and come with explicit rubrics and checklists.
AI.result: Continued pre-training on their trajectory-augmented corpus, followed by supervised fine-tuning on public data, yields broad gains on writing benchmarks, while maintaining general reasoning capabilities and improving long-document reading. These writing improvements hold even when all models are fine-tuned on a strong, specialized writing SFT dataset. Adding their SFT data into that fine-tuning setup further boosts academic-writing performance. The new PAW-Bench benchmark and SFT corpus provide structured evaluation and training resources for academic writing.
AI.conclusion: Reverse-engineering the writing trajectories of scientific papers into multi-turn synthetic data is an effective way to enrich training signals for language models. This approach scales to large arXiv corpora, yields useful CPT and SFT datasets, and supports a dedicated academic-writing benchmark. Models trained with these resources show consistent improvements in writing quality and long-document handling without sacrificing general reasoning, indicating that document-level thought reconstruction is a powerful paradigm for enhancing academic-writing abilities.

title: ProgRouter: Online Progress-Guided Orchestration for Multi-Agent LLM Workflows under Quality-Cost Tradeoffs
comment: Accepted in Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026. Index Terms: Collaborative agentic workflows, LLM agent orchestration, Quality-cost trade-off, Task progress prediction, Online decision-making
summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) workflows have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving complex, open-ended tasks through collaborative reasoning among specialized LLM agents, but they incur substantial operating costs due to repeated LLM invocations and long-horizon context accumulation. Existing cascade routing methods make one-shot, query-level decisions and cannot adapt to the dynamic, state-dependent nature of multi-step workflows, in which the right LLM at each step depends on evolving task progress, remaining task difficulty, and cost-efficiency requirements. We present ProgRouter, an online progress-guided routing framework that adaptively selects LLM agents across workflow steps to preserve task-solving quality while adhering to time and cost budgets. ProgRouter introduces a multi-view task progress scorer that combines coarse workflow outcome regimes with fine-grained signals on subtask completion, progress trends, and workflow state quality.
