Then, a dual-path task progress predictor and an adaptive meta-gating mechanism estimate the progress gain for each candidate routed LLM. ProgRouter makes online step-wise routing decisions that balance progress gain, task time budgets, and long-term operating cost efficiency. Experiments on HumanEval Plus, MBPP, MATH-500, and ASQA, spanning agentic code generation, mathematical reasoning, and retrieval-augmented long-form question answering, demonstrate that ProgRouter reduces the operating cost relative to key baselines while maintaining strong task-solving performance.

AI.tldr: ProgRouter is a progress-aware router that adaptively selects among multiple LLM agents at each step of a multi-agent workflow to save time and cost while preserving task performance.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM workflows are powerful for complex, open-ended tasks but are expensive because they require many LLM calls and long context histories. Existing cascade routing schemes decide once per query which model to use and cannot adapt as the task state evolves across multiple steps. There is a need for a routing method that can respond to dynamic task progress, remaining difficulty, and budget constraints throughout the workflow.
AI.method: The authors propose ProgRouter, an online routing framework that operates step-by-step over a multi-agent LLM workflow. It first defines a multi-view task progress scorer combining high-level outcome regimes with finer-grained indicators of subtask completion, progress trends, and workflow state quality. Using this representation, a dual-path task progress predictor plus an adaptive meta-gating mechanism estimate the expected progress gain from using each candidate LLM agent at the current step. Based on these estimates, ProgRouter makes online, step-wise routing choices that trade off predicted progress gain against time and cost budgets, aiming for long-term cost-efficiency while maintaining solution quality.
AI.result: On benchmarks including HumanEval Plus and MBPP (agentic code generation), MATH-500 (mathematical reasoning), and ASQA (retrieval-augmented long-form QA), ProgRouter achieves similar task-solving quality to strong baselines but with reduced operating cost. The experiments show that dynamic, progress-aware routing across workflow steps is more cost-efficient than static or one-shot cascade routing while keeping performance competitive.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, progress-guided routing in multi-agent LLM workflows can significantly cut time and monetary cost without sacrificing problem-solving quality. By explicitly modeling task progress and predicting per-step progress gains for each candidate LLM, ProgRouter provides a more efficient alternative to traditional, static cascade routing for complex multi-step LLM applications.

title: Skill Issue: Are Skills Language-Invariant in LLMs?
summary: Large language models access knowledge inconsistently across languages, but to what extent do they differ in their skill sets when interacting with different languages? This work quantifies cross-lingual skill inconsistency orthogonally from knowledge and general benchmark performance. We do this via multilingual self-play: two instances of the same model compete in a text-based game, each interacting through a different language interface. Since the model, opponent, rules, state space, and available actions remain fixed, this setting isolates the effect of language on the model's realized behavior. We build a multilingual extension to TextArena and evaluate three open-weight models across eight languages and six games covering spatial reasoning, imperfect information, resource allocation, and repeated interaction. We find that the same model can exhibit markedly different playing strength across languages, with systematic variation in win--loss margins, invalid actions, and strategic tendencies. Detailed analyses reveal language-specific failures in spatial reasoning, card-conditioned decisions, and optimal move selection. In some settings, changing only the intermediate reasoning language recovers much of the lost performance, suggesting that language can affect different stages of the decision process. These results show that skill discrepancies are a measurable major roadblock in the development of truly multilingual models. Better understanding these discrepancies can help us design models that perform more equitably across languages.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the same large language model shows different levels of skill depending on the language it uses, independent of its stored knowledge.
AI.motivation: While multilingual LLMs are known to have uneven knowledge across languages, it is unclear whether their underlying decision-making and problem-solving skills are also inconsistent across languages when knowledge and tasks are held constant. This hinders the development of fair, truly multilingual systems.
AI.method: The authors introduce a multilingual self-play setup using a multilingual extension of TextArena. Two instances of the same model play against each other in text-based games, each using a different language interface. Because the model architecture, opponent, rules, state space, and actions are fixed, any performance differences can be attributed to language. They evaluate three open-weight models across eight languages and six game types that test spatial reasoning, imperfect information, resource allocation, and repeated interaction, and they analyze win–loss margins, invalid moves, and strategic patterns. They also vary the language used for intermediate reasoning to test its effect on performance.
AI.result: The same model shows significant variation in playing strength across languages, reflected in different win–loss margins, frequencies of invalid actions, and strategic behaviors. Specific language-dependent weaknesses appear in spatial reasoning, card-based decision-making, and choice of optimal moves. Changing only the intermediate reasoning language can substantially recover performance losses in some settings, implying that language affects internal decision steps, not just input/output surfaces.
AI.conclusion: Cross-lingual skill inconsistency is a measurable and substantial obstacle for multilingual LLMs, distinct from knowledge gaps or aggregate benchmark scores. Language itself can shape the model’s realized reasoning and decision-making processes. Understanding and mitigating these discrepancies is important for building multilingual models that behave reliably and equitably across languages.

title: AsymSpec: Context-Asymmetric Speculative Decoding for Agentic LLMs
summary: Agentic LLM pipelines face escalating inference costs as context accumulates across retrieval, tool use, and multi-turn interactions. To control latency, deployments routinely compress inputs, but this degrades task accuracy. Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates generation losslessly, yet it assumes the drafter and verifier share an identical context, preventing SD from resolving the accuracy-overhead trade-off. We propose AsymSpec, an asymmetric speculative decoding framework that breaks this symmetry: a lightweight drafter reads the full input while the large verifier operates on the compressed view. The drafter steers the verifier via a contrastive $δ$-fusion of logits, modulated by a divergence-aware acceptance gate that preserves verification stability and high draft acceptance rates. Evaluated across four agentic capabilities and two end-to-end agent benchmarks, AsymSpec reaches $\approx 90\%$ of full-context accuracy on average, delivering $1.3$--$1.7\times$ throughput speedups at $0.2$--$0.3\times$ the compute cost on isolated text capabilities. These results show that asymmetric context access yields substantial gains precisely when compression discards critical reasoning signals.

AI.tldr: AsymSpec is an asymmetric speculative decoding framework where a lightweight drafter sees full context and a large verifier sees compressed context, achieving near full-context accuracy with significantly lower compute and higher throughput.
AI.motivation: Agentic LLM pipelines suffer from rising inference cost and latency as context grows via retrieval, tool calls, and multi-turn interactions. Existing input compression reduces latency but harms accuracy, while standard speculative decoding assumes both drafter and verifier share the same (typically full) context, so it cannot address the fundamental trade-off between context size, accuracy, and compute. A new approach is needed that leverages speculative decoding while allowing different context views to reduce cost without sacrificing much accuracy.
AI.method: AsymSpec introduces asymmetric speculative decoding where a small drafter model accesses the full, uncompressed input and proposes drafts, while a larger verifier model operates on a compressed representation of the input. The drafter’s logits are fused contrastively with the verifier’s logits using a delta (δ-) fusion mechanism that biases the verifier toward the drafter’s predictions in a controlled way. A divergence-aware acceptance gate monitors discrepancy between drafter and verifier to maintain verification stability and ensure high draft acceptance rates, even under asymmetric context. The system is evaluated on multiple agentic capabilities and end-to-end agent benchmarks.
AI.result: On four agentic capabilities and two end-to-end agent benchmarks, AsymSpec recovers about 90% of the accuracy of a full-context large model on average, while delivering 1.3–1.7× throughput speedups and reducing compute cost to 0.2–0.3× on isolated text capabilities. The gains are especially notable in scenarios where input compression would otherwise discard important reasoning information.
AI.conclusion: AsymSpec demonstrates that breaking the symmetry of speculative decoding—letting the drafter see full context and the verifier see compressed context—can effectively mitigate the trade-off between inference cost and task accuracy in agentic LLM pipelines. Asymmetric context access, combined with δ-fusion and divergence-aware gating, enables substantial efficiency improvements while retaining most of the accuracy of full-context inference, particularly in settings where naive compression harms reasoning performance.

title: Key Point Analysis Needs Structure Recovery: Task Definition, Dataset Diagnosis, and a Structure-Aware Benchmark
summary: Key Point Analysis (KPA) aims to identify a concise set of key points that summarize a collection of arguments together with their prevalence. We argue that KPA is fundamentally a structured prediction problem that requires recovering semantic groupings, generating representative key points, ensuring coverage, and estimating prevalence. Under this formulation, we show that existing KPA benchmarks suffer from limitations in grouping quality, redundancy, coverage, and argument-key point mappings, causing ceiling violation and selection failure in reference-based evaluation. To support future research on true KPA, we introduce a structure-aware, distribution-sensitive benchmark built via a human-in-the-loop re-annotation. Human and LLM evaluations consistently show that the resulting structures yield more coherent groupings, higher-quality key points, better coverage, and more reliable prevalence estimates than existing annotations. We further release several annotation resources to support research on KPA evaluation, argument-key point matching, explainable KPA, and LLM-as-a-judge methodologies, and outline a research agenda for true KPA.

AI.tldr: This paper redefines Key Point Analysis (KPA) as a structured prediction problem and introduces a new, human-in-the-loop, structure-aware benchmark that fixes major flaws in existing datasets, yielding better groupings, key points, coverage, and prevalence estimates.
AI.motivation: Existing KPA benchmarks have serious issues in semantic grouping quality, redundancy, coverage of arguments, and the correctness of argument–key point mappings. These issues break standard reference-based evaluation (ceiling violation, selection failure), making it hard to properly train or evaluate models that perform true KPA. The authors are motivated to provide a more realistic and reliable benchmark that captures the full structured nature of KPA and supports future research on both modeling and evaluation.
AI.method: The authors first conceptualize KPA as a structured prediction task involving four components: (1) recovering semantic groupings of arguments, (2) generating representative key points, (3) ensuring coverage over arguments, and (4) estimating prevalence of each key point. They then analyze existing KPA benchmarks and empirically identify multiple limitations. To remedy this, they build a new benchmark via human-in-the-loop re-annotation that explicitly enforces structure-aware and distribution-sensitive properties. They validate the new resource using both human evaluations and large language model (LLM) based evaluations, and they prepare additional annotation layers to enable research on evaluation schemes, argument–key point matching, explainability, and LLM-as-a-judge techniques.
AI.result: The new benchmark produces more coherent semantic groupings, higher-quality and less redundant key points, better coverage of the underlying argument space, and more reliable estimates of key point prevalence than earlier datasets. Both humans and LLM-based judges prefer the new annotations over existing ones. The resource also includes extra annotation artifacts useful for studying evaluation and matching, which the community can directly use for developing improved KPA systems and assessment methods.
AI.conclusion: KPA should be treated as a structured prediction problem rather than a simple summarization or clustering task, and existing benchmarks fall short of this standard. The authors’ structure-aware, distribution-sensitive benchmark—built with human-in-the-loop re-annotation—provides a more valid testbed for “true KPA” and helps remedy issues such as ceiling violations and selection failures in evaluation. By releasing this benchmark and related annotation resources, they aim to catalyze research on more faithful KPA models, better evaluation metrics, and robust LLM-as-a-judge practices, and they outline a broader research agenda grounded in this more principled view of KPA.

title: Imitation Learning for Connection-Tableau Construction
summary: An automated theorem prover builds a proof step by step, choosing at each point what to add and what to remove. We cast this construction as a policy acting in a transition system induced by a formal calculus, which fixes which steps are sound: for clausal connection tableaux, leanCoP-style search and plCoP/rlCoP-style planning then become stateful policies over one interface, and policy-learning methods apply directly. We equip such policies with a graph neural network that scores proof edits from structure that transfers across problems, train it by imitation learning from found proofs, and measure how performance holds as we remove search scaffolding, from full symbolic backtracking to a policy the network drives alone. Within a fixed step budget on M2k, MPTP2078-bushy, and TPTP v9.2.1, learned policies solve up to 46% more problems than leanCoP, and reach proofs in an order of magnitude fewer steps.

AI.tldr: They treat proof search in automated theorem proving as a learned policy over a transition system, using graph neural networks and imitation learning to guide leanCoP-style provers, achieving large gains in solved problems and proof length reduction.
AI.motivation: Automated theorem provers typically rely on hand-crafted heuristics and symbolic backtracking to explore large proof spaces, which can be inefficient and hard to optimize across varied problem families. There is a need to integrate modern learning methods with existing calculi (like clausal connection tableaux) in a way that is both sound and general, and to reduce reliance on exhaustive search while improving performance on standard benchmarks.
AI.method: They formalize proof construction as a policy acting in a transition system defined by a sound calculus (clausal connection tableaux). On top of leanCoP/plCoP/rlCoP-style search, they build a unified stateful policy interface and attach a graph neural network that assigns scores to possible proof edits using structural information about the current proof state and problem. The network is trained via imitation learning from proofs found by existing search procedures. They then progressively remove symbolic search components (like full backtracking) to test how much of the search the learned policy can reliably perform on its own.
AI.result: On standard benchmarks (M2k, MPTP2078-bushy, and TPTP v9.2.1) and under a fixed step budget, the learned graph-neural policies solve up to 46% more problems than the classical leanCoP prover. Additionally, they find proofs using up to an order of magnitude fewer proof steps compared to the baseline, demonstrating substantially more efficient search.
AI.conclusion: Casting proof search as a learned policy over a calculus-defined transition system and guiding it with graph neural networks trained by imitation learning can significantly improve automated theorem prover performance. This approach generalizes across different connection-based provers, reduces dependence on heavy symbolic backtracking, and yields both higher success rates and shorter proofs, suggesting a promising path toward more data-driven, efficient theorem proving systems.

title: Anchoring Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge Systems: Prior Scores Compromise Evaluation Independence
comment: 10 pages, full research paper, to appear in proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM '26), 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assess generated content, giving rise to the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm. These systems now score outputs, filter content, and gate iterative refinement in production pipelines, where each judgment is often assumed to be independent of earlier evaluations. We test this assumption using three prompt conditions: no metadata, revision framing, and anchored metadata containing revision, attempt, and prior-score fields. We show that prior scores, even when included only as context metadata, anchor judgments and systematically shift ratings toward their values. Across 192,000 attempted evaluations (185,271 successful), seven out of the eight evaluated models have 95% task-stratified bootstrap intervals below zero for the total anchored-metadata effect on 20 fixed texts. Cohen's $d$, a standardized measure of the difference between score distributions, reaches an absolute value of 0.71. Token-level analysis of selected model-task probes suggests a threshold-like response pattern: introducing anchored metadata produces a marked redistribution of output-score probabilities, while changing the anchor value within the tested below-threshold range produces comparatively little additional variation. On categorical industry data with human-labeled ground truth, anchored metadata blocks 48% of error corrections and flips 10.18% of correct judgments toward an assigned wrong label, demonstrating the bias extends beyond numerical scoring to categorical decisions. Neither Chain-of-Thought nor a metadata-disregard warning reduces the total effect, although the warning improves the paired accuracy effect relative to baseline in the industry experiment. Reliable LLM evaluation demands careful context engineering rather than an assumption of impartiality. Effective mitigation must be validated for the intended model and task or domain.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that including previous scores as metadata strongly biases LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations, shifting current judgments toward prior scores and harming accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to judge and score content, and many pipelines assume each evaluation is independent of prior ones. The authors want to test whether this assumption holds when previous scores or attempts are given as metadata, and to understand how such context influences LLM judgments.
AI.method: The authors design an experiment with three prompt conditions: no metadata, revision framing, and anchored metadata that includes prior revision, attempt number, and prior-score fields. They run about 192k evaluation attempts across eight LLMs on 20 fixed texts, measure how scores shift under different conditions, and quantify effects using statistics like bootstrap confidence intervals and Cohen’s d. They also perform token-level analyses to examine how probability distributions over scores change, and test on categorical, industry-labeled data to see how anchored metadata affects classification decisions. They further test mitigation strategies such as Chain-of-Thought prompting and metadata-disregard warnings.
AI.result: Seven out of eight models show a significant anchoring effect: prior scores in metadata systematically pull current ratings toward those values, with Cohen’s d up to 0.71. The token-level analysis indicates a threshold-like shift when anchored metadata is introduced, with relatively small changes when varying the specific anchor value below a threshold. On real categorical industry data, anchored metadata prevents nearly half of potential error corrections and flips about 10.18% of correct labels to incorrect ones that match the anchor. Mitigation attempts like Chain-of-Thought and simple metadata-disregard warnings do not eliminate the overall effect, though the warning improves paired accuracy in the industry setting.
AI.conclusion: LLM evaluators are not impartial when exposed to prior scores or judgments; such metadata systematically biases both numeric and categorical decisions. Therefore, reliable use of LLMs as judges requires deliberate context and prompt engineering that avoids or controls anchoring effects, and any mitigation needs to be specifically validated for each model and task or domain rather than assumed to generalize.

title: Trace Integrity for LLM Data Agents: A Vision for Auditable Structured Reasoning in Real-World Systems
summary: Answer accuracy is an insufficient reliability signal for LLM data agents. In structured-data tasks, a benchmark-correct answer can be produced by an invalid trace. This paper introduces Trace Integrity, a deployment reliability criterion for evaluating whether the computation recorded behind an answer is explicit, executable, schema-valid, operator-faithful, replayable, answer-consistent, and auditable. We identify the Structure Gap as the deployment failure mode that makes Trace Integrity necessary: natural-language reasoning and free-form rationales do not reliably specify the operator-level programs required by real-world systems. We operationalize Trace Integrity with execution contracts, structured artifacts that bind user intent to schema elements, operator plans, assumptions, executable queries, verification status, and final-answer linkage. We also introduce CAIT (Correct Answer / Invalid Trace) Rate, which measures how often answer-only evaluation counts computationally unsupported outputs as successes. In an empirical demonstration on BIRD Mini-Dev, Direct SQL, Operation Summary + SQL, and Contract-First SQL achieve answer accuracies of 20%, 22%, and 24%, while their Trace Integrity Pass Rates are 39%, 43%, and 40% and their CAIT Rates remain high at 55%, 59.1%, and 45.8%, showing that answer accuracy, trace validity, and silent-failure risk are distinct evaluation signals. Real-world LLM data agents should, therefore, be evaluated not only by whether their outputs match a reference answer, but by whether those outputs are backed by auditable computation.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that just checking whether a large language model (LLM) data agent gets the right final answer is not enough; you must also check whether the underlying computation (its trace) is valid and auditable.
AI.motivation: In real-world structured-data tasks (like database querying), LLMs can sometimes output the correct final answer even when the intermediate reasoning or query (the trace) is wrong or invalid. This is dangerous in deployment because it hides silent failures: systems may appear to work when evaluated only on answer accuracy, but actually rely on incorrect or non-replayable computations. The authors want a principled way to measure the reliability of the computation process itself, not just the outcomes.
AI.method: The authors define a new reliability criterion called Trace Integrity, which requires that the computation behind an answer be explicit, executable, schema-valid, operator-faithful, replayable, consistent with the final answer, and auditable. They formalize Trace Integrity via “execution contracts,” structured artifacts that connect user intent to database schema elements, operator plans, assumptions, executable queries, verification status, and linkage to the final answer. They also introduce a new metric, CAIT (Correct Answer / Invalid Trace) Rate, to quantify how often a system obtains a correct answer with an invalid or unsupported trace. They then test several prompting strategies (Direct SQL, Operation Summary + SQL, Contract-First SQL) on the BIRD Mini-Dev benchmark and evaluate both answer accuracy and Trace Integrity-related metrics.
AI.result: On the BIRD Mini-Dev dataset, Direct SQL, Operation Summary + SQL, and Contract-First SQL achieve relatively low answer accuracies of 20%, 22%, and 24%. However, their Trace Integrity Pass Rates are significantly higher: 39%, 43%, and 40%, respectively. At the same time, CAIT Rates are high—55%, 59.1%, and 45.8%—indicating that a large fraction of seemingly correct answers rely on invalid traces. These empirical results show that answer accuracy, trace validity, and the risk of silent failures are distinct and sometimes misaligned evaluation signals.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that for LLM data agents used in real-world structured-data applications, answer-only evaluation is insufficient and potentially misleading. Systems should be evaluated on whether their outputs are supported by computation that is explicit, executable, schema-consistent, operator-faithful, replayable, answer-consistent, and auditable. Trace Integrity and execution contracts provide a framework and metrics (including CAIT Rate) to reveal and manage silent failure modes that are invisible to traditional accuracy-based benchmarks.

title: Loss-Based Active Learning for Neural Abstractive Summarization
summary: Fine-tuning abstractive summarization models requires high-quality annotated data. However, obtaining such corpora is expensive and time-consuming, as it requires human annotators to read and comprehend long documents to create accurate summaries. Active learning mitigates this issue by selecting only the most informative instances for annotation, allowing models to achieve competitive results with significantly fewer labels. However, the application of active learning to summarization remains under-explored, and existing studies often suffer from instability and significant computational bottlenecks. To overcome these challenges, we propose LOBSTER (LOss-BaSed acTivE leaRning), a novel active learning framework designed specifically for abstractive summarization. LOBSTER improves performance by prioritizing unlabeled instances semantically similar to the model's current high-loss training examples, enabling the model to explicitly correct its specific weaknesses. Our empirical evaluation across three benchmark datasets and two summarization backbone models demonstrates that LOBSTER consistently matches or outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches while achieving a query selection speedup of up to 665x.

AI.tldr: Proposes LOBSTER, an active learning framework for abstractive summarization that selects unlabeled texts similar to high-loss examples, achieving comparable or better performance than SOTA with far faster query selection.
AI.motivation: Abstractive summarization models need large amounts of high-quality human-annotated data, which is costly because annotators must read and summarize long documents. Active learning can reduce annotation needs by selecting the most informative instances, but prior work in summarization is limited, unstable, and computationally expensive. There is a need for a more efficient, stable active learning approach tailored to summarization.
AI.method: Introduce LOBSTER, a loss-based active learning framework. It monitors which training instances currently incur high loss for the summarization model, then searches the unlabeled pool for instances that are semantically similar to those high-loss examples. These similar unlabeled instances are prioritized for annotation, aiming to help the model explicitly improve on its weaknesses. The approach is evaluated on three benchmark datasets using two different summarization backbones, comparing against existing active learning baselines.
AI.result: Across the three benchmarks and two backbone models, LOBSTER consistently matches or surpasses existing state-of-the-art active learning strategies for abstractive summarization. Additionally, its query selection procedure is highly efficient, achieving up to 665x speedup in selecting which unlabeled documents to annotate compared to competing methods.
AI.conclusion: Loss-based, similarity-driven active learning can effectively target a summarization model’s weaknesses while being computationally efficient. LOBSTER demonstrates that such an approach yields state-of-the-art or better performance with substantially faster query selection, suggesting it is a practical and scalable solution for reducing annotation costs in abstractive summarization tasks.

title: SwarmWorld: Stigmergic technological evolution in societies of language-model agents
summary: Collective intelligence can emerge when individuals coordinate through a shared environment, allowing local actions to accumulate into durable social organization. Language-model agents offer a new substrate for this process, yet most multi-agent systems rely on direct conversation, predefined roles, or centralized workflows. It remains unclear whether decentralized agents can build functional technologies and outperform independent search. Here, initially homogeneous LLM agents in SwarmWorld self-organize without assigned roles or recipes into evolving technological societies. Agents explore a spatial environment, process resources, test materials, construct persistent artifacts, and write executable controllers evaluated by a deterministic simulator under unseen disturbances after the agents are removed. SwarmWorld splits cognition from consequence: agents propose architectures and controllers within fixed action and material schemas, while the simulated world determines function. Shared societies develop broader, more resilient technological portfolios than a strong best-of-N isolated-search baseline, although isolated search remains competitive for the strongest artifact. Agents differentiate into exploration, construction, maintenance, and coordination behaviors, transitioning as the world matures. Technologies accumulate through collaborative construction, executable inheritance, and persistent agent-artifact networks, with most reuse beginning through physical observation rather than communication. Explicit cultural mechanisms amplify collaboration and organization, but functional benefits depend on outcome and timescale. Physical stigmergy alone supports capable societies, while interaction drives persistent technological ecologies rather than universally superior individual inventions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SwarmWorld, a decentralized environment where homogeneous LLM agents self-organize via a shared world to build and test persistent technologies, outperforming independent search in portfolio breadth and resilience.
AI.motivation: To understand whether and how collective intelligence can emerge in decentralized language-model agents that coordinate only through a shared environment (stigmergy), and whether such systems can build functional, resilient technologies that surpass independent LLM search strategies.
AI.method: The authors create SwarmWorld, a spatial simulation where initially identical LLM agents interact only through actions on the environment: exploring, gathering resources, testing materials, building artifacts, and writing executable controllers within fixed schemas. Artifact functionality is evaluated by a separate deterministic simulator under unseen disturbances, after agents are removed. They compare decentralized societies against strong best-of-N isolated search and manipulate cultural mechanisms (communication, explicit sharing) to assess their impact.
AI.result: Decentralized LLM societies in SwarmWorld self-organize into differentiated behavioral roles (exploration, construction, maintenance, coordination) that shift over time as the environment changes. These societies produce broader, more resilient portfolios of technologies than a strong isolated best-of-N search baseline, though isolated search can match or exceed them for the single strongest artifact. Most technological reuse emerges via physical observation of artifacts rather than direct communication, and added cultural mechanisms increase collaboration and organization with outcome- and timescale-dependent benefits.
AI.conclusion: Physical stigmergy via a shared environment is sufficient for homogeneous LLM agents to form functional technological societies with role differentiation and cumulative technological cultures. While explicit communication and cultural scaffolds enhance organization, durable technological ecologies arise primarily from environment-mediated interaction, and decentralized societies excel in technological diversity and robustness rather than universally superior individual inventions.

title: From Passive Response to Proactive Correction: Enhancing LLM Robustness Against Input Fact Perturbations
comment: Accepted to the Main Conference of EMNLP 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) frequently produce confident yet factually incorrect responses when user inputs contain misleading premises, a phenomenon we attribute to fact perturbations in the input. Existing approaches to hallucination mitigation typically assume reliable user inputs, overlooking how such factual errors can actively mislead model reasoning. To address this vulnerability, we propose DEDUCE, a three-stage framework that transforms LLMs from passive responders into proactive error correctors. DEDUCE operates in three stages: (1) detect errors through fine-grained fact extraction and verification; (2) devise correction strategies via multi perspective deliberation; and (3) correct misconceptions while delivering reliable answers. We also present MisFactQA, a dataset containing factual errors of varying degrees, and propose new metrics for evaluating model robustness. Experiments on TruthfulQA, FalseQA, and our MisFactQA benchmark demonstrate that DEDUCE significantly improves both accuracy and error correction capability. Consistent gains across Qwen, LLaMA, and Gemma families confirm its effectiveness and scalability.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DEDUCE, a three-stage framework that enables LLMs to detect and correct factual errors in user queries, improving robustness to misleading premises.
AI.motivation: LLMs often accept misleading or factually wrong user premises and generate confident but incorrect answers. Existing hallucination-mitigation methods mostly assume that user inputs are factually reliable, leaving models vulnerable when the input itself is wrong. The motivation is to make LLMs robust to such fact perturbations and capable of actively correcting user misconceptions rather than merely responding to them.
AI.method: The authors propose DEDUCE, a three-stage framework: (1) Detect: perform fine-grained fact extraction from the user input and verify each fact against external knowledge or tools to identify potential errors; (2) Devise: use multi-perspective deliberation to plan how to address the identified errors, considering different ways to correct or respond to them; (3) Correct: revise the user’s misconceptions explicitly and provide a reliable final answer. They also create MisFactQA, a benchmark dataset with systematically constructed factual errors of varying severity, and define new metrics to quantify robustness to misleading premises and error-correction ability.
AI.result: On benchmarks including TruthfulQA, FalseQA, and the new MisFactQA, DEDUCE-equipped models show higher answer accuracy and stronger ability to detect and correct false premises. The improvements hold across multiple LLM families (Qwen, LLaMA, Gemma), indicating generality and scalability.
AI.conclusion: Transforming LLMs from passive responders into proactive fact checkers via the DEDUCE framework substantially enhances robustness against factually flawed user inputs. The approach consistently improves both correctness and misconception-correction across models and benchmarks, and the MisFactQA dataset plus new robustness metrics provide useful tools for further research in this area.

title: Planetary Prediction Engine: Autonomous Geospatial Prediction via Intelligent Data Selection and Foundation Model Embeddings
summary: Addressing critical global challenges, from food security and disaster risk to disease outbreaks and socio-economic vulnerability, demands high-fidelity geospatial modeling. However, building predictive planetary models remains bottlenecked by a fragmented data ecosystem, requiring manual data retrieval, multimodal data curation and fusion along with iterative model selection. We present the Planetary Prediction Engine (PPE), an autonomous AI system that executes this end-to-end workflow directly from natural-language queries. PPE synthesizes multimodal datasets on the fly, retrieving spatiotemporally relevant covariates across open-web and Earth observation platforms (Data Commons, Google Earth Engine) and fusing them with geospatial foundation model embeddings (PDFM, AlphaEarth). Simultaneously, it searches over task-tailored model architecture families with automated overfitting guards. Across diverse tasks, geographies, and scientific domains, PPE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art or manually tuned expert baselines. For US spatial regression, PPE improves mean $R^2$ across 21 CDC health indicators (76.8% vs. 60.0%), FEMA national risk indices (64.9% vs. 60.0%), and the Social Vulnerability Index (66.2% vs. 58.6%). For spatial downscaling in data-scarce settings, PPE integrates localized proxies to double baseline accuracy in Nigerian food security indicators ($R^2$ of 66.1% vs. 31.5%). For epidemiological nowcasting of the 2026 DRC Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, PPE achieves a Recall@10 of 83.3% (identifying 15 of 18 newly invaded health zones across five weekly forecasts), a +10.3 percentage-point improvement over the public state-of-the-art modeling (~73%). By combining autonomous multimodal planetary data discovery with targeted model optimization, PPE lowers the technical barrier to planetary-scale analytics, enabling rapid, customized, expert-level deployment.

AI.tldr: They propose an autonomous AI system, the Planetary Prediction Engine (PPE), that turns natural language queries into end-to-end geospatial prediction pipelines, outperforming expert and state-of-the-art baselines across multiple global tasks.
AI.motivation: Global challenges such as food security, disasters, disease, and socio-economic vulnerability require accurate, scalable geospatial prediction. Current workflows are slow and fragmented, relying on manual data search, curation, fusion of heterogeneous data, and ad hoc model selection. This bottleneck prevents timely, expert-level planetary modeling for many users and applications.
AI.method: They design PPE, an autonomous AI system that: (1) parses natural-language queries; (2) automatically discovers and retrieves spatiotemporally relevant multimodal data from open-web sources and platforms like Data Commons and Google Earth Engine; (3) fuses these data with embeddings from geospatial foundation models (e.g., PDFM, AlphaEarth); and (4) performs automated model search across task-specific architecture families, including mechanisms to avoid overfitting. The system builds complete end-to-end prediction pipelines without manual intervention.
AI.result: Across various tasks and regions, PPE surpasses state-of-the-art or expert-tuned baselines. In US spatial regression, it yields higher mean R^2 for 21 CDC health indicators (76.8% vs. 60.0%), FEMA national risk indices (64.9% vs. 60.0%), and the Social Vulnerability Index (66.2% vs. 58.6%). For spatial downscaling of Nigerian food security data, PPE doubles baseline performance (R^2 66.1% vs. 31.5%). In epidemiological nowcasting of a Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in DRC, it achieves Recall@10 of 83.3%, improving ~10.3 percentage points over the public state of the art (~73%).
AI.conclusion: Autonomous multimodal data discovery combined with automated, task-tailored model optimization can substantially lower the technical barrier to planetary-scale geospatial analytics. PPE demonstrates that natural-language-driven, end-to-end systems can deliver rapid, customized, expert-level predictive performance across diverse scientific and policy-relevant domains.

title: One Form to Transfer Them All: Pretraining Multilingual Language Models Beyond Native Orthography
summary: Multilingual language models transfer knowledge across languages through shared subword vocabulary, a mechanism that breaks down when related languages use different writing systems. Prior work addresses this via script equalization (romanization or IPA transcription), but direct comparisons are rare; the focus has been on encoder-only models, with most work adapting existing pretrained models. We systematically compare different input representations in autoregressive multilingual pretraining, comparing orthographic text, IPA, and romanization in a controlled setup across three scales (467M, 709M, and 1.03B) on eight languages in four typologically motivated pairs. Across a wide range of downstream tasks on seen and unseen languages, romanized pretraining yields the strongest cross-lingual transfer, and the advantage over text widens with scale. IPA improves over text in most settings but trails romanization. Surprisingly, finetuning a text-pretrained model on romanized data hurts performance on languages already covered by the base model, only marginally helping when the model lacks script coverage. Our results indicate that for multilingual models spanning typologically diverse scripts, to obtain maximum benefits, romanization should be treated as a core design choice applied at pretraining rather than a post hoc fix.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how different input representations (original scripts, IPA, and romanization) affect cross-lingual transfer in multilingual autoregressive language models and finds that romanization at pretraining time yields the best transfer, especially at larger scales.
AI.motivation: Multilingual models usually share knowledge across languages via a common subword vocabulary, but this breaks for related languages written in different scripts, limiting cross-lingual transfer. Existing fixes like romanization or IPA have been studied mostly for encoder-only or adapted models, with few systematic, controlled comparisons. There is a need to understand, in a principled way, which representation best supports transfer in generative multilingual models and at different scales.
AI.method: The authors pretrain autoregressive multilingual language models under a controlled setup using three kinds of input representations: original orthographic text, IPA transcription, and romanization. They train models at three parameter scales (467M, 709M, 1.03B) on eight languages grouped into four typologically motivated pairs that differ in script but share linguistic similarities. They then evaluate these models on a broad set of downstream tasks covering both languages seen during pretraining and unseen languages, comparing cross-lingual transfer performance across the three representation choices.
AI.result: Romanized pretraining consistently achieves the strongest cross-lingual transfer across tasks and languages, and its advantage over original-script text grows as the model size increases. IPA usually improves over the original orthographic text but performs worse than romanization. When a model first pretrained on text is later finetuned on romanized data, performance degrades on languages already covered in the base model and only marginally improves transfer to languages whose scripts were absent from pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Romanization is most effective when integrated as a core design choice during multilingual pretraining, particularly for models that span typologically diverse scripts, as it maximizes cross-lingual transfer. Post hoc script equalization—such as finetuning a text-pretrained model on romanized inputs—is not an effective strategy and can even harm performance on covered languages. IPA offers some benefits over original text but is less advantageous than romanization overall.

title: SAMpLE: A SystemC-AMS Machine LEarning-based Framework for Virtual Prototyping
summary: Machine Learning (ML) is increasingly used in virtual prototypes of embedded systems to model behaviors that are difficult to capture analytically. However, integrating ML models into virtual platform simulation is still typically done through ad hoc solutions, which limits reuse, comparability, and reproducibility. This paper presents \textbf{\textit{SAMpLE}}, an open-source SystemC-AMS-based framework that integrates ML models as first-class Timed Dataflow (TDF) components through a standardized plug-and-play interface. SAMpLE provides two execution backends: a native C++ backend for online training of lightweight models, and an offline backend for executing externally developed models without requiring re-implementation in C++ or manual integration steps. The framework uses ONNX as a standard model exchange format to enable integration of externally trained ML models into SystemC-AMS simulations, and allows the evaluation of different ML-based solutions within the same testbench, dataset, and simulation workflow. The modular design and unified and reproducible environment will allow future extensions of SAMpLE to new models, without modifying the SystemC-AMS structure.

AI.tldr: Introduces SAMpLE, an open-source SystemC-AMS framework that integrates ML models as standard Timed Dataflow components via a plug-and-play interface using ONNX.
AI.motivation: ML is increasingly used to model complex behaviors in virtual prototypes of embedded systems, but current integration into virtual platform simulations is ad hoc, hindering reuse, comparability, and reproducibility. A standardized, modular way to plug ML models into SystemC-AMS simulations is needed.
AI.method: Design and implementation of SAMpLE, a SystemC-AMS-based framework that treats ML models as first-class TDF components. It offers two execution backends: (1) a native C++ backend for online training of lightweight models, and (2) an offline backend for executing models developed externally, imported via ONNX, without re-implementation or manual integration. The framework standardizes interfaces and uses a modular architecture for easy extension.
AI.result: SAMpLE enables plug-and-play integration of ML models into SystemC-AMS simulations, supports both online training and offline inference of externally trained models, and allows evaluation and comparison of different ML-based solutions within a unified testbench, dataset, and simulation workflow.
AI.conclusion: By providing a modular, standardized, and reproducible environment that treats ML models as first-class TDF components and leverages ONNX for model exchange, SAMpLE simplifies integration and comparison of ML models in SystemC-AMS virtual prototypes and can be extended to new models without changing the underlying simulation structure.

title: Query-Side Attacks on GNN-Based KGQA: Tracing Failures from Entity Linking to Answer Generation
summary: GNN-based Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) pipelines process queries through four discrete stages: entity linking, subgraph retrieval, GNN reasoning, and answer generation. Standard robustness evaluations conflate stage-level failures into a single end-to-end metric, obscuring both the source of brittleness and the appropriate mitigation target. We ask which stage fails, and why, when the pipeline is subjected to adversarial perturbations on the input question. We introduce a stage-isolation protocol with two answer-preserving adversarial perturbations verified against the knowledge graph: Compositional Restructuring (CR) and Relation Synonym Swap (RS) target distinct stages while leaving entity seeds intact. Evaluated across ComplexWebQuestions and WebQSP, the results run counter to prevailing assumptions: the GNN reasoning stage retains near-baseline accuracy when the subgraph is intact, while subgraph construction accounts for over 99\% of the end-to-end collapse under CR, occurring even when the gold answer is present in 74\% of retrieved subgraphs. This exposes a fundamental distinction between answer presence and answer reachability that end-to-end metrics cannot detect, and places the mitigation target firmly at the subgraph construction stage rather than the reasoning model. Perturbed datasets and evaluation infrastructure are released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/atkgrag-E85C .

AI.tldr: The paper dissects robustness of GNN-based KGQA pipelines by isolating which stage fails under adversarial question perturbations, showing subgraph construction—not GNN reasoning—is the main bottleneck.
AI.motivation: End-to-end robustness metrics for KGQA systems obscure which component (entity linking, subgraph retrieval, GNN reasoning, or answer generation) is responsible for failures, making it hard to design effective robustness improvements. The authors want to pinpoint stage-specific brittleness under controlled adversarial attacks.
AI.method: They propose a stage-isolation evaluation protocol using two knowledge-graph-validated, answer-preserving adversarial perturbations on the input questions: Compositional Restructuring (CR), which alters question structure, and Relation Synonym Swap (RS), which swaps surface forms of relations. These are designed to target different pipeline stages while keeping entity seeds fixed. They then measure per-stage and end-to-end performance across KGQA benchmarks (ComplexWebQuestions and WebQSP), contrasting intact vs perturbed questions and analyzing answer presence vs reachability in retrieved subgraphs.
AI.result: Under the proposed adversarial perturbations, overall end-to-end performance drops sharply, but detailed analysis reveals that the GNN reasoning stage maintains near-baseline accuracy whenever the retrieved subgraph already contains the necessary information. In contrast, the subgraph construction stage is highly fragile: over 99% of the end-to-end performance collapse under Compositional Restructuring is due to errors in subgraph retrieval, despite the gold answer being present in 74% of retrieved subgraphs.
AI.conclusion: Robustness weaknesses in GNN-based KGQA pipelines primarily stem from subgraph construction rather than from the GNN reasoning module itself. This demonstrates that answer presence in a subgraph does not guarantee answer reachability by the reasoning model, and that end-to-end metrics are insufficient to reveal this gap. Robustness efforts should therefore prioritize improving and stress-testing the subgraph retrieval stage. The paper also releases perturbed datasets and infrastructure to facilitate such fine-grained robustness evaluation.

title: Unveiling Spectral Mechanisms in Training-Free LLM Text Detection
summary: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) makes it increasingly difficult to distinguish human writing from machine-generated text. Training-free detection offers a scalable solution, yet common confidence-based metrics mainly measure average token probabilities and often miss the signal fluctuations that characterize human writing, which we call "generative vitality". Spectral analysis offers a way to capture this vitality, but its mechanism and practical boundaries remain underexplored. In this paper, we analyze spectral detection from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. We connect spectral energy to variance in proxy log-probability trajectories and explain how broader human token choices create the fluctuations used by frequency-domain indicators. We further show that the strength of this signal depends on text length and sampling range: spectral evidence is clearest for long, continuous, constrained generation, while short, fragmented, mixed, and edited settings require complementary confidence and fluctuation views. These findings clarify when frequency-domain detection works and provide guidance for future multi-dimensional detector design.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when and how spectral (frequency-domain) methods can detect machine-generated text by focusing on signal fluctuations in token probabilities, termed "generative vitality."
AI.motivation: Traditional training-free detectors for LLM-generated text mostly rely on average confidence (token probabilities), but they overlook fine-grained fluctuations that differentiate human from machine text. There is a need to understand the theoretical basis and limits of spectral analysis methods that might capture these fluctuations and improve detection reliability.
AI.method: The authors perform a theoretical analysis linking spectral energy to variance in proxy log-probability sequences over tokens, explaining how broader human token choice distributions induce stronger fluctuations observable in the frequency domain. They then empirically study how spectral detection behaves under varying conditions such as text length, continuity, constraint level, and the presence of mixing or editing, comparing spectral indicators with conventional confidence-based metrics.
AI.result: They find that spectral evidence for distinguishing human and machine text is strongest for long, continuous, and relatively constrained generations, where fluctuation patterns are stable and measurable. In contrast, for short, fragmented, mixed, or edited text, the spectral signal weakens or becomes unreliable, and confidence-based and fluctuation-based metrics need to be combined for robust detection.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-domain (spectral) detection methods work best under specific conditions—mainly long, coherent segments with consistent generation dynamics—and should not be used in isolation for more complex or shorter scenarios. The work clarifies the mechanism behind spectral detection, outlines its practical boundaries, and suggests that future detectors should integrate both confidence and fluctuation (spectral) perspectives into multi-dimensional detection frameworks.

title: Lost but not erased: Finding traces of a forgotten language in neural speech models
summary: International adoptees retain phonological traces of a birth language they can no longer speak or comprehend, a persistence typically attributed to a biologically-timed critical period. We asked whether it could instead reflect the ordinary dynamics of learning, using automatic speech recognition models that simulate the international adoptee experience without maturational confounds. Models were trained on one language and then abruptly switched to a second. We found that traces of the first language persisted throughout second-language training, but mainly in the lowest, pre-phonemic layers. These traces were functional, as models with early exposure re-learned their lost first language 14% faster than naive models; this advantage held even against models adopted early from a related language and disappeared when the earliest layers were substituted from a non-adopted model. We argue that these critical-period effects reflect entrenchment of foundational representations rather than a maturational loss of plasticity, and that experience plays a central role in critical periods in language acquisition.

AI.tldr: The paper uses speech recognition models to show that early exposure to a language leaves functional phonological traces even after complete ‘loss’, suggesting critical-period phenomena arise from entrenched early representations rather than a hard biological loss of plasticity.
AI.motivation: International adoptees show long-lasting, implicit retention of their birth language’s phonology despite no conscious knowledge or use. This has been taken as evidence for a biologically fixed critical period. The authors aim to test whether these effects can instead be explained by standard learning dynamics and representational entrenchment, using computational models that avoid human maturational confounds.
AI.method: The authors train automatic speech recognition neural models first on one language (L1) and then abruptly switch training to a second language (L2), simulating international adoption. They analyze representational traces of L1 across the network’s layers during L2 training, focusing on whether and where L1 information persists. They then test whether this residual L1 knowledge is functionally useful by measuring how quickly models can relearn L1 compared to L1-naive models, to models pre-trained on a related language, and to models whose earliest layers are replaced with those from non-adopted models.
AI.result: L1 traces persist throughout L2 training but are concentrated in the lowest, pre-phonemic layers of the model. These traces are functionally meaningful: models with early L1 exposure relearn L1 about 14% faster than fully naive models. This relearning advantage exceeds that of models adopted early from a related language and disappears if the model’s earliest layers are swapped out with those from a model that never saw L1, implicating these foundational layers as the locus of the preserved traces.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that phenomena often attributed to a biologically determined critical period—such as adoptees’ residual birth-language phonology—can arise from the entrenchment of early, low-level representations under ordinary learning dynamics, rather than from a sudden maturational loss of plasticity. Thus, critical periods in language acquisition may be strongly shaped by experience-dependent stabilization of foundational representations, highlighting experience, not just maturation, as central to understanding critical-period effects.

title: When Personality Meets Quantization: A Layer-wise MBTI Analysis of Quantized LLMs
summary: Personality is increasingly important in large language models (LLMs), as it shapes users' trust, engagement, and emotional experiences. While the Myers--Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) has emerged as a common framework for assessing LLMs' personality, existing studies focus primarily on full-precision models and evaluate only final outputs. They overlook the widespread deployment of quantized LLMs requiring low memory footprints, whose personality traits remain underexplored. In this work, we present a systematic MBTI analysis of open-source LLMs across multiple precisions, including mainstream 4-bit methods (GPTQ, AWQ) and extreme 2-bit settings (AQLM variants). Beyond output-level evaluation, we examine how personality emerges across layers through option-level entropy and confidence-gap dynamics, and introduce Uncertainty-Amplified Layer Decoding (UALD) to study decoding-induced personality drift at inference time. Our results reveal a key insight: LLMs' personality is not a static property, but an emergent, layer-dependent decision process sensitive to quantization, prompting, and decoding. Specifically, we find that (1) ENFJ remains dominant across model families and precisions; (2) 4-bit quantization largely preserves coarse personality structure, while 2-bit quantization disrupts fine-grained prompt consistency and cross-precision agreement; (3) personality decisions emerges in upper layers, following substantial ambiguity in early layers; and (4) inference decoding can shift personality, while personality-aligned conditioning improves robustness. These findings provide a new perspective on the behavioral reliability of quantized LLMs and highlight the importance of considering internal dynamics and inference strategies in personality-sensitive chatbot applications.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how personality traits of large language models (LLMs), measured via MBTI, change under different quantization levels, across layers, and under different decoding strategies.
AI.motivation: Personality perceived in LLMs affects user trust, engagement, and emotional experience, and MBTI is widely used to characterize it. However, prior work concentrates on full-precision models and final outputs, ignoring the increasingly common quantized LLMs and the internal, layer-wise dynamics that shape personality. This leaves a gap in understanding the behavioral reliability of memory-efficient, quantized models used in real-world deployments.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate open-source LLMs using the MBTI framework across multiple numeric precisions, including standard 4-bit schemes (GPTQ, AWQ) and more aggressive 2-bit schemes (AQLM variants). They do both output-level MBTI assessments and internal analyses across layers using option-level entropy and confidence-gap trajectories to see where personality decisions form. They also propose Uncertainty-Amplified Layer Decoding (UALD) to probe how different decoding strategies at inference time can alter apparent personality ("personality drift").
AI.result: They observe that ENFJ is the dominant MBTI profile across model families and precisions. 4-bit quantization tends to preserve the broad personality pattern of the base model, but 2-bit quantization significantly disrupts consistency across prompts and agreement between precisions. Personality-related decisions mainly crystallize in upper layers, after substantial ambiguity in lower layers. Moreover, decoding choices can noticeably change the expressed personality, while conditioning the model with personality-aligned prompts improves stability and robustness of the expressed traits.
AI.conclusion: Personality in LLMs should not be treated as a fixed, monolithic property of a model but as an emergent, layer-dependent decision process influenced by quantization level, prompts, and decoding strategy. For quantized LLMs, especially at extreme low precisions, this leads to reduced behavioral reliability and consistency. Designers of personality-sensitive chatbots should account for internal dynamics, precision choice, and decoding methods, and may need personality-aligned conditioning to maintain stable user-facing traits.

title: Distinct dynamics of conceptual and referential disruptions in human reading and large language model processing
summary: Linguistic meaning is grounded in conceptual content, from which reference to particular entities emerges as words enter discourse. To examine the processing dynamics associated with these two dimensions of meaning, we selectively disrupted conceptual or referential information in short narratives and traced the resulting effects in human self-paced reading and in the predictive and representational processing of large language models. In human reading, conceptual disruptions produced a strong but localized processing cost, emerging immediately after the distorted word, reaching an early maximum, and then declining rapidly. Referential disruptions produced weaker effects, which decreased more gradually across subsequent words, and were more strongly modulated by sentence boundaries. In the language model, both disruptions emerged immediately at the manipulated word. Contextual model surprisal showed a pattern closely paralleling human reading: conceptual disruption produced a larger, more locally concentrated effect that decayed rapidly, whereas referential disruption produced a smaller and more gradual downstream effect. Output-layer representations showed a different pattern: referential disruption produced a larger initial displacement, while both distortions were subsequently characterized by power-law decay. Together, these results provide convergent evidence for distinguishable processing dynamics of two types of meaning: conceptual information imposes a more locally concentrated integration cost, whereas referential information engages a more distributed process of maintaining discourse-level identity.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how conceptual meaning and referential meaning are processed differently by humans and large language models using controlled disruptions in short narratives.
AI.motivation: To understand whether and how the processing of conceptual content (general meanings of words) differs from the processing of referential content (tracking specific entities in discourse) in both human readers and large language models, and to see if models mirror human dynamics.
AI.method: The authors create short narratives in which they selectively disrupt either conceptual information (making a word conceptually anomalous) or referential information (making it unclear which entity is being referred to). They then measure processing costs: in humans via self-paced reading times, and in large language models via surprisal (predictive processing) and changes in output-layer representations at and after the manipulated word.
AI.result: In humans, conceptual disruptions cause a strong, immediate, and localized processing cost that peaks right after the distorted word and then rapidly declines; referential disruptions cause weaker effects that decay more slowly and are influenced by sentence boundaries. In language models, surprisal patterns closely match human reading: conceptual disruptions yield larger, more localized spikes in surprisal, whereas referential disruptions yield smaller, more gradually decaying effects. However, in output-layer representations, referential disruptions cause a larger initial displacement, with both disruption types showing power-law decay over time.
AI.conclusion: Conceptual and referential meaning reflect distinguishable processing dynamics. Conceptual information mainly incurs a local integration cost when the anomalous word is processed, while referential information involves a more distributed, longer-lasting process of maintaining and updating discourse-level entity identities. Large language models partially mirror these human processing patterns, especially at the level of surprisal, though their internal representations show distinct behavior.

title: VISA: Agentic Self-Evolving Data Synthesis for Multimodal Instruction Following
summary: Multimodal instruction-following models require training data that is accurate, diverse, verifiable, and challenging. Existing synthesis pipelines typically follow a one-pass generate-and-filter paradigm, discarding feedback from failed samples, verifier outcomes, and target-model errors. We present VISA (Visual Instruction Synthesis Agent), an agentic framework that reformulates multimodal instruction synthesis as a self-evolving loop. At each round, VISA analyzes an image to filter incompatible constraints and discover new verifiable ones, samples diversity- and difficulty-aware constraint sets from persistent memory, generates candidate instructions, and verifies the resulting samples with executable tools and structured large language model judges. Failed samples trigger diagnostic-guided recovery, while accepted samples are probed against the target model to estimate difficulty. The resulting verifier signals and target-model failure profiles are written back to memory, allowing subsequent rounds to adaptively expand the constraint space, reduce template repetition, and focus on unresolved model weaknesses. The same verifier contracts further provide reward signals for reinforcement learning without a separately trained reward model. Experiments on MM-IFEval show that VISA consistently improves multimodal instruction following over strong baselines, while preserving general multimodal capability across seven public benchmarks.

AI.tldr: VISA is an agentic framework for generating high-quality multimodal instruction-following data via a self-improving loop that uses verifiers and model feedback.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal instruction data generation uses one-shot generate-and-filter processes that waste information from failures, verifier feedback, and target-model errors, leading to less effective and less adaptive training data.
AI.method: VISA runs a self-evolving loop: for each image, it filters incompatible constraints and discovers verifiable ones, samples diverse and difficulty-aware constraint sets from a persistent memory, generates candidate instructions, and verifies them using executable tools plus structured LLM judges. Failed samples undergo diagnostic-guided recovery; successful samples are tested on the target model to assess difficulty. All verifier signals and model failure profiles are written back to memory to adapt future rounds, expand constraints, avoid template repetition, and target model weaknesses. The same verifier contracts also produce rewards usable in RL without a separate reward model.
AI.result: On the MM-IFEval benchmark, VISA-generated data leads to consistent improvement in multimodal instruction-following performance compared to strong baselines, while maintaining general multimodal abilities across seven public benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: An agentic, self-evolving instruction synthesis framework that leverages verifier feedback and model errors can generate higher-quality multimodal training data, improve instruction following, and provide RL rewards without additional reward models, all while preserving broad multimodal capability.

title: Beyond Local Surprise: Grounded Dialogue as Selective Belief Revision under Referential Uncertainty
summary: When a speaker refers to a scene that the listener cannot directly see, the listener must decide whether to preserve its current understanding or revise it as new utterances arrive. Many language systems treat local mismatch as a cue for updating: divergence from the current understanding encourages adjustment. Yet conversational understanding may be more conservative, interpreting mismatching evidence relative to prior understanding rather than immediately revising it. We introduce a controlled, data-driven framework for turn-by-turn preserve/revise decisions in dialogue, where competing revision policies are learned under otherwise identical conditions. We compare four theory-driven revision strategies, each reflecting a different assumption about when listeners should preserve or revise. Two findings stand out. First, a mismatch-driven policy that updates solely based on local divergence reacts strongly to mismatch but destabilizes grounding and degrades retrieval. Second, an uncertainty-sensitive policy extends mismatch-based updating with accumulated evidence, preserving coherent understanding while maintaining strong retrieval performance. Surprisingly, coherent understanding emerges from a counterintuitive pattern: local mismatch promotes preservation, whereas accumulated uncertainty promotes revision, suggesting that listeners maintain prior understanding despite local mismatch and revise only when uncertainty sufficiently accumulates. This pattern is consistent with conceptual pact theory.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how listeners decide whether to keep or revise their current mental picture of an unseen scene as dialogue unfolds, finding that conservative, uncertainty-based revision yields more coherent understanding than immediate mismatch-based updating.
AI.motivation: To understand and model how conversational partners maintain or update shared understanding (grounding) about things they cannot both see, and to evaluate different theoretical accounts of when listeners should preserve or revise their interpretations in the face of mismatching utterances.
AI.method: The authors build a controlled, data-driven dialogue framework where a listener model receives turn-by-turn utterances about a scene it cannot see and must decide to preserve or revise its current interpretation. Within this framework, they implement and compare four theory-driven revision policies that differ in how they respond to local mismatch and accumulated uncertainty, then evaluate these policies on measures like grounding stability and retrieval performance.
AI.result: They find that a purely mismatch-driven revision policy, which updates interpretation whenever local evidence diverges from the current understanding, aggressively reacts to mismatch but leads to unstable grounding and worse retrieval. In contrast, an uncertainty-sensitive policy that combines mismatch cues with accumulated evidence yields stable, coherent interpretations and strong retrieval performance, revealing that effective listeners often preserve interpretations despite local mismatch and only revise when global uncertainty becomes high.
AI.conclusion: Listeners in dialogue appear to use a conservative, uncertainty-accumulation strategy rather than reacting immediately to local mismatches: local mismatch tends to trigger preservation, while only sufficiently accumulated uncertainty triggers revision. This pattern aligns with conceptual pact theory, in which conversational partners maintain established understandings unless there is strong evidence to renegotiate them, and it has implications for designing dialogue systems that manage grounding more robustly.

title: Fine-Tuning Whisper for Automatic Speech Recognition in Baniwa: A Preliminary Study
summary: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) technologies have achieved remarkable performance in recent years through the use of large multilingual foundation models. However, most advances remain concentrated on high-resource languages, while indigenous languages continue to suffer from a lack of speech resources and language technologies. This work presents a preliminary study on the adaptation of Whisper for Automatic Speech Recognition in Baniwa, an indigenous Arawakan language spoken in Brazil, Colombia, and Venezuela. The experiments were conducted using a corpus of 1,373 manually transcribed recordings obtained from a linguistic documentation project. The corpus contains approximately 0.54 hours of speech and consists primarily of isolated words and short elicited utterances. The Whisper Small model was fine-tuned using supervised learning and evaluated using Word Error Rate (WER) and Character Error Rate (CER). The best model achieved a WER of 37.5% and a CER of 7.45%, demonstrating that multilingual foundation models can be successfully adapted to extremely low-resource indigenous languages. The results establish an initial baseline for Baniwa Automatic Speech Recognition and provide a foundation for future research involving larger datasets, language-specific adaptation strategies, and post-processing techniques.

AI.tldr: This paper explores fine-tuning OpenAI’s Whisper model for automatic speech recognition (ASR) in Baniwa, an extremely low-resource indigenous language, and shows that a multilingual foundation model can be adapted successfully, establishing a first ASR baseline.
AI.motivation: Most progress in ASR with large multilingual foundation models benefits high-resource languages, leaving indigenous languages under-served due to scarce data and tools. Baniwa, an Arawakan language with very limited resources, lacks ASR systems. The authors aim to see whether a pre-trained multilingual model like Whisper can be effectively adapted to Baniwa using a tiny corpus, thereby addressing digital marginalization and supporting linguistic documentation and revitalization.
AI.method: The authors use a corpus of 1,373 manually transcribed Baniwa recordings (about 0.54 hours of speech, mainly isolated words and short elicited utterances) collected from a linguistic documentation project. They fine-tune the Whisper Small model with supervised learning on this corpus. Performance is evaluated using standard ASR metrics: Word Error Rate (WER) and Character Error Rate (CER).
AI.result: After fine-tuning, the best Whisper Small model for Baniwa achieves a Word Error Rate (WER) of 37.5% and a Character Error Rate (CER) of 7.45% on the evaluation set, which is notable given the extremely small amount of training data. These scores constitute the first reported quantitative baseline for Baniwa ASR.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that multilingual foundation models like Whisper can be adapted to extremely low-resource indigenous languages even with very limited training data. This provides an initial ASR baseline for Baniwa and suggests that with larger datasets, language-specific adaptation techniques, and improved post-processing, performance could be further enhanced, supporting future research and language technology development for Baniwa and similar languages.

title: Prefix Sliding for efficient test-time scaling
summary: Test-time scaling uses extra test-time compute to improve performance, such as letting language models reason longer when solving a problem. As models keep the entire reasoning trace in memory via full attention, hard tasks that need long thinking can be prohibitively expensive. However, we find most intermediate reasoning tokens lose importance as the model continues reasoning. This calls into question whether retaining them is worth the cost. Based on this insight, we propose Prefix Sliding, which discards tokens during reasoning that are not part of the prefix or the window of the last few thousand tokens. The prefix has key instructions and tools available to the model, while the most recent tokens are the current reasoning the model is working on. This caps the total memory requirement regardless of how long the model reasons, allowing for efficient long-horizon test-time scaling. Without training, Prefix Sliding can make existing models 3x faster while maintaining performance. Training with Prefix Sliding using reinforcement learning can achieve better performance by enabling scaling to reasoning traces beyond a hundred thousand tokens. Ablations show Prefix Sliding outperforms summarizing intermediate tokens or vanilla sliding window. Our code is at https://github.com/Muennighoff/prefix-sliding

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Prefix Sliding, a method to efficiently scale test-time reasoning for language models by keeping only an initial instruction prefix and a moving window of recent tokens, discarding older intermediate tokens to cap memory and speed up inference without sacrificing performance.
AI.motivation: Test-time scaling improves model performance by letting language models think longer, but full attention over the entire reasoning trace makes long-horizon reasoning computationally and memory expensive. The authors observe that many intermediate reasoning tokens become unimportant as reasoning progresses, questioning the need to retain all tokens and motivating a more efficient attention/memory strategy.
AI.method: They introduce Prefix Sliding, which maintains (1) a fixed initial prefix containing key instructions and available tools, and (2) a sliding window of the last few thousand tokens representing the current reasoning. All other intermediate tokens are discarded from the context. They first apply this at inference time without retraining, then additionally train models with Prefix Sliding using reinforcement learning to better adapt to very long reasoning traces. They compare against summarization of intermediate tokens and a standard sliding-window approach.
AI.result: Without any training, applying Prefix Sliding to existing models yields about a 3x speedup while preserving performance. With reinforcement learning finetuning under the Prefix Sliding regime, models achieve higher performance and can effectively reason with traces longer than 100k tokens. Empirical ablations indicate that Prefix Sliding performs better than methods that summarize discarded tokens or use a naive sliding window over all tokens.
AI.conclusion: Discarding non-essential intermediate tokens during reasoning and retaining only an instruction prefix plus a recent-token window enables efficient long-horizon test-time scaling for language models. Prefix Sliding caps memory usage irrespective of reasoning length, accelerates inference, and, especially when combined with RL training, supports very long reasoning traces and outperforms alternative context-management strategies.
